text: Movie: How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies (2024) 2h 5m| Official Rating: 7.9/10 | Rating: 7.9/10 | It is somewhat depressing to think that we see each other's values once we are close to losing one another. In this case, the melancholy comes back multiplied.It hurts to know that there are grandparents out there who spend most of their time paying attention to their family, to the point that they feel absolutely nothing about being solitary anymore. There's this huge amount of devotion that they shared with their loved ones that all they think is for their children and grandchildren to wake up with no worries in the future even if it takes their lives to pay for it. There's just something about the love that they have that's way different from any form of love out there. Because of that, I am pretty certain of the fact that there's no other love that could sit proportional to that level.Even way before we were born, we were already connected to this special soul. My heart already knew where it belonged and where it should foster kindness, acceptance, passion, and above all love. This defines what home really should be. An environment where there is space for growth and familial adoration. Just like they all say, there's no place like home. For that, I am thankful to this film for making me realize that my truest home resides in the purest heart of my grandmother.Thinking that today is my birthday, I've deeply thought about the beautiful things that I achieved and also thought about the things that I want for this special day. This movie tapped my shoulder and told me that there's no other gift in this world that I could even ask for, because my special gift was already given to me. That's when it was pretty much conceivable that the greatest gift of all time was indeed my own grandmother.It has come to my realization that it really doesn't matter if you can't figure out what to do in your life and that it's okay to play video games while live streaming all day. It's okay not to get a decent profession in the early days of your career, and it's okay not to make millions of pesos before grandma dies. This taught me not to look for things from a conspicuous angle because the most genuine value lies deeply in their core. With that, I am convinced that the kind of millions I should be making with my grandma is the amount of memories with care and love, enough for her not to feel lonely. Because she was really there at times when you needed someone to provide these qualities for you. The least that you could do is to appreciate their existence while they're still here.If you're lucky enough, give it a go, hug your grandmother tightly, and whisper in their ears how much you love them. To those who were left with good memories, your grandparents will always look after you in a serene place.After countless times looking for the most authentic love from other people, I spent so much effort on them that I forgot to see the value in my grandmother's love. Because of that, I came to the conclusion that she really is the love of my life.There's nothing more I could ask for for my birthday gift than watching this Thai movie with my very own grandmother  she's the gift of my life.I love you so much mommy. Hope we could spend years of happiness together.shoutout to my cousin, ate lai for making this dream come true.

text: Movie: How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies (2024) 2h 5m| Official Rating: 7.9/10 | Rating: 7.9/10 | How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies (Lahn Mah) is an evocative and tender exploration of family ties, cultural heritage, and the poignant inevitability of loss. Anchored in the traditions and quirks of Thai Chinese communities, the film weaves a heartfelt story that resonates universally while staying true to its unique setting.At its heart is the bond between M and his amah (grandmother), a woman steeped in the wisdom and customs of her Chaoshan heritage. From the congee she sells in Talat Phlu's bustling market to her reverence for Guanyin and her habit of storing money in tin cans, amah embodies the spirit of resilience and sacrifice. M's relationship with her unfolds across a rich tapestry of cultural details, from shared meals at a spinning Chinese dining table to lessons about frugality, tradition, and love.The film masterfully uses symbolism, with pomegranates and congee taking on deeper meanings. The amah's insistence on planting pomegranates for prosperity and her frequent use of the Tiociu phrase 'biji beras sudah menjadi bubur' highlight her acceptance of life's unchangeable realities. Similarly, the sudden rain during moments of disappointment or grief adds an emotional layer to pivotal scenes, reinforcing the film's atmospheric storytelling.The narrative is steeped in cultural specificity, from the use of the Tiociu language to the rituals surrounding death. The depiction of amah's grand burial complete with sprawling land and intricate flower arrangements is both a testament to her life and a reflection of her hope that her children will honor her memory. Yet, the irony of a family fractured by inheritance disputes underscores the tension between tradition and modernity.Visually, the film is striking, particularly in its use of transitions. A sequence where a train moves backward into a flashback of M's childhood, only to surge forward into the present, mirrors the cyclical nature of memory and legacy. The climactic moments, such as the dropping of a pomegranate coinciding with amah's passing, are both poetic and heartbreaking.The performances, particularly from the actor portraying amah, are deeply moving. Her small gestures like unbuttoning her shirt to ease her pain or folding her hands in a parting gesture reminiscent of her younger self speak volumes about her character's journey. M's quiet rebellion, as seen in his messy flower scattering at her grave, reveals his complex emotions of love, guilt, and grief.

text: Movie: How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies (2024) 2h 5m| Official Rating: 7.9/10 | Rating: 7.9/10 | There are things in life more important than money, but sometimes we lose sight of that, unwittingly allowing our perspectives to become seriously skewed. Unfortunately, this usually happens most often when family related considerations are involved. And those flawed perceptions, in turn, can become even further distorted when money is tied up with those familial matters, particularly when inheritance concerns loom. Such is the case for a Chinese Thai family facing the prospects of what will happen to the assets of its terminally ill matriarch (Usha Seamkhum) who has recently been diagnosed with Stage IV intestinal cancer. Several relatives vie for control of her money and property, but the most ambitious among them is her financially strapped grandson (Putthipong Assaratanakul), who suddenly and miraculously manages to shed his generally indifferent attitude toward her and eagerly volunteers to step up as her full time caretaker, all in hopes that this generous gesture will translate into a sizable windfall upon her passing. However, even though Grandma may be a bit old fashioned in some of her thinking and outlooks, she's no naïve dullard, either, quickly recognizing this shift as the transparent move that it is. And she's determined to have her way about this scenario, using it as an opportunity to not only get her needs met, but also to give her often lost grandson valuable lessons in tough love and finding much needed direction in life. So how will this unfold? Will these allegedly altruistic efforts ring true? Moreover, can they be carried out without undue interference from other relatives, most notably his two uncles (Sanya Kunakorn, Pongsatorn Jongwilas), who each have self serving agendas of their own? And how will Grandma respond to these diverse family dynamics and a host of unforeseen developments that emerge at a time when her health is failing fast? Writer director Pat Boonnitipat's debut feature represents an impressive big screen premiere, one that's thoughtful, sensitive, incisive and touching without becoming schmaltzy, manipulative or overly sentimental. The picture's finely constructed narrative and superbly written screenplay tell this engaging story with a skilled hand for a first time filmmaker, yielding a production that's evenly paced and knows precisely when to employ its dramatic and comedic touches for maximum effect. And, on top of all this, this offering's gifted ensemble, gorgeous cinematography and suitably atmospheric background score all combine to make the most out of the well crafted foundation underlying this material. If there's anything that could use some improvement, it might be in tweaking the picture's slightly stretched out closing act, which could have benefitted from some modest editing, but that's an easily overlooked shortfall in light of all of the film's other outstanding attributes. 'How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies' is truly a cinematic gem that has somehow flown well below the radar thus far, but it's one of those pictures genuinely worth a look. Thankfully, it's now widely available for streaming online and truly makes for a worthwhile watch, serving up meaningful observations for those times when we might be on the verge of losing perspective.

text: Movie: How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies (2024) 2h 5m| Official Rating: 7.9/10 | Rating: 7.9/10 | It's not every day you come across a film that so authentically captures the emotional chaos and complicated bonds of a family like 'How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies.' Directed by Pat Boonnitipat, this Thai dramedy dives headfirst into the conflicts, little gestures, and moments of tenderness that surface in times of extreme vulnerability. It balances sentimentality and humor with a surprising lightness, delivering a movie that doesn't reinvent the wheel but reminds us why family stories always hit so deeply.The narrative's backbone is M., played with a kind of lazy charisma by Putthipong Assaratanakul. M. is your classic case of someone dodging responsibilities until they become impossible to ignore. A failed video game streamer, he steps up to care for his grandmother, Amah (Usha Seamkhum), after learning about her terminal illness. At first, his intentions are as transparent as they are funny: to secure a slice of her inheritance. But Boonnitipat and Thodsapon Thiptinnakorn's script is sharp enough never to let M. Feel like just an opportunist. As the story unfolds, what begins as a convenient act evolves into something genuine, and it's in this arc of transformation that the film finds its heart.Amah is the kind of character who lingers in your memory. Strong, stubborn, and quick witted, she faces her terminal illness with a mix of pragmatism and resignation that makes her instantly lovable. Through her eyes, the film explores not just dysfunctional family dynamics but also the quiet impact of mortality on everyone around her. Amah serves as the emotional anchor, connecting her children, grandchildren, and even the audience, all while navigating the small betrayals and manipulations of those who are supposed to care for her.What really sets the film apart, though, is the attention to detail. Boonnitipat is a director who knows that the setting can tell as much of a story as the dialogue. The bustling streets of Chinatown in Bangkok, hospital corridors, casual poolside conversations all of these moments build a living, breathing world beyond the core plot. Each scene is so vivid you can almost smell the steaming broth at the local market or hear the distant hum of tuk tuk engines. This strong sense of place, combined with the rich tapestry of sounds and visuals, elevates the movie beyond a conventional melodrama.Of course, there's sentimentality, and at times the film leans into a few predictable jokes about aging and bodily functions. But even these choices, which might feel clichéd elsewhere, are handled with a disarming honesty. One particularly memorable scene shows M. Helping Amah with a mundane task that quickly turns into a quiet moment of connection between the two. It's in these smaller, intimate moments that the film truly shines, showing how fragile yet powerful family bonds can be.Another highlight is the way the film tackles M.'s growth without resorting to easy fixes. He starts out selfish and aimless, but his journey is never sugarcoated. Instead, the script demonstrates how constant presence and care even when fueled by questionable motives have the power to change both the giver and the receiver. M. doesn't become a saint; he remains a deeply flawed character. But as the film so sensitively suggests, transformation lies in the small gestures, not grand epiphanies.Despite its heavy theme, 'How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies' is ultimately a film about reconciliation and acceptance. It reminds us that the people we love will never be perfect and that family is as much a source of conflict as it is of comfort. There's something deeply reassuring in the way the movie wraps up, offering a sense of hope without ignoring the messiness of real life.Whether it's through the screenplay's sensitivity, the genuine performances, or the thoughtful direction, 'How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies' stands out as one of the year's most rewarding surprises. It doesn't settle for just making you cry or laugh; instead, it delivers an honest, warm portrait of the pains and joys of being part of a family. By the time the credits rolled, I couldn't help but think of my own grandmother, my own moments of disconnect and reconnection. And in the end, that's what cinema does best.

text: Movie: How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies (2024) 2h 5m| Official Rating: 7.9/10 | Rating: 7.9/10 | The desire for inheritance has always been a strong narrative driver, but How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies (2024) is not limited to a game of interests; it builds a drama about personal transformation and family bonds. M, the protagonist, sees his grandmother's illness as a financial opportunity and decides to care for her, inspired by a cousin who did the same for an elderly man. However, what begins as an opportunistic calculation soon turns into a genuine relationship, as their time together reveals layers that go beyond the coldness of a will. The film traces this evolution with sensitivity, avoiding excessive cynicism or easy sentimentality.The film's richness also lies in the portrayal of family relationships. The grandmother is the central figure of a network of affections and distances: the oldest son, financially successful but emotionally absent; M's mother, who seems to balance herself in this scenario; and the younger brother, in debt and always in need of maternal care. The tensions are subtle but revealing, and they contribute to the emotional weight of the narrative.Is there a catch? For those who prefer stories with a greater balance of drama and humor, the film might feel a bit linear. There are light moments, yes, but only as brief respites. How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies is a full fledged drama, diving deep into emotions without resorting to striking comedic relief. For those who appreciate this type of narrative, it's a real treat. For those, like me, who prefer a bit more tonal variation, it might lack a certain spice.But regardless of personal genre preferences, How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies is a beautiful and well crafted film that makes us reflect on aging, loneliness, and the importance of bonds. In the end, the inheritance that truly matters here is not financial, but emotional.

filename: How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies
text: Movie: How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies (2024) 2h 5m| Official Rating: 7.9/10 | Rating: 7.9/10 | How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies arrives with the deceptive label of 'dark comedy,' but anyone expecting equal measures of darkness and levity will find themselves profoundly mistaken. This Thai film is overwhelmingly heavy on the dark, with comedy so minimal it feels almost accidental. Perhaps if you've never experienced the complexities of family dynamics, never witnessed illness ravage a loved one, or never felt the profound weight of love intertwined with loss, you might find moments of lightness. But for those who have lived through these universal human experiences, this film hits with the force of unfiltered reality.A Pomegranate of Grief The story unfolds like a sheltered pomegranate initially contained within the deceptively simple premise of M, a university dropout who volunteers to care for his terminally ill grandmother Mengju in hopes of securing her inheritance. But as the narrative progresses, this seemingly straightforward tale explodes into a million uncontainable pieces of grief, each seed representing a different facet of human suffering and love. The film doesn't just explore grief; it dissects it with surgical precision, revealing its many flavors and textures across multiple contexts.The Spectrum of Human Sorrow What makes this film extraordinary is its unflinching examination of grief in all its manifestations. We witness sadness in its purest form as M watches his grandmother deteriorate, guilt as he grapples with his initially selfish motivations, and despair as the family confronts the inevitability of loss. There's respite in the quiet moments of connection between M and Mengju, relief when pain temporarily subsides, and agony in the raw confrontation with mortality. The film captures the deep, penetrating love that exists between family members even when complicated by money, pride, and past wounds.The acceptance that comes isn't peaceful or easy it's earned through witnessing every stage of the dying process, every family argument over inheritance, every moment of genuine care that transcends material concerns.Lost in Translation, Found in Emotion Watching with English subtitles likely meant losing nuances of Thai cultural expressions and familial dynamics, yet the film's emotional core transcends language barriers. The authenticity of the family interactions, particularly the way households navigate love, frustration, and obligation, creates a universal resonance that doesn't require perfect translation to understand.Cycles of Trauma and Healing Perhaps most powerfully, the film illustrates how trauma and healing perpetuate through family cycles. We see how Mengju's role as caregiver to her own parents shaped her expectations, how M's initial selfishness mirrors broader family patterns of treating relationships as transactions, and how genuine care can break these cycles. The nursing home sequence, Soei's gambling debts, and Kiang's wealth driven manipulations all demonstrate how family dysfunction repeats across generations until someone chooses differently.A Masterpiece of Emotional Honesty 'How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies' succeeds not as the dark comedy it's marketed as, but as an unflinching portrait of family, mortality, and the messy reality of love. It covers the full spectrum of human experience: sadness and relief, endings and renewal, the continuation of life even in death. The film's greatest achievement is showing how the circle of life isn't a gentle, Disney fied concept, but a brutal, beautiful, and ultimately redemptive force that shapes us all.This isn't a film you watch for laughs it's a film you experience for truth. And in that truth, despite the overwhelming darkness, there's something profoundly life affirming about witnessing authentic human connection in the face of inevitable loss.

text: Movie: How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies (2024) 2h 5m| Official Rating: 7.9/10 | Rating: 7.9/10 | The premise itself is a delicate balancing act: it's part lighthearted romp, part emotional rollercoaster. The film doesn't shy away from exploring the more serious, bittersweet aspects of dealing with terminal illness and the impending loss of a loved one. However, it manages to keep the tone from becoming too heavy by focusing on the protagonist's often ridiculous attempts to get rich quick.The script is smart, with plenty of witty dialogue and unexpected twists. The humor often comes from the protagonist's misguided entrepreneurial efforts, which range from outlandish to surprisingly inventive. Yet, underneath the comedy, there's a real exploration of the meaning of family, legacy, and the pressures of life, especially when time seems limited.The performances are stellar, with the lead actor delivering a heartfelt portrayal of someone who is desperately trying to secure a future for himself and his family, even as the clock is ticking. The chemistry between the lead and the grandmother is touching, and their relationship forms the emotional core of the film.The pacing, while fast at times, allows for moments of introspection that prevent the movie from feeling like a mere slapstick comedy. There's a genuine emotional payoff toward the end, making it clear that this is more than just a film about getting rich it's about understanding what truly matters before it's too late.

text: Movie: How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies (2024) 2h 5m| Official Rating: 7.9/10 | Rating: 7.9/10 | It is not far fetched today to say that most relationships are superficial and people view them only in terms of their greedy personal benefits. The story starts with Mui, M.'s cousin, inheriting nearly all of Grandpa's wealth after becoming his number one, upon nursing him in his last days. This inspires the indolent and failed game streamer, M., to chase his Grandma's wealth and property. There is no shortcut to this but by winning her heart gradually within the predicted timespan of a year, so M. Sets off to do that.Though driven by selfish motives and shallow actions, the movie beautifully captures the transformation of the relationship between an ageing Grandma and her only grandson. Her offspring are in the race to acquire the best of her inheritance. The plot makes us question whether actions belie incentives and intentions, casting even minimal humanity aside.This piece of art is not an emotional rollercoaster. Yet it makes you laugh and cry; it touches the nooks of your whimpering heart and fills it with reminiscences of your loved ones. The plot unfolds most gently, at a warm and tender pace. It is compelling with exceptional cinematography and equally outstanding acting, particularly by Putthipong Assaratanakul who plays the grandson and Usha Seamkhum as the most lovable Grandma. The story is relatable. The story is about all of us; happening all around us. There were moments where I felt frustrated while reflecting on whether human relations have bottled down to the Bahts you can count. There were moments when I felt my gut wrench in disappointment and disgust. The transition in the climax, however, is sure to leave you wailing   with hope and comfort. Maybe Amah was the luckiest soul, for her devout worship finally granted her a dedicated grandson to shower her with untarnished love.

text: Movie: How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies (2024) 2h 5m| Official Rating: 7.9/10 | Rating: 7.9/10 | 'How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies' tugs at the heartstrings with its poignant exploration of family, loss, and regret. The film's emotional core, centered around a grandson's evolving relationship with his dying grandmother, is undeniably powerful and will likely leave viewers reaching for tissues. However, while the film excels in delivering tear jerking moments, it falls short in other aspects, ultimately resulting in a mediocre cinematic experience.The film's premise, while simple, offers fertile ground for emotional exploration. A young man, driven by financial desperation, sets out to win over his estranged grandmother in hopes of inheriting her wealth. As he spends time with her, his motivations gradually shift from greed to genuine affection. This transformation is portrayed convincingly, and the emotional bond that develops between the two characters is genuinely touching.However, the film's execution falters in several areas. The plot feels predictable and lacks narrative depth, relying heavily on sentimental tropes to elicit emotional responses. The supporting characters are underdeveloped, and their actions often feel contrived to serve the main storyline. Furthermore, the film's pacing is uneven, with certain scenes dragging on while others feel rushed.Despite its shortcomings, 'How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies' is saved by its genuinely moving portrayal of love and loss. The film's exploration of family dynamics and the complexities of grief resonates deeply, offering a poignant reminder of the importance of cherishing our loved ones.Verdict: If you're looking for a tearjerker that will tug at your heartstrings, 'How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies' might be worth a watch. However, be prepared for a predictable plot and mediocre execution. The film's emotional core is its saving grace, offering a touching exploration of family and loss that will resonate with many viewers.

text: Movie: How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies (2024) 2h 5m| Official Rating: 7.9/10 | Rating: 7.9/10 | A sweet, sentimental & sincerely crafted comedy drama that's packed with heart, depth, charm & emotion, How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies is as tender as it is amusing and is finely elevated by honest performances from its cast to deliver a crowd pleasing delight in addition to offering a sensible portrait of Asian family life & relationship dynamics.Co written & directed by Pat Boonnitipat in his feature film debut, the story is rather simple and easy to predict what road it might take & how the events may unfold but what makes it gripping is the grandma grandson chemistry that's earnest enough. The plot gradually plays out, isn't in any hurry and keeps the interest alive despite the slow & deliberate pacing.But the glacial pace has its downsides too as it almost brings the story to a standstill even if the investment in the drama & characters isn't affected. Performances are where it scores the most marks and both the protagonist play their roles with conviction, mainly Usha 'Taew' Seamkhum who plays the grandmother in what's her acting debut. And they are well supported by the rest.Overall, How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies touches on themes of ageing, generational divide, gender roles, familial disputes & Thai cultural experience and is held together by the fab interplay between its leading duo. An emotionally rich & resonant dramedy that's brought to life with care, warmth & affection, this Thai crowdpleaser is one of the better offerings of 2024 and comes recommended.

text: Movie: How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies (2024) 2h 5m| Official Rating: 7.9/10 | Rating: 7.9/10 | It's tempting to say that 'How To Make Millions Before Grandma Dies (2024)' is emotionally manipulative, but it isn't really any more manipulative than entries in its genre usually are. Yes, it has tearjerking piano tracks under most important scenes, but it also focuses on a very flawed central character and allows his connection with his eponymous Grandma to build slowly over time. As a weepy, albeit a life affirming (or, I suppose, relationship affirming) one, it feels as though it genuinely earns your tears, no matter how many times the closed captions say something to the effect of 'sentimental music plays'. With unassuming but compelling, and ultimately powerful, performances and a tendency to prefer restraint over unsubtlety, the flick crafts a story that slowly but surely works its way into your heart and all but ensures there won't be a dry eye in the house by the time it's over. At once satisfyingly specific and necessarily universal, the narrative makes up for its general predictability with a competency that's far more impressive than that word makes it sound. Plus, there are enough wrinkles in its emotional journey for its final destination not to feel quite as much like the foregone conclusion it essentially is, and its final few scenes put the cherry right on the top of the proverbial cake by doing something you should have expected but likely plain forgot to. It isn't a complicated or especially novel experience, but it gets to the core of an emotional truth without feeling cloying or overly sentimental. It has the ability to completely devastate you, while also leaving you happy and hopeful at the same time. It's almost like the cinematic equivalent when you think back on a lost relative and cry because you miss them, but smile because you knew them. It's really quite moving, and it's relatively entertaining for its entire (slightly too long) duration   despite, or perhaps because of, its general subtlety and borderline mundanity. It's a really strong effort, to be honest. Its effect creeps up on you, but ultimately can't be denied. Above all else, it reminds you that, if you can, you should visit your grandma. I know I'll be giving mine a big hug the next time I see her.

text: Movie: How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies (2024) 2h 5m| Official Rating: 7.9/10 | Rating: 7.9/10 | This movie, How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies, shows the lifestyle of a Thai Chinese family in a very real and emotional way. It focuses on how family relationships can slowly change over time. As people grow older, they move out, start their own families, or become busy with work. Even differences in age can create a gap between family members. All of these things can make people drift apart without even noticing it.The story mainly follows two characters, M and Ama. At the beginning, their relationship feels a bit distant and awkward. However, as they spend more time together, their bond gradually becomes stronger. Through small everyday moments, we can see how their relationship grows. The movie clearly shows that even if love and connection seem to fade away, they can always come back if people are willing to spend time together again.Another strong point of the movie is how it presents Chinese family culture in a very natural way. The way the family members talk and interact with each other feels realistic and relatable. Ama, who represents the older generation, doesn't openly express her feelings. She speaks very little and may seem strict or distant, but deep inside, she is full of love, care, and concern for her family. The film also highlights how elderly people often feel lonely and quietly wish for more attention and love from their children and grandchildren.As the story goes on, it makes the audience reflect on their own family relationships. It reminds us to think about the people we love, especially our grandparents. While watching, I couldn't help but think of my own Ama when she was still alive, which made the experience even more emotional and meaningful.Overall, How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies is a very well made and deeply touching movie. It feels honest and realistic, as if we are part of the story ourselves. Even though the story is simple, it carries a powerful message about family, love, and time. It reminds us that no matter how busy life gets, spending time with our loved ones is something we should never take for granted.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | In terms of sheer athleticism and martial artistry, Tony Jaa certainly lives up to his billing as 'the Next Bruce Lee'. He puts the kick into this quick fry Thai fightfest that mixes dynamic set pieces with skull splitting one on ones. It should also remind fans of the Crouching Hero, Flying Dagger brand of Eastern blockbuster (including myself) that Oriental action cinema was founded on action without safety nets, never mind all that fancy wirework and colour coordinated mysticism.But for all his physical prowess, Jaa falls short of Bruce Lee (and even Jet Li) when it comes to charisma, sounding nervous and looking slightly uncomfortable in the action free scenes. Director Pinkaew perhaps recognises that Jaa will need time to build his own screen persona, so wisely gives him very little to say. I wish the same could be said of screechy female sidekick Muay who is both an irritation and a distraction. However, quibbling too much about the acting would be churlish.Who cares that the plot's straight out of The A Team when the adrenaline flows this thick and fast? The foot pursuit through Bangkok's backstreets is not just five minutes of pure exhilaration, it turns a few chase clichés on their heads (uh oh, look out for those two guys carrying panes of glass across the road hold on a minute!). There are even replays of the most jaw dropping bits so that you can believe what you just saw.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 9/10 | Version: Edko's Hong Kong VCD releaseIn only their first movie, director Prachya Pinkaew and lead actor Tony Jaa have created a very impressive, awesome action movie in 'Ong Bak'. Jaa plays Ting, a muay thai fighter from a small village in Thailand. The villagers revere Ong Bak, a statue of Buddha kept in the village's temple, and believe it guarantees the safety of the village. Don, a former villager turned criminal, removes the head from the statue and takes it to Bangkok, to curry favour from the crime lord Khom Tuan. Ting follows Don to Bangkok and fights for the return of Ong Bak.Story wise, its a pretty standard action movie   it touches briefly on serious social issues in Thailand, but only very briefly. Action wise, its a pretty awesome action movie. Tony Jaa is pretty good showing off his muay thai skills on screen as he fights a range opponents. Most of the one on one fights are well choreographed and quite intense. As for stunts: some of them would make even old school Jackie Chan green with envy. Jaa and Pinkaew have hit the nail right on the head when it comes to action movies, and in only their first go!    Hopefully I can catch it on the big screen some time.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 10/10 | I've seen some of the negative comments people have made, and they are really off base, and quite frankly, stupid.This movie is filled with incredible fight scenes, from the multitude of fights in the fighting circle, to that final fight in the cave. Those people who think that there aren't any action scenes in it are blind, obviously.As another user has said, the whole point of Ong Bak was to display Tony Jaa's skill at martial arts, which is utterly incredible. Tony Jaa is the best martial artist I have had the pleasure of watching on the big screen.While the plot wasn't the most original, why on earth did you go into Ong Bak expecting some sort of Oscar winning drama, such as Titanic? This movie was merely introducing Tony Jaa's skill to the North American audience.People really need to lighten up. Just because a movie doesn't have an incredibly detailed and complex plot, that doesn't mean it's a bad movie! There is nothing wrong with a so called 'mindless' action movie, such as Ong Bak! Just because it isn't some sort of drama, or another plot saturated film, that doesn't mean it is garbage! While it may not have the best plot around, in terms of pure martial arts, this is the king. There is not a single martial arts movie out there that I have seen, that is more enjoyable than this movie, and I've seen a lot of martial arts movies.If you are not stuck up, and you are able to enjoy a good martial arts movie, than Ong Bak is definitely for you! text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | Imagine you and your buddies are in high school, and one of your friends is Tony Jaa, and you want to make a little movie to show off Tony's awesome talents, like that ninja guy you see on youtube. Then imagine that the Thai government gives you a couple of million dollars to do it professionally. That's how this movie comes off.The plot and characters are pretty forgettable. I guess if you know nothing about Buddhism or Thailand you might get something out of it, I don't know. The real reason to watch this movie of course is for Tony Jaa. And don't worry, you won't miss anything. Every time Tony does something cool, which is often, you get to see it two or three times in slow motion. I didn't mind it here because this is my introduction to Jaa, but now that he's got a few movies under his belt he should probably cut back on that stuff.The fight choreography was a mixed bag, IMO. There was a lot of pausing between moves, which made it seem a bit old fashioned. The opponents were pretty uninspired too; I don't think much thought went into them.It's exciting to see a talented young martial arts performer like Jaa come along, but for anyone who thinks Jackie Chan (who Jaa borrows heavily from) or Jet Li have something to worry about, you're dead wrong... at least for now. I look forward to the next one.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 10/10 | Tony Ja is the new Jet Li and Jackie Chan with a thai boxing background. This guy moves as quick as Jackie, has the strength of Jet Li, put packs a more violent, deadly assault   he uses his knees and elbows for pure annihilation. Why does he use his elbow and knees so much? Because they are the hardest parts of the human body. And god damn in Ong Bak he proper messes up everyone he comes across. Thai boxing is proper hardcore, they don't mess about.In Ong Bak, the story is pretty non existent, basically some gangstas from the city come to our heros poor village and steal the Buddha's head statue, and so Tony Ja commits to bringing it back and restoring peace. Now with that out of the way, let's talk about the fighting as this is where the film excels. WOW, this IS the most realistic fighting you will ever see. The only thing I can compare it to is Ultimate Fighting, but ten times worse. Tony Ja will become a legend this is fact. His flexibility in fighting is so extreme, and this film is basically just crammed up with the biggest, most violent stunts you will ever see. For instance, in a scene where Tony and his newly met friends run away from a group of hoodlums, he gets away in style. This is done by jumping through the tiny gaps, either backwards sliding underneath cars, jumping feet and hands outstretched through a hope, running across people's heads, flippin, kicking, somersaulting absolutely everywhere. Remember when you first saw the matrix and you were like `woah', well this is so much better. For starts, the stunts in this film are REAL. Everybody gets injured. There are no wires, pulleys, fake punches, fake blood. This is how it should be. Hollywood take note. The best scenes come where there is a kinda of street fighter style arena, where the deadliest fighters compete to be champion. Tony gets accidently caught up in this, and doesn't mess around by defeating the champion with a single powerful knee thrust into the opponents chest as Tony bends forwards and twists to avoid the ensuing punch from the opponent then unleashes the killer blow. Everyone in the arena is stunned and Tony gets booed for bad sportsmanship.. But don't worry about that has the biggest fights of his life coming up.You need this film in your life. I haven't seen anything as violent and hardcore as this ever before. But even though its hardcore and low budget, the direction is slick. Double takes are often used for the incredible action so you can really appreciate, for example, taking out three men with a triple, twisting back flip and smashing their heads in with your knees and elbows at the same time with pure accuracy. I have watched this four times now and cannot get enough. Overall, the story line is weak and there are some hilarious cheesy moments, but this all works perfectly well as instead of going `god damn thats sick!' at the beginning, you will end up saying `ha ha! Did you see his elbow get torn backwards then snapped! Ha ha! This is genius!'. It's like CKY2 with all the accidents, but here it is intentional for someone to do themselves in. This is a film you will watch over and over again, and show your mates everytime they come round.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7/10 | I saw Ong Bak for the first time on the Stockholm Film Festival in November of 2003, and now recently saw it again on DVD. I usually see at least 4 5 Asian films on the festival every year and each one is a gamble. At worst Asian action films can be unbearably slow and dull with uninteresting action scenes and horrible acting. At their best they can be like a wonderful ballet with astonishing moves and moods. Ong Bak falls somewhere inbetween these two.The story and set up in Ong Bak is nothing very original. The head of the village Buddha statue (named Ong Bak) is stolen which spells bad luck for the village. So they send their best man to the city to find the son who moved away, and they can search for the head together. Of course the villager is completely lost in the city and soon gets himself into trouble.So the story is nothing new, neither is the setup which is more or less van Damme standard fare movies like 'Lionheart' except in Thailand. We see some street fighting and some tournament style fighting in seedy bars. So, what makes Ong Bak stand out? Well, the fighting! I have seldom seen such well made fighting scenes. Both well choreographed and plentiful! The thai boxing done here might be very stylized to look good, but it really does the trick. The fights are simply put amazing! The lead actor really knows his moves and his acrobatics, and many times you can really feel the crushing hits as kicks and elbows hit home. Also the pace is very high with almost constant fighting in the last half of the movie. And it all looks very very nice.So, Ong Bak is definitely for those of you who are suckers for martial arts and fighting. Don't expect an original story or terribly solid acting. But expect a fun ride, lots and lots of violence. And for me that's enough. Ong Bak receives a .

All I want to see is people getting knocked unconscious and high speed car chases without all the mind numbing character development and complicated plot twists. text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | That 'Thai Warrior' is Worowit/Panom Yeerum, AKA Tony Jaa, and he's the reason for watching this movie. He's an amazingly gifted young Muai Thai kick boxer and stunt man who did all his leaps and jumps and dives. My favorite moment of all is the one where he's chasing through the streets and dives under a car, slides out the other side, and pops up again all in one smooth motion. Do you think that's easy? It's barely even conceivable. And he does all this without digital manipulation or the wires we've gotten all too familiar with in Chinese martial arts movies. Look for the real thing here, no arty made for westerners romances à la 'Crouching Tiger' or 'Flying Daggers.' This is like finding a dirty little restaurant in San Francisco's Tenderloin that has really authentic Vietnamese or Pakistani food. No frills just the joy of truly unmediated experience. The story, something about the head from Ting's (Jaa's) village temple's Buddha statue (or ONG BAK) whose theft by a gangster's low level employee disgraces the village and must be restored, is a mere formality, just enough to get things going and give Ting a back story.Tony Jaa's face is pretty, almost feminine, and his body is stocky and incredibly flexible and strong. Despite a poster for the movie that shows his broad tapered back, you may not notice how well muscled he is at first. None of this movie is about superficial show so much as it's about accomplishment. Jaa's expressions are intent and sensitive, but unlike the 'Beautiful Boxer' star Asanee Suwan (whose character, Nong Toom, is supposed to be a cross dresser fighting to earn money for a sex change), Jaa doesn't mug in an attempt to act and isn't called upon to do so.This was a relaxing way to end a movie marathon of three films in one day the other two were the Kazakhstan charmer 'Schizo' and the doc of US soldiers in Iraq, 'Gunner Palace' because you don't need to take it seriously. In fact you must adopt a mindless attitude watching 'Ong bak' (which I couldn't for 'Sin City' or 'Oldboy,' hence my difficulty with those two productions) because it contains a lot of bone crushing violence. Sometimes you can even hear the bones being crushed. The movie has been called 'insanely brutal' and that's about right, though all the brutality is pretty much in hand to hand fighting and stays close to the kick boxing techniques. You have to focus exclusively on Tony Jaa's physical prowess and remember that this is just a movie that people are not really being killed or their heads mashed in but if you do so you will be amply rewarded. There are car chases, battles, competitions, sexy girls, and evil gangsters, the kingpin of them all, Khom Tuan (Sukhaaw Phongwilai), being a depraved cripple with a scary voice box. It's not that there's no plot, just that you'd waste your time taking it seriously.The other most purely enjoyable sequence in 'Ong bak' comes even earlier than the street chase, when Ting is demonstrating his training for his Buddhist teacher through adopting a sequence of ritualized positions. This is sheer physical grace, like a dance broken into a series of sudden tableaux, and you realize what a heap of actual ART there is in the martial arts. You can't fake this kind of thing, and what impresses in this scene is not the moves and positions in themselves, but the clear sense you get that Tony Jaa knows all this deep in his bones. More than just showing off a series of carefully memorized moves this sequence is like someone with a beautiful voice and perfect diction reciting a long, awesome prayer. It's beyond words, and beyond interpretation. It just IS.It's said that 'The Making of Ong bak' is even better. Could be. Also it's said that Tony Jaa's going to be bigger than Jackie Chan and Jet Li. That's not too far fetched either. But even if this was only a unique moment in time, it'd be a movie that's fun to watch for anyone who enjoys seeing the body in graceful, powerful, acrobatic motion. In the world of martial arts stunts, it just doesn't get any better than this.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior, is a Thai film with English subtitles. The film takes place in a village in Thailand, where an evil businessman cuts the head off of the village's Buddha statue (named Ong Bak) and takes him for his boss. The village is very upset to have it gone and fears that it will bring them back luck and they need it back before they can have a special ceremony. A young man named Ting, volunteers to travel to Bangkok, to get the head back from the man who stole it. In Bangkok, Ting meets up with his cousin Humlae, who gets Ting, to fight in several fights to win him money and then agrees to help him find the head. Along the way they have to battle gangs in the city and more fighting matches till they finally get the head. Winner of The Orient Express Award for Prachya Pinkaew (the film's writer, director and producer) at The Catalonian International Film Festival and The Action Asia Award at The Deauville Asian Film Festival. Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior, has a very simple story and there really isn't a lot to the film other than some very nice looking fight scenes with good choreography but there is some humour mixed in and the film is full of action and is never boring. I would have liked to have had a little more of a complex story but I guess the film wants to be entertaining and that is what it comes out being. Overall an entertaining movie that looks good and will certainly impress martial arts fans and action film fans alike.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 8/10 | Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior more than exceeded my expectations. I have been waiting for nearly a year since I first heard of it to actually see it and it did not let me down. Although the movie started a bit slow, after about half an hour, things began to pick up and the movie never looked back.Ong Bak is about a small town villager named Ting (Tony Jaa), who sets out to find the head of his beloved sacred statue, which was stolen. Ting finds his long lost cousin from the village, Humlae (Perttary Wongkamlao), who at first claims to not know Ting until he sees that his village did not send him alone, but with a bag of cash to use as he sees necessary to get the statue head back. This is our first real look at Tony Jaa's talents, as the first chase scene begins after Humlae takes off with the bag on his motorcycle. Amazingly, Ting follows Humlae all the way to a pit fighter type of place where the real action begins.Although the plot is pretty thin, it is more than made up for by Jaa's entertaining and seemingly impossible stunts. The movie plays up the stunts big, as it claims no stunt men, no wires, no CGI, etc. With all that in mind, this movie is pretty mind boggling. Comparisons to Jackie Chan are going to be inevitable, and not undeserving. I can only imagine what the two of them could have accomplished if they did a movie together while Chan was younger. Simply amazing.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | There really is nothing new to see in Ong Bak when it comes to acting, directing, plot or any other filmatic aspects. There's some emotion and tension that builds up as the simple plot unravels and the final scenes rounds up the movie nicely. Other than that, what makes Ong Bak so good is Tony Jaa's honed fighting skills.This is a martial arts movie, expecting a fantastic plot or fantastic drama is silly. If you are put off by the idea of watching various guys either getting their ass kicked or kicking the hero's ass spectacularly with a little plot thrown in to tie(a ha)it all together then this is not the movie for you. Chinese action movies with fancy wires and fantastic colours and poetry instead, maybe? That's the other part Ong Bak wins a lot on. As cool as it is seeing someone fight over a lake in the air, or slicing a million arrows with their dress, you feel it's not real. Ong Bak proudly boasts with it's 'No wires, no CG, no stunt doubles' policy, and they should. Seeing a man getting a tremendous kick to the throat in slow mo delivers even more when you know it's not a trick(or as close to not a trick a movie can get you).After four years of training(for real, that is), Tony Jaa's Ting is ready to take on the world, and he does. The 'Muay Korat' fighting style looks exotic and fresh after the overuse of Kung Fu and the like in American movies. There are some pretty lethal looking moves that really makes you go 'ouch!' The usual obvious plot holes, such as 'why does no one use a gun?' and 'why do they attack him one and one?' are avoided as well.If you like these sorts of movies then Ong Bak is a fresh breath of air, just as good as any Hong Kong movie. I kinda wish my home country had any fighting styles worth making a movie of...

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | Ong Bak is a one man show and Tony Jaa is that show, bringing the art of Muay Thai to the mainstream in all its bone crunching glory. While it certainly struggles with giving many of its characters coherent motivations or personalities outside of stock archetypes, Jaa's violent strikes and sheer versatility keep it from getting boring. The first knee to the face is enough to make anyone wince. Jaa manages to combine the brutality of Bruce Lee, with the sheer speed of Jet Li and the wild athleticism and sheer determination of Jackie Chan into set pieces that manage to showcase the man's skills as a fighter and out and out action star. It contains all the classic hallmarks of Hong Kong cinema but lacks the writing, acting and glossy filmmaking to fully back it up. It's not terribly original but as entertainment goes, Ong Bak delivers with an effortless proficiency for brutal violence and inventive action scenes that remain endlessly engaging for fans of martial arts cinema.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | Now this is rare, am actually reviewing a movie I watched on TV. But how can I miss Ong Bak when Tom Yum Goong is around the corner, and I'd actually missed this movie during it's run at the local theatres! I'm not going to go through the details of the story   it's a simple plot about an ancient Buddha statue called Ong Bak, whose head is stolen by artifact hunters, and it's up to local village folk hero Ting who volunteers to retrieve it back from Bangkok. There, he meets up with some friends and embarks on a fight laden journey to the bowels of the city in order to fulfill his mission.What's appealing is that the main lead, played by Tony Jaa, impresses with his brand of real kung fu. Make that Muay Thai boxing, the real deal. He's today's Bruce Lee and Jackie Chan, the latter being older and wanting to move on to drama. So Tony Jaa should claim the mantle of Asia's kung fu king from Jackie Chan, and perhaps Jet Li too. Jaa's reflexes is lightning fast, and martial arts moves, lethal and deadly. I can never forget the strong punches, knees, elbows, and the feints with the kicks. Awesome, violent stuff there. No holds barred.But that's not all, besides martial arts, he's quite nimble and shows off his skills with some acrobatics during a chase scene along the back streets of Bangkok. The runs, squeezes, side splits, jumping side splits, under and sliding splits. Wow. The scenes get repeated in slow motion and in different angles, but I'm not a bit disturbed by the 'show offy' sequences. It's the real   no wires, no stunt doubles, all Jaa! And as if to emulate a typical Jackie Chan movie, there's always that bit of humour some of the acrobatic scenes, the tuk tuk chase, and also courtesy of a sidekick. But when it comes down to the fighting arena, it's all dead serious action, which many action fans will definitely enjoy.Tom Yum Goong, I'm already in the queue!

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | Since the demise of Bruce Lee, martial arts films have to an extent hovered between Jackie Chan comedy and the extensive wireworks fighting of Crouching Tiger and its follow ons. There have been relatively few attempts to show martial arts at their most developed (Bruce Lee was a pretty hard act to follow, after all).Ong Bak reverses the trend somewhat by dispensing with wire works and using a Thai expert who then apparently trained even further for several years before making the film. The effect is impressive and realistic. Ting (played by Tony Jaa) accepts the mission of his village to recover a the head of a Buddha stolen from the village temple. He tracks the thieves to the backstreets of Bangkok and comes up against the local crime operation   that deals drugs, shady gambling dens, legal and illegal fight clubs and in valuable Buddhist artifacts. Inasmuch as Ting has to wade through a veritable army of 'baddies' to achieve 'justice' it is too similar in theme to a swathe of other movies to count for much in plot originality, but setting the action in Thailand gives it a new and colourful edge. At the end of the day, mostly a film for martial arts fans though.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | This movie has the hallmarks of being a classic and firmly putting Tony Jaa up with the cult heroes of Bruce Lee, Jackie Chan and Jet Li.The story is simplistic but thats part of the beauty. The fight scenes are energetic, awesome and totally realistic. The crunching deadly elbows, powerful knees and even the leg checks and guarding are excellent. It is rather brutal in places and you will find yourself cringing; glad you are not the recipient of some of the blows. Ong bak has it all as an action movie   good guy vs bad, bare fisted, with weapons, rather unique chase scenes, comedy, brutality, explosions etcTony Jaa is like Jackie Chan on Steroids... this is one martial artist that you feel would kick Bruce Lee's behind. He performs all his own stunts, they proudly market; no strings, CGI, stand ins, etc. On the 2 DVD set the audience is treated to so many extras which is compelling. The Documentary 'Born for the Fight'; an incite into the world of the real Thai Boxer and the role of Muay Thai is magnificent.It must be noted that Ong bak is subtitled as it in Thai. But on the whole it doesn't detract from the enjoyment of the film. However, without spoilers, there's only one thing to say. If you are a Martial Arts fan.. definitely see it. If your not   see it anyway :)

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | With the preceding success of such slightly artsier fair   in the vein of beauties Hero and House Of Flying Daggers   Ong Bak is a welcome return to the old fashion exploitation movies made all too familiar by Bruce Lee. Zhang Yimou may have made poetic beauties, but nothing makes popcorn taste sweeter than a good old fashion kick em up like Ong Bak. And BOY does it kick em up! Overshadowed on it's release by the more mainstream   yet somewhat ramshackle Kung Fu Hustle   our faithful protagonist is played by Tony Jaa   a Muay Thai master in his native Thailand. After a fantastic opening involving various other hapless hopefuls attempting to climb a tree and win an honorary race, the sacred head of the village God 'Ong Bak' is stolen from the statue and taken to Bangkok. The faithful Ting (Jaa) offers to retrieve the stolen prize   apparently worth millions   and on the way meets former clan member Humlae (who now prefers the name George) and his lady friend.As the 20 minute build up should now have you foaming at the mouth in anticipation for the impending punch ups   fret not. They are fantastic. There are GREAT fight scenes. There are chase scenes involving glass sheets being carried across roads (always a favourite), gangsters chasing each other on three wheeled taxis and then tipping off the edge of an incomplete highway. It really is rib tickling fun. But the greatest joy is watching Tony Jaa roundhouse kick his way through the film in brutal fashion the likes of Van Damme only dreamt about. It's no wonder Muay Thai had perturbed censors in the past   it really does look brutal.When a films is so refreshingly honest in it's exploitative ideology it's hard to criticise its many faults. Tony Jaa may not be the best actor in the world but has all the head cracking aptitude to bypass the likes of Jet Li. Zhang Yimou's Hero looked great and had wonderfully choreographed sword fights, but it is really refreshing to see a film that sends you back to the glory days of Enter The Dragon. You're not going to get a vacuous and slightly pretentious story about spiritual enlightenment. What you do get is a little bit of plot, a little bit of comedy and then 45 minutes of people kicking each other in the head. And when it's this much fun who cares if Petchtai Wongkamlao is wasted in a boring stock comedy sidekick role? Or if some of the jokes are just off peg? Go see it. It's a terrific actioner. And all the more impressive for it's reliance on stunts instead of CGI trickery.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 6/10 | This is a martial arts film with a lot of stunts in the manner of Jackie Chan films. Except that it's not Jackie Chan. It's Tony Jaa, starring as country bumpkin awesome Muay Thai fighter, Ting.First of all, this film is a general film and it has no aspirations to be anything more. The story is very simple: Buddha's head ('Ong Bak') was stolen from village. Ting is dispatched to recover the head. Ting meets corrupted former villager Humlae who gets them into trouble. Ting kicks ass. Humlae is redeemed. Ting kicks ass. They recover the Buddha's head. Ting kicks ass. The end. The character with the most depth is Humlae, of course, as he has two dimensions (scoundrel and loyal villager) and some amount of emotional turmoil.So with the entire story out of the way, let's talk briefly about the acting. It's completely unbelievableespecially any English speaking part (including many of the brawlers that Ting goes head to head with). Humlae is portrayed with simple acting that doesn't evoke depth or permit any serious belief in his character, but adequately enough for the purposes of the film. Tony Jaa has enough charisma to carry him through his few lines, but with those components over with, we get to what this film is really about: the action.This is a martial arts film. The majority of the film's highlights occurs during some of the amazing stunts or fight sequences. The stunts are pretty impressive (one example is Tony Jaa leaping through a coil of barbed wire right after jumping completely over a set of cars) and the fights are almost as impressive. Unfortunately, you can tell from the start that none of the contending fighters are really a match for Ting, so a lot of the dramatic potency of the fights is lost.As for the direction, it's pretty workmanlike, although in some cases it becomes a little pornographic in style, with it's slow motion repeating of spectacular feats of athletic prowess. It's nothing that detracts from the film, but it's not anything that's particularly praiseworthy either.So it's a martial arts film. After you watch it once, you may want to watch it again, but the odds are that you're going to skip to the 'good parts,' namely the fight sequences and the stunts, as nothing else about the film is notable. It's not much of a movie overall, but it makes for decent spectacle. It's okay enough the first time through. .

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | First, I have to put you in my mind set when I watched this film. I had just come home from watching the Transporter 2 (one of the most hollow movies I have ever seen.) which was incomparable to the first Transporter on any level. So having just witnessed that debacle I had to redeem my evening. My brother had purchased Ong Bak but, had not yet watched it so we set about reclaiming our Friday evening. Spastic chimpanzee seizures are the only description of the anguish I had to suffer through to get through this film. Comparing Tony Jaa to guys like Jet Li and Jackie Chan is just unforgivable; those guys are in a different league than he is. Now I am not saying that he can't one day reach their level but, even mentioning his name in the same sentence as Bruce Lee is a shame. Bruce Lee helped reinvigorate martial arts movies and make them accessible to a wider audience. Tony Jaa studied Muay Thai for four years in preparation for this film (http://www.tonyjaa.org/bio.shtml). All the previous martial arts legends I listed previously had years of experience before they started making films. In the end all the hype for this film should have been toned down so that people could accept Tony Jaa for what he is, a possible future legend not a replacement for the old guard. So, it is possible that I was already dumb no plot action movied out by the time I watched this movie or it could just be a dumb, slow, nothing new venture into old familiar territory.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | Ting lives in a village where they worship the statue of Ong bak. When an unscrupulous young man comes to the village to buy valuable goods, he steals the head and returns to Bangkok where he gives it to his boss  a crime lord who presides over illegal pit fights and steals historical artefacts. Ting goes to Bangkok to join up with former villager Humlae (who now is a street hustler and calls himself George). However, once there, he finds that the only way to get the head back is to kick and elbow people. Lots.Before I talk about the main (only?) reason to see this film, let me at least pretend that it is meant to operate like a normal film and look at the traditional aspects that give a film value  plot, acting, characters etc. First off, the plot is very basic, so basic that really I could have done it in a sentence and still given you more than you needed to know. Happily it only really last 15 minutes before we are given the first of many, many action scenes. Within this basic frame it is no surprise that none of the characters work or are developed to a point were we care about them  this is a given, but why then did the film still labour under the idea that we did? I didn't care that much for any of them, because none were written as people  only action figures or one note characters (ie the girl who is suffering due to crime, the crimelord, the middleman etc etc).With this, perhaps it is no surprise that the performances are roundly average. Wongkamlao is pretty funny but can't do much more than that  but he looks like Brando at his best compared to the wooden and unconvincing Yodkamol. The rest of the cast fill their genre cliché shoes well enough; leaving us with the reason we are here  Jaa himself. Now, as an actor, he needs work  he can't really deliver a character, seems unsure of how to handle comedy and, despite having a good screen presence, didn't convince delivering dialogue neither. However, none of this really matters does it? I didn't come for plot, narrative, script, acting or directing  I came to se people get kicked and, by god, that is what this film delivers.Without wires and without special effects, the fight scenes had the cinema audibly reacting with gasps and groans as Jaa did things that did not seem possible but also delivered some very, very brutal moves that made even the toughest in the room wince. Of course, a film that relies solely on action is never going to be one that manages to win praise beyond the bounds of the genre, but it helps that, within that genre it blows away a lot of competition and justifies its UK wide cinema release. Rest assured, it is stunning at times and, although it niggles that the film is set around the action (as opposed to vice versa) it is forgivable when it is this enjoyable! Overall, not a brilliant film by any means but one that really delivers in terms of what it sets out to do. Action fans will love it and those that thing martial arts started with the Matrix will find out just how much more compelling action is whenever it isn't being produced on a hard drive somewhere. With a plot so basic, acting so poor and characters so thin, it speaks volumes about the quality of the action that I was engaged and entertained from start (well, ten minutes in) to finish.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.5/10 | From the first time I viewed the trailer I was blown away and knew I had to see this movie. I wanted to see it in the theater, but it stopped playing near me the day I had planned on seeing it, so I bought it on ebay. It just wasn't paced as well as some of the more popular martial arts movies (my favorite is Fist of Legend), but it did have some great acrobatics. I think future movies from Tony Jaa will be more amazing and polished than Ong Bak, and Jaa will hopefully rise as the new martial arts movie master. He just needs some acting lessons and a better script to work with.Overall

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | Back in the early nineties, there seemed to be an abundance of good action vehicles and there were some powerful action stars. Names like Jean Claude van Damme and Steven Seagal (who threw punches) and Sylvester Stallone and Arnold Schwarzenegger (who shot many guns) stood for some pretty good action films and good fight sequences. Since halfway the 1990's however, there was a tide of good action films and action fans like myself (I was 14 to 15 at the time) had to turn elsewhere. John Woo became my number one (after seeing Hard Target) and then I started watching more and more Jackie Chan. That guy is simply amazing and even over the last few years he has made some very good action films (First Strike, Shanghai Noon and Rush Hour).Of course, as of late there have been numerous wire fu films, but they are not exactly my cup of tea. Some style is great of course, but those films (like The House of Flying Daggers and Hero) simply overdo it and become unrealistic and to an extent boring. I like my action rough, realistic and if possible well filmed (not too poetic though) and as of late Jackie Chan seemed the only one able to provide me with that. But Jackie Chan cannot go on and make films forever and when he said he would quit making action films soon, I thought there was no hope for the good old fighting action film. I mean Arnie and Sly have sort of found their replacements in Vin Diesel and The Rock, but who I wondered would take over the torch from Jackie Chan? The answer came to me tonight...TONY JAA!!!!! This guy is really great. Van Damme was good some time ago, Seagal was amazing in his day, Chan was crazy and Jaa is simply insane. His moves are great and combined with Pinakaew's skilled directing they fuse into a violent blow that will rock your world. But there is more to the film than the action. The story is good as well and the acting is about as great as the fighting scenes. In my mind, Ong Bak is not only the new standard for action films, but also the new standard for incorporating believable fighting, skilled film making, a good story and great acting. Forget XXX, Exit Wounds, The Fast and the Furious, The Savage and The Chronicles of Riddick! Stop contemplating Rocky 6 and Rambo 4. This is the new standard and I will accept nothing less in the future. text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | It's not that Ong Bak: Muay Thai Warrior is an unexciting film because it is; it's just that it's so fabricated and guilty in the sense it wants to move onto the next set piece so urgently that it forgets to give us some of the basics we may want. I wouldn't say I was a fan of kung fu or martial arts films in general but whenever I watch one, I seem to come away with a more than positive opinion. I like films like Enter the Dragon and Kung fu Hustle; I also liked more western attempts such as The Matrix and Equilibrium but each of these four films give us something to focus on, something to care about and ultimately, something to read into. Whether it's an attack on the everyday man living a life of monotony and taking up a 'point of no return' opportunity to rid his basic, computer driven existence as seen in The Matrix or whether it's the scathing attack on censorship of classical texts and what that does to us in a strict, state controlled nation as seen in Equilibrium or maybe even the hybrid beast that is Kung fu Hustle with its mixture of genres and eastern and western ideas all mixed into one, most other films I've seen in Ong Bak's genre offer something in return on top of the fight scenes  but there is nothing really here in the long run.Ong Bak is a film that carries the moral idea that 'with great power, comes great responsibility.' Ting (Jaa) is a fighter of immense strength from an isolated Thai village that is close enough to the hustling an bustling Eastern metropolis that is Bankok for thieves to come and steal a sacred head belonging to a statue. Despite being located so close to Bankok, the city that it is, there is no sign of modernity in this Thai village. In fact, the film makes so much of a point that it is still in the ancient and pre modern world that transforming the archetype of the story is made all that much more easier.As a space within the film; the village is full of Thai people into religion, morals and equality  it is the ultimate 'good on the inside, everything outside is evil.' Contrast this to the space of Bankok again inhabited by Thais as you'd expect but this time they are more into the opposites of the village: hustling, fighting, crime and greed. It amazes me that the influence or possible Americanisation has not trickled down to smaller towns and villages such as Ting's. What also amazes me is how obvious the story is in the sense it is a 'fish out of water' concept, something that is relatively straight forward to spot but dealt with here in a pretty bland and basic manner again tempting me into thinking that the film really just exists for the stunts.As a MacGuffin, the statue head works well in the sense it is a good excuse for this home grown warrior to leave what is safe and venture to 'the city' in an attempt to prove himself worthy as a fighter or indeed, as a 'man' as these stories go. If you can get your head around the fact they only send one guy then that's one thing but if by any chance you apply a scrape of logic to the stunts and general choreography then that's another notch on your futility cap. The stunt scenes, whilst impressive for what they are, are fabricated and false. Instead of simply dodging a chasing pack of enemies the film sees fit to have its hero fault athletically and ballet like through a tight spot surrounded by people carrying glass panes. Surely a simple dodge or walk around would've been just as affective, but no and a similar occurrence happens involving spears.Scenes like this play out purely for the audience's pleasure. The characters on screen are obviously not aware of our gaze and yet Ting plays out the set pieces purely for our pleasure; either that or he is a show off but why would you toy with your life like that? Twinned with these stunts are other such gimmicks that break reality like the 'double take' and on one occasion from memory, a 'triple take'. The scenes play out in a guilty fashion, more so a 'look what we can do' rather than an unfolding of events for a reason.Ong Bak is a film in which its antagonist must talk through a voice enhancer, not because there's any logic behind it but because it's just different; it's range for the audience and different for the sake of being different. It's the sort of film in which the 'good' guys wear white and the 'bad' guys wear black during the fight club scenes and it's also the sort of film in which a daft car chase played for laughs will play out on an empty freeway in a casual and unrealistic manner  the chase also leads to certain plot revelations while assuming exploding cars have never been funnier.And so Ong Bak is the sort of film in which a stone faced hero complete with die hard morals will venture out of his boundaries to track down a sacred object, culminating in a battle against evil. I don't actually expect the Americans to remake this one because it feels American enough as it is and that is perhaps the most disappointing thing about Ong Bak, a Thai produced; Thai funded film about issues and beliefs that clearly still mean so much to them.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | The story is about a young man in a remote village who has been sent to the city to retrieve Ong Bak's head. Ong Bak is the village's local buddhist statue and is looked on by the village as it's deity. The village is suffering hard times and it is believed that unless the head is retrieved, no salvation will ever be in sight. I saw this movie in the US had I not been studying Lao (the Lao language is very closely related to thai, quite a bit of the two languages is shared) I would have missed out on what I believe are quite a few of the best parts of the movie due to them not being translated in the subtitles. For instance, upon arriving in the Bangkok, Ting played by Tony Jaa meets his goofy sidekick whose name (nickname?) is Hum Lae, which quite literally translates to 'Black Penis', or whatever other word you want to substitute for the male genitalia. There are several places in the movie where this is extremely hilarious, but not if you don't know it. All in all I would have to say I truly enjoyed the movie. The characters aren't particularly complex. They are in fact rather simplistic caricatures that most movies employ, but let's get real, this is a muay thai flick, and the fight scenes are quite possibly the best I've ever seen. They definitely rank in the top five. Almost as interesting in my opinion is the subtlety with which the thai culture is exposed to the audience. You don't have to be paying attention to enjoy the movie, but some scenes when paid close attention to leave one with a deeper understanding of Asian cultures in general. In one of the last scenes a buddha head (not ong bak's) is broken exposing what appears to be at first glance lava or some golden substance, but in actuality represents the inner light of buddha, this isn't explained, but is commonly understood by buddhists everywhere. All in all I highly recommend this movie to anyone with an interest in films of this type. The acting is mediocre but given that it's still a great movie.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | Martial arts films don't come with more action than Ong Bak. Tony Jaa is by no doubt an astonishing fighter, and Prachya Pinkaew (director) & his cinematographer Nattawut Kittikhun do well in milking his talents for all their worth. The pair stun us with astonishingly detailed fight sequences, choreographed to perfection by Tony Jaa   the leading man himself. Cinematography is pin sharp, and the Thanat Sunsin Thanapat Taweesuk editing team fly the banner of their craft high with jaw dropping cuts and manipulations   foremost being ingenious use of instant replays.All that being considered, Ong Bak falls far too short in an area arguably more important than technical mastery of filmmaking: the script is terrible. Gaps in the fighting sequences and landscape fills play out like a painful Jackie Chan overdub without the Chan. Kittikhun manages to stun us with majestic landscape cinematography   which does somewhat make up for the shocking script; though cannot ever restore the potential destroyed by the shoddy framework.Technically speaking, Ong Bak is convincing   it certainly lives up to its expectation as martial arts eye candy; though if story and depth are what you seek, then you can give it a miss. But if mindless thrills portrayed with majestic technical mastery are what you seek, then Ong Bak is for you.
