text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | 'Bruce Lee was the first. Jackie Chan took it to a new level. And now . There's a new superstar of martial arts'The above tagline comes courtesy of the North American trailer for the new martial arts film Ong bak (new to American audiences, but two years released in Asia) and refers directly to the star of the film, Tony Jaa. You may not know of Tony Jaa yet, but if Hollywood has its way, his name will be on marquees for the next 10 years as Jet Li was the decade previous. He is a good looking, ass kicking martial arts contortionist who's stunts pay homage to the Jackie Chan of the 1970's and early 80's before stunt men and special effects began to share some of his credits. In Ong bak, the producers boast 'No stunt doubles. No computer graphics. No strings attached.' And who would have thought that this would have been such a refreshing change. For as much as I thank The Matrix trilogy for bringing us five years of incredible action entertainment, it also revolutionized how special effects and more specifically, hidden wires were used in films so that ordinary people can do extraordinary stunts. This has, in my opinion, cheapened action films of the new millennium as it is now common place to see someone jump in the air, do more flying rotations than a professional ice skater and kick unconscious five or more men before having their two feet again hit the earth. The technique has become such commonplace that the invisible harness has been used for comedic purposes in movies like Scary Movie and Austin Powers.But Ong bak will have none of that. Ong bak tells the story about a young man (Booting) that leaves a small village for the big city in the pursuit for the head of a religious statuette (the Ong bak) that is stolen from the temple by a corrupt crime lord. Ong bak's story is a simple one: Booting must track down the thieves and retrieve the head. In fact, the story is so simple that you could believe that these were the only words written in the script and to fill in the extra time, they would have Jaa jump, climb, punch and kick until the inevitable showdown at the film's conclusion. But what do we care? When was the last time that you knowingly set out to watch a bare knuckled martial arts film and cared about story, sub plots, love interests and foreshadowing? This movie is about Jaa, giving him a vehicle to strut his stuff and boy, do we get what we've paid for.Ong bak has some remarkable action sequences with Jaa sliding under vehicles, jumping through barbed wire, running on people's shoulders and in his own patented move, smacking his elbow on the top of the head. He moves with incredible speed and seems to have eyes in the back of his head. His grace is choreographed with the precision of a craftsman but with the ferocity of an untamed animal. When Booting fights in a match, which seems ripped from the kumite underground fighting of Bloodsport, you could almost turn the volume off in the theatre and you will still believe you are hearing cracking bones and audience gasps. If you were to use one word for Ong bak it would probably be 'cool'. Tony Jaa is the epitome of cool. You will leave the theatre excited, pumped up and in the mood to listen to Carl Douglas' Kung Fu Fighting over and over again on the way home. Just don't expect to tell anyone about the story the next day, for after three viewings, I still can't notice, remember or care.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | I decided to give this movie a watch after reading the rave reviews on numerous websites. Being a martial arts fan, I was confident that this would be the movie I've been waiting for. The United States hasn't seen a good import for awhile, minus the cure for insomnia 'Hero.' Good beat'em up flicks are hard to come by in the new millennium, so I was looking forward to Ong Bak.The movie starts off confusing enough: we get to watch a bunch of dirty people climbing up a huge tree, racing for a flag or something. I'm sure this is easily understandable in Thailand, but it just did not translate well for an opening scene for the States. Shortly after, we get to meet Ting (or as my subtitles read, 'Tim') played by newcomer Tony Jaa. Ting is apparently the go to guy of the village when trouble starts, for we soon find a thief stealing the head of statue Ong Bak, and immediately Ting puts it on himself to recapture the stolen head. Ting grabs money from the whole village, and decides to blindly search for the guy in Bangkok. He meets up with a former villager Humlae who is a little down on his luck with gambling, and his partner in crime, a girl named Muay. After agreeing to let Ting stay at his house, Humlae takes Ting's money to a boxing bar to ante up. Ting follows Humlae to the strangely diverse bar, and gets suckered into fighting. Naturally, Ting has little trouble grounding the 'champion.' This does not go over well with the crowd, or with a mob leader, who loses a ton of money from a bet made on the fight. This brings Ting to keep fighting one ridiculous baddie after another, concluding with a guy who seems to be more focused on destroying everything in sight than fighting Ting. Interesting scenes follow, with Ting and Humlae still searching for Ong Bak. Yadda yadda yadda.After watching the movie, I had mixed feelings. The action scenes were really good, but they came off just too reminiscent of a Van Damme flick from the early 90's. An impressive kick from Ting was met with an instant replay or two, adding to the cheese factor and kind of ruining the moment. The rest of the movie has every requisite scene for an action flick: a foot chase throughout town, a car chase, a bad sub plot involving drug lords, etc. Even with the impressive fighting scenes, the movie still seemed to drag on. The humor doesn't translate well, and the rest of the dialogue just leaves us nodding our head waiting for the next fight scene. For having such little plot, they sure pile on the dialogue and storytelling, especially in the first half of the film.It seems the director of the movie is a little behind the times. This is easily something that would have went over well in 1997, but watching it now just feels redundant. We've seen this before. Tony Jaa is a fresh face, and I am looking forward to seeing some more work from him, even in something produced in the States (he will have to work on his English and get rid of that horrid accent, though). But Ong Bak is really just a made for TV movie in disguise. It will fit in nicely during a Martial Arts marathon on the USA network, and that's about it.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | Evoking the duality of good and bad through the pastoral simplicity of the Thai countryside and the seedy underbelly of Bangkok's prostitution and drug trade, 'Ong Bak' argues its principles with a brutally honest knee to the face of the West's creeping cultural domination of Asia. The filmmakers present this as a homage to the visual masters in Besson, Spielberg and most of all the glut of Bruce Lee and Jackie Chan fighting vehicles that saw them fleeting from hordes of non descript assailants through literally tight spaces. Tony Jaa's prototypical monastic role as an avenging warrior for the lower rung of Thailand is no different from his role in this film's follow up international moneymaker, 'Tom Yum Goong' or more particularly known as 'The Protector'.Other than its similarities in characters, Jaa has to retrieve his temple's talismanic Buddha statue head (the titular Ong Bak) that is being held for ransom by Bangkok druggist, Don instead of being commissioned to rescue his elephants from animal traders in its structural and thematic progeny, 'Tom Yum Goong'. The stoic (by choice?), reticent country boy is thrust into a dodgy and faced with dangers at every corner, mostly by evil and greedy men trying to make a quick buck from Jaa's expertise with his elbows and knees.The most apparent hint of the veracious nationalism that 'Ong Bak' suffuses between its prolonged chase sequences and high kicks to head are set in the dingy underground fighting club where patrons of all nationalities and races huddle together, hand on each other's shoulders while corralling a motley collection of ribald pugilists hoping to best each other blow for blow to receive that plate of prize money.In steps Jaa with his tattered temple habits, unaware of the monetary reverence for such an occasion. As the newly crowned fighting champion rushes towards Jaa with his fists clenched, up goes Jaa's knee to deliver a knockout that silences the raucous crowd. In yet another scrap at the same club, a brawny Aussie lout bellows across the room to Jaa's disinterested character after nearly decimating his previous opponent who jumped in to rescue a damsel as said lout was groping her repeatedly. Rounding off his character as best the writers could, his soft spot for rescuing distressed women prevails and Jaa unleashes a torrent of body blows onto the racist, sexist and eventually vanquished miscreant, resulting in the long overdue return to the main plot.Playing as though through a series of video game levels varying in difficulty, the settings and pliable environments start to change but not the fighters. Each opponent are nothing but fodder to the invincible Jaa as he dispatches each one of them with astonishingly legerdemain and a refreshingly straightforward temerity unseen in any city boy that knows what's best for him and his limps. This machine of a man probably leaves behind a hundred men in his wake until he reaches the tough final boss stage, the right hand stooge of the villainous old man with a neat idiosyncrasy suggesting either a barely breathing, handicapped warning label or a 'live every moment till life crashes down on you' type of attitude. 'Ong Bak' is appropriately billed as brilliantly choreographed escapist fare that presents to us a man without personality and without emotions, just a moral imperative that transcends life and death.Rating: 3½ out of 5

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | The story is better than most martial arts films made in Asia, but the cinematography is a bit amateurish. The story utilizes elements of Thai culture that may not translate well for Westerners though the plot has some heart and meat to it unlike many martial arts films that seem to be a fight looking for a pretext. The camera work is a little hokey with common use of double (or triple, etc.) takes of action shots. This wasn't cool when used in Lionheart and it still isn't. Overall, however, the production value is high for the genre and the sound track is decent.Next up are the fight scenes. Jaa's form is perfect and he has real presence. He doesn't really act, though, and it appears they have used the early Jean Claude van Damme technique. One can forgive this minor transgression as I am sure we would much rather see an incredible martial artist trying to act rather than an actor faking a martial art. I used to study Muay Thai and it is very poor for film work. There are not that many forms and it doesn't lend itself to drama in a battle. The art doesn't have a traditional sense of blocking so it appears as if it is a slugfest a la Rocky. Jaa pushes the art to the limit and he has amazing form. The fight scenes are very good. There are also amazing chases and the obligatory secondary tragedies.The movie reminds me very much of earlier Jackie Chan films. It's not bad, but it doesn't stand out too much among the crowd.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7/10 | 'Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003)' focuses on a young martial artist who travels to the big city to retrieve a religious statue stolen from his village. He comes across an illegal fight circuit and clashes with its host, who turns out to be smuggling precious national artefacts. The movie has an uneven tone and a sort of 'back and forth' plot that keeps returning to the same central concept of underground fighting. It also has very simple characterisations and is occasionally haphazardly constructed. However, much like with 'Warrior King (2005)', these issues come secondary to the flick's fantastic action sequences. Though the organised fight aspect is only ever so compelling from a narrative point of view, it allows the film to indulge in some good old fashioned fisticuffs. These scenes showcase some satisfying, unexpectedly brutal choreography and are highly entertaining. Not all the fights take place inside the ring, though; the movie's fantastic finale brings things to a whole new level with a final confrontation that only gets more fun (and violent) as it goes along. It also ends in a surprisingly emotional way. Another highlight is a foot chase that sees Jaa perform all manner of near impossible athletic feats, navigating though increasingly dangerous obstacles as his pursuers fall at each hurdle. The film elects to show us each of these multiple times, just to make sure we don't miss any of them. Overall, the picture is flawed but fun. It's probably more consistent than the aforementioned 'Warrior King (2005)', but it certainly isn't quite as exciting. Still, it's a more than solid action film that deserves to be seen. .

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | I grew up with martial arts movies watching almost everything under the sun (SHAOLIN TEMPLE, PROJECT 'A', KILL OR BE KILLED, FLYING GUILLOTINE, FIST OF THE WHITE LOTUS, THE 36 CHAMBERS, ENTER THE DRAGON, blah, blah, blah.) I walked into the theater with high expectations since everyone lauded the film ONG BAK, saying it was better than Jackie Chan's films, even better than Bruce Lee's. I walked out of the theater upset that I just wasted good money and some time out of my life on a film that brought nothing new to the table, save a promising action talent, Tony Jaa. I expect that people won't agree with me on this issue and I don't care. Sure the movie was filled with acrobatic stunts and the fight choreography was well done. Was it better than Jackie Chan's films? No Way. Chan was doing stuff like this 20 years ago. I'm not doubting Tony Jaa's ability as a martial artist. I have tremendous respect for Muy Thai as an effective fighting art. He has great potential in future action films. Was it better than Bruce Lee's Films? To a degree yes. The story was better, but not by much. And no actor to this date is able to capture his audience with the same raw screen intensity that Bruce Lee portrayed way back in the day. Although Tony Jaa's performance was much more 'gymnastic' than Lee's, Lee was all street. He was the type of guy, actor or not, that you wouldn't want to go toe to toe if you crossed paths with him in an alley   and that's just from looking at his face. text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | Let's get one thing straight from the off; I really wanted to like Ong Bak. I'd seen several trailers and read many independent reviews that hailed it as the greatest thing to hit martial arts film making in years. Maybe that was the problem. I was so looking forward to seeing this film that it was almost inevitable that it was going to end up a disappointment. The fact that the plot is paper thin is not a problem for me. The majority of martial arts films are not exactly defined by their intricate plotting and depth of character. We're dealing with stock heroes and villains here, with a couple of sidekicks thrown in to provide comic relief. Ting's simplistic quest is also an ideal one on which to hang the fight/chase set pieces that the genre demands. And that's really where the problem lies. The set up is adequate, it's in the execution of the rest of it's job that the film fails. The editing is all over the place and the general pacing is far too slow. It is no exaggeration to say that the first major fight of any kind doesn't occur until 45 minutes in, almost half the movie's running time! The Muay Thai styled action is brutally impressive at first but it's cinematic limitations soon show through. As for the films two chase sequences, the car chase is plain boring and poorly handled and the alley chase staged just to show how acrobatic Jaa can be. There's nothing wrong with this, but better filmmakers have managed to fit this kind of sequence into their films more organically(i.e. Jackie Chan). On the positive side, the film generally looked great due to the excellent cinematography and the actor who played the role of comedy sidekick George/Dirty Balls did so to the hilt and was definitely the heart and soul of the movie. Tony Jaa is an impressive action performer with a bright future ahead of him, but to talk of him being in the same company as Jackie Chan and Bruce Lee at this time is nonsense. Ong Bak is a commendable first effort, but it's a long way from Enter the Dragon or Drunken Master 2.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | How many movies nowadays do you see that contain over the top stunts with obvious wire work and CG effects? Doesn't it get to a point where you just want to stomp the producers head for making it so stupid? Well, Ong Bak is here to kick that producer as well as yourself in the face with some of the best action ever seen on film, no strings attached. Of course, it's a complete shame that the editors have bastardized them.Not that you really care, but there isn't really much of a story to go along with these action scenes. Basically, greedy drug dealer Don (Sirioput) has stolen the head of the statue of god Ong Bak from a small village in Thailand after the chief refused to sell him his Buddha amulet. So the village sends out their prize fighter with a terrible name, Ting (Jaa), to retrieve Ong Bak's head. The chief also says to recruit the help of his wayward son Humlae (Wongkamlao), who has run to Bangkok and become a heavy gambler and conman. What they find is a scandal involving a rich socialite (Pongwilai) and hundreds of stolen articles.It's all ridiculous, and it doesn't try to hide it. It exists to simply string together multiple scenes that involve Ting (what a terrible name) being chased, attacked and attacking. Jaa is an exceptional martial artist, so it is hard to blame the movie for the shallow plot. In fact, if there was a plot, odds are we'd have less scenes of Jaa kicking some ass.And we do get a lot of Jaa kicking ass. There are around 10 or so long fight sequence in the film, with many other short ones in between. They involve a cab chase across a bridge with Jaa jumping between cars, a boxing match which results in a destroyed arena, a fight with mine workers carrying machetes and a ring fight with an extremely hopped up bodyguard. Even more intriguing is that Jaa did all of his own stuntwork for the movie, and no special effects or wirework was used. It's truly a spectacle, and Jaa is easily the next Bruce Lee, Jackie Chan or Jet Li (in fact, he's probably better than all of them).It's somewhat of a shame, however, that while Jaa is exceptional and no one can deny that , the editors have tried to take away some of that effect by using excessive slow downs and replays. In fact, it makes it feel like sporting event instead of a real movie. It also gets annoying as sometimes replays are used for cool, but not especially excellent stunts, such as sliding under a truck or jumping over a parked car. It all becomes so chopped up that a lot of the effect is gone.As for the acting, since it is in Thai, I cannot be the best judge of it. I could tell that Wongkamlao was pretty bad as Humlae, over exaggerating every sentence he spoke. The rest of the cast's acting relies mainly on fighting skills, and it all looks real and professional. On a side note, the English dubbing for this film is traditionally horrendous, so Thai audio with English subtitles is the way to go.Basically, if you can get around the terrible plot and the choppy editing, Ong Bak contains some of best fight sequences seen in quite a while. However, there are many little things that will bug you while watching them. It's really isn't worth letting them annoy you to a point where you don't see the fights, so it is a worthwhile rental for the action freak in all of us.Overall Rating  72%

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | I have little problem with the simple story; it was acceptable for such a feature, though it could have used a little more heart. The technical aspects (direction, acting, etc ) were good enough too but the music in the American version consisted of lame, generic, techno music courtesy of Luc Besson (who also annoyingly cut some parts out). But onto the action now. The chase sequences were actually pretty entertaining, if nothing all that special. The foot chase gave a good opportunity to show off Tony Jaa's skills (more on him in a moment) and the multiple cart chase provided some admirable wrecks and explosions. The fights were decent too and it's nice to see some 'real' stunt work back on the screen. Now, while what I've wrote so far is mostly positive, the point I'm trying to make is even though I found Ong Bak to be an adequate action movie, it certainly wasn't as great as the hype led me to believe. The fights, aside from them being 'real,' were not much better than what you'd find in a modern Jet Li flick. In other words, they were mostly typical and not all that thrilling, and the moves became dull and repetitive (many of them shown three times in slow mo!). Seriously, Tony Jaa must have only learned two stances, three spinning flips, and about eight strikes. Now, to Jaa's credit, he does display some quality acrobatic skills à la Jackie Chan, mainly in the street chase. However, as far as that goes, it's the kind of stuff Chan could do in his sleep. Also, I must say that I didn't appreciate the cut on Chan on the back of the DVD case, which was totally false. Back to Jaa, despite his athletic talent, he lacked screen charisma, which is quite important in these kinds of movies. He just didn't make for all that interesting of a character. Plus, he looks like the lovechild of Gollum and Tattoo from Fantasy Island, which doesn't help matters any. Don't get me wrong, folks, I enjoyed the movie and Tony Jaa may have a future in the genre but this wasn't the serious, brutal fight flick I was expecting, and hoping for.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | Not to insult Tony Jaa, but one has to think someone is a little, shall we say, light headed, to do some of the stunts he does in ONG BAK. That said, anyone who sits through the wafer thin and often meandering story to watch Jaa (Panom Yeerum) do what he does here and isn't completely stunned by what they see, can't be a real action fan, IMHO.There's certainly a lack of money on screen and the seams show often enough (especially in the film stock/color timing areas, where the image is often overly dark or something approaching monochrome). In this day of CROUCHING TIGER, HERO, HOUSE OF FLYING DAGGERS and KUNG FU HUSTLE I'm starting to get used to the idea of bigger budgets, rich colors, beautiful lighting and sets, and more character development in fight films. But you won't find any of that in ONG BAK. The film when I saw it, looked bad enough to be an old '70's film print, run on TV way too often.However, the fights are the focus, and they're mostly done right. The big stunts are often presented with multiple camera angles in succession, which I found saved me a few times from blurting out, 'what just happened? I wanna see that again.' Usually, you see it a couple of times. At least the filmmakers know why we watch the movie.I must mention a very annoying problem with the US DVD release: the only English subtitle track is for the hearing impaired (although not listed as such   clearly a mistake), which means that all the sound effects and several music cues gets spelled out as well, often filling up the bottom and into nearly the center of the screen   very annoying for an action movie. The subtitles run over the frame, not below it as is more common in widescreen presentations on DVD, so it makes matters worse. I found myself trying to look through them to see what was happening in a few scenes. It became so annoying (at least to me, whose hearing is fine and is not used to so much subtitle clutter), I almost broke down and went for the dubbed English track, but came to my senses and stuck it out. (You have been warned, however.)I understand Tony Jaa's next film will have a much larger budget. Let's hope they keep the raw feel to the fight scenes and put the money into a decent script and better film stock. It's pretty hard to sit through at times. The bottom line for this one is: If you need a good story, look elsewhere; if you want to see the amazing Tony Jaa in action, you won't be disappointed. He and the fine stunt crew/actors might be the only great thing about ONG BAK, but when you can do what they do, without wires or stunt doubles, that's probably enough.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | I haven't been this impressed with a martial arts movie in a long time. Doubly so since it isn't the typical Japanese or Chinese martial arts. We are treated to Muay Thai Kickboxing which is an extremely hard form of fighting involving lots of elbows and knees.Tony Jaa is amazing. While his character spends a majority of looking rather sulky, he is an incredible athlete. Early in the film there are a number of scenes reminiscent of Jackie Chan's movies while he evades the bad guys. When he really starts fighting it is hard core martial arts. For the fights I am reminded of the Streetfighter movies. Scenes where it really looks like the actors are getting damaged. Sure the fight scenes are cinematic with plenty of gratuitous spins and airborne maneuvers, but even the most ridiculous seeming moves really look like they would hurt.The story is pretty simple. A young man from a small village, who is trained in Kickboxing, and sets off to find the man who stole the head from the village idol (Ong Bak). He is also to find a village elders son who is living in Bangkok. The son is a lowlife con man who wants nothing to do with his past. The man who stole the head of the idol works for a mob boss, who collects artifacts and bets of fights. So the hero gets sucked into a fight against the underworld figure, and against his fighters.If you are a fan of martial arts movies, this is the must see movie of the year, if not of the decade. text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | This movie does for tuktuks what The Blues Brothers did for Dodge Monaco police cruisers.In one of many thrilling chase scenes, the venerable little three wheeled motorcycle taxis are put to the test, tipping over, sliding around, popping wheelies and ending up in a big pile at the bottom of an unfinished highway exit ramp. Anyone who's ever been ripped off by the driver of these insane vehicles will take much delight in their destruction.The action hardly lets up in this, from a thrilling opening sequence involving a capture the flag match in a tree to an unsanctioned muay Thai boxing match set on Bangkok's infamous Khao San Road.Other comments about how the star is destined to be the next Jackie Chan, to how the director is the greatest ever, etc, etc, tend to over rate this film. Yeah, it's pretty darn good, and one of the best action films to come out of the Thai film industry yet. Up until this one, the best Thai films have been historical epics, like Bangrajan and Suriyothai. Even the ghost story, Nang Nak, had some good battlefield scenes. Ong Bak is more in the vein of Hollywood or Hong Kong actioners, but it's hardly on par with the likes of say Jackie Chan or John Woo.The big problem for this film in the international market is that the DVDs are being marketed without any subtitles   not that they are really needed with all the action going on   but they would help improve the accessibility of this movie to foreign audiences.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | Ong Bak (2003) is a throwback film to the yesteryear of the glorious reign of Shaw Brothers action films and the rising productions of Golden Harvest. This is a straight forward, hard hitting no holds barred type of kung fu film that pulls no punches. I miss these films and I'm glad to see this one has finally made it to the big time. Instead of burying or putting films like these on the independent or art house circuit, it's finally available for the mass market.The movie is about a young villager who must bring back a religious relic that a former resident stole for financial gain. Ting, a extraordinary fighter leaves his hamlet to head off towards the city of Bangkok and find a cousin of his who left is impoverished country life to seek his fortune in the big metropolis, Ting doesn't know that his cousin is a rascal who's involved in all kind of scams and bad dealings with the local syndicate. Can Ting find his village's idol and restore spiritual order within their tight knit community? Will Ting be able to handle himself in the big city as well?If you love action films or the kung fu genre this is a do not miss. The film is in Thai with English sub titles. The movie hasn't be tampered with that much. Don't be turned off by the fact that this is a foreign film. It's in the original language so the audience wont have to suffer with cheesy dubbing and shoddy editing. I guarantee you will not be disappointed. From Thailand, of course!Highly recommended!

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | While it starts out slow, Ong Bak eventually delivers on all of its promises as a 'nuclear bomb of cool'. By the end of this film, Tony Jaa establishes himself as the heir to Bruce Lee's action film legacy, an artist who can dazzle with feats of physical prowess as well as humble with some of the most brutal and intense beatings ever handed out on film. The director does not get in the way of the stunts, and the raw and rough directing style assures you of the stunt work's gritty authenticity. The utter audacity of some of the knees to the face or elbows to the skull delivered by Tony Jaa make you wonder how many stunt men were hospitalized by this film. Its a feeling I haven't had since Bruce leveled a kneeling Han with a kick to the face during Enter the Dragon or sent someone flying by 'kicking from the hip'.This movie will make old school, gritty Bruce Lee fans grin with joy and drop the jaws of any martial arts film newcomers. A welcome break from the flowery dance and painterly cinematography of modern martial arts films, Ong Bak will satiate any gnawing hunger for raw, ass kicking action.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | This is without a doubt the best martial arts film since 'Enter The Dragon'. text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | I'm a fan of all types of martial arts films, from the 1970s efforts of the Shaw Brothers to the 1960s Samurai films to Tzui Hark to Jet Li to Ringo Lam to to Donnie Yen to Jackie Chan. text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | I've not enjoyed a martial arts film as much as 'Ong bak' since Jackie Chan's amazing 'Kwai tsan tseh' ('Wheels On Meals').'Ong bak' is a splendidly entertaining action film that avoids the downfalls of CGI and wires, relying instead on the talents of its cast, particularly the amazing Tony Jaa. text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | There's a quick way to sum up whether you're the sort of person who might enjoy this film:Does the idea of a man, with his leg on fire, leaping a good twelve feet through the air and landing, knee first, on an assailant, appeal to you?If the answer is emphatically 'Yes!' watch this film and love every second (like me)! If it is 'Maybe...' watch it and be amazed though somewhat underwhelmed at the extraordinary lack of sensible plotting, bizarre repetition of brief sequences and annoying slow motion moments. If your answer would be a definite 'No.' this is most definitely not the film for you. Ong Bak contains the most incredible martial arts and gymnastics you are ever likely to see committed to film. Unfortunately it sacrifices a great deal to achieve this, mostly by failing to offer much in the way of sensible plot and occasional pacing problems. text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | With Jackie and Jet having virtually abandoned the world of pure martial arts action film in favour of more lucrative lighthearted Hollywood fodder and the occasional lavish historical epic, fans of no nonsense, no holds barred, bone crunching fight fests were left looking for the next star to fill the void.Enter stunt man Tony Jaa, whose athleticism and outstanding Muay Thai fighting skills impressed producer director Prachya Pinkaew sufficiently for him to cast the unknown in the lead role for his latest project Ong Bak. Martial arts fans had found their new hero, and the rest, as they say, is history.As Ting, the villager charged with the job of finding and returning the stolen head of Ong Bak, the village's stone Buddha, Jaa displays an energy not witnessed since the heydays of Chan and Li. Pinkaew's incredible understanding of action cinema, combined with Jaa's precision, power, and speed, delivers a level of excitement and inventiveness that had been sorely missing from the genre for quite some time.From the spectacular opening scene, in which Jaa and his fellow villagers battle to claim a flag from the top of a tree, with numerous bodies tumbling awkwardly onto the tree's limbs before hitting the ground hard, and the star hopping with ease from branch to branch to avoid the same fate, it is clear that this is going to be something special. Throughout the film, Pinkaew requires his star to perform increasingly amazing physical feats, but nothing seems impossible for the talented Thai, who leaps through coils of barbed wire, between plate glass sheets, over and under moving cars, and battles a variety of imposing foes with seeming ease, and completely without the aid of namby pamby wirework or CGI trickery.By the end of the brutal final showdown against the big bad boss and his most evil of henchmen, Jaa has more than proved himself as a worthy successor to the martial arts movie crown. Long live the king!

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | STAR RATING: Unmissable Very Good Okay You Could Go Out For A Meal Instead * Avoid At All Costs In Ting's (Tony Jaa) village in Thailand, the festival of Ong Bak, the great Thai warrior, is about to begin. But then, disaster strikes when the head of Ong is severed from his statue and stolen. Vowing to return it, Ting heads out to Bangkok and tracks down his drug pushing, bike racing screw up cousin Humlae (Petachtai Wongkamlao) and heads after the crook he's pretty certain is behind it all.I'm not sure who they're going around touting as the new Jackie Chan, but I have an idea it may be this Jaa guy. If it's true he did all his own stunts in this without the aid of effects or stunt doubles, then that's a real achievement. The stunts and martial arts on display here are truly breath taking. The film also manages to be funny in a really simple way at times.Aside from this, it also pays great homage to the classic Bruce Lee MA actioners of the 70s, right down from the dubbed voices that don't always match up to the words coming out of the characters mouths, to the simple villains, from the dastardly Don (Wannakit Sirioput) to some wheel chair bound guy who has to place what looks like a miniature inhaler up to his throat to talk. It also moves them from their Chinese origins to a Thailand one. Trust me, everything you see here is authentic Muay Thai.It basically succeeds in every way it meant to. With all the computer aided stunts and effects out there nowaday, it's very good to watch something that is pure and great all the way.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: .10/10 | Thailand Muay Thai boxing master, stuntman, and actor Tony Jaa is quickly rising to become the new 'it' star of martial arts cinema. We get many dazzling stunts and foot chases through Jaa's native Thailand (which are used to great extent in showing us this country's exotic beauty), and many brutal bouts between himself and a legion of disposable bad guys, I mean sparring partners.One thing I've learned in recent years is that Thailand has yet to pop up on the radar of the martial arts circuit in a big international way, and with Jaa's star making crossover hit, 2003's 'Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior,' they may have just gotten their due. Another interesting tidbit I've picked up: it may be the first in a glorious revolution of Thai made martial arts movies.Jaa is a really little guy too. So little that in fact, you could put him in a crowd of people and if you passed him, you wouldn't notice him. But don't let his size fool you; he has some pretty impressive and spectacularly dizzying moves of his own, and I've learned that the fighting style he's mastered, Muay Thai boxing, is different from other significant styles such as Aikido, Karate, Jeet Kune Do or Wushu (what we're all used to), in that it largely utilizes the artist's arms, elbows, and knee joints so that he can deliver some pretty punishing blows to an opponent's midsection, face or skull.With all this said, 'Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior' is a real jolter when it comes to its displays of action. When punches land, with the combined force of muscle and pure strength, they sound like they hurt. I said HURT. You can HEAR the sounds of a fist pounding into flesh. Many times in these movies, you hear some exaggerated sound when a fighter strikes an opponent, but here it sounds like these guys are really going at it, and it looks like it hurts.And it has a plot that's not all that unfamiliar with much of martial arts cinema (not that the plot really matters, all 10 minutes of it). In a small Thai village, Jaa plays Ting, a devout Buddhist who is forced to travel to the city when the head of a sacred statue is stolen. It is here on the streets of Bangkok that he takes on the ruthless criminal underworld and a legion of gangsters.In Bangkok, he frequents after hour fight clubs and engages in impressive and brutal bouts with other fighters, each one more over the top than the last. He is at first reluctant to fight, as he was warned by his master to not use his skills for money or entertainment purposes, and vowed to never do so. But with all these bad guys around that are all asking for a licking, he's left with no choice.Surprisingly, this really is an entertaining martial arts actioner from one of the last places to spring up on the kung fu scene. Jaa is an incredible stunt person, as I'm sure from the previews, that no wires, CGI or fancy camera tricks were employed to exaggerate the feats of real stunt work, which is something missing in the increasingly desperate genre of martial arts movies.Just watch the film's opening sequence for example, which opens up at a tree climbing contest. An establishing shot shows us the height of the tree (it's pretty tall, with many branches sticking out) and we can very easily tell that when guys are knocked off, they fall a great distance and then they hit the ground  hard  and it looks AND sounds like it really hurts.Guys get beat up in some very brutal and entertaining ways in martial arts movies; 'Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior' is no exception. I checked out the '8 Movements of Muay Thai' and Jaa's live stage performance in France on the special features section of the DVD and I can guarantee even the most skeptical viewers that much of what goes on here is indeed real (and if it isn't, which I doubt, well, they've done a good job of concealing any effects trickery). However, in a time when 'Matrix' fu or wire fu rules nearly everything around us, it's good to see a movie from a far off and little known place show the world how an action movie is supposed to be made

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 9/10 | Ong Bak is a really a fantastic debut for Tony Jaa and others. Though it isn't strong on the story or character development which is very basic, it is all about the brutal full contact, graceful well choreographed action scenes ever present in this film. The story is basically Ting (Jaa) a country boy goes to Bangkok to retrieve a sacred stolen 'artifact'. That's all there is to it really. Now the action however is the strong point of Ong Bak, what they say is true, no wires, no special effects...everything you see is real and people really get hurt. Tony Jaa really is the next action hero, and at this rate, he'll be a superstar within less then 5 years, probably even the first Thai superstar. Critics say that he incorporates all the likes of Bruce Lee,Jackie Chan and others. Though it is true Jaa is inspired by them, his style is quite different, sure he has the amazing stunts (like Chan) and the full contact brutal force (like Lee) but he has his own trademark, Thai Boxing, different to any Chinese films, completely different and somewhat more realistic. He uses knees and elbows, and as being a martial artist myself I can say this is simply because they are the hardest part of the body. I am very keen on this new star, and Iwish him every luck, I'll be following his career closely, for I know he will be successful.Watch Ong Bak, it won't disappoint, .

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | Rest assured if 8 year olds were old enough to see 'Ong Bak' there would by a Muay Thai studio in every American town. Yes, Mommy, I want to vault over cars; yes, I want to jump feet first through hoops; yes I want to beat people up—err, defend myself—with what amounts to the strength of my elbows.'Ong Bak' is a martial arts showcase in this regard; any of the action scenes could be used as a recruitment video for the sport/art form. And then there's Tony Jaa, who aside from instantly elevating himself to modern equivalents such as Jet Li and Jackie Chan, plays a character in Ting who could teach every action hero that ever was a thing or two about humility. In fact, we could all learn a thing or two from the Buddhists.Ting lives in rural Thai village centered around a Buddhist monastery. When the head of the town's precious Buddha statue, Ong Bak, is ripped off and stolen, Ting is tasked with heading to Bangkok to retrieve it lest the village see bad luck forever. Men have kicked ass over less.Filmmaker Prachya Prinkaew surrounds Ting with a vibrant ensemble. Ting's first order of business is to seek out his cousin, Humlae (Petchai Wongkamlao), a deceitful and shallow money grubber of the worst kind and his little sister Muay (Pumwaree Yodkamol) with whom he runs cons. When Humlae realizes Ting could be a top prize fighter, he agrees to help Ting get the Ong Bak back. It's currently in the possession of Komtuan, a wheelchair bound crime lord with a tracheotomy. Although the dynamics between them could be described as cliché, this is a rather unique core cast of characters.With someone of Jaa's ability, it's not difficult to conceive of some creative action sequences and grin inducing stunts. The smartest decision, however, is easily Prinkaew's choice to reveal Jaa's skills to us slowly, to tease his ass kicking potential. The chase scene through Bangkok that shows off Jaa's acrobatic side gives us our first taste and leaves us hungry for what this guy can do when someone needs to be put in their place (a.k.a the floor).The fights don't disappoint either. Although they can get repetitive toward the end, Jaa provides a spectacle and the fight choreography is legit. And despite the 'R' rating, 'Ong  Bak' avoids getting brutally violent, instead more interested in the artistry of the fighting. The only poor technique choice is the use of the 'let's see that again!' shot after Jaa does anything the film wants you to see as miraculous. This is a film, not a live sporting event, but that's not to take anything away from the cool moves they highlight. If they happened in live sports, I'd want to see them again too.The most enjoyable part of 'Ong Bak' aside from the martial arts is that the creativity is not limited to the fight choreography. Scenes like the street chase or the Thai taxi bikes chase make the film something that can be enjoyed by more than just martial arts connoisseurs.And everyone who watches 'Ong Bak' will walk away from the screen completely in awe of Tony Jaa. He's the kind of talent playing the kind of character that's impossible not to love.~Steven CThanks for reading! Visit moviemusereviews.com

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | I think critics have missed another point from this wonderful film. Not only is their the visual displays, which is only scratching the surface of what this movie offers, it also gives a lot of philosophical and theoretical insight to modern society and how globalisation is affecting south east Asian culture. Ong Bak is no Bruce Lee movie which is abundant with spiritual offerings, but it does focus on how sacredness is becoming a thing of the past. It points out that Asian civilisations which have managed to keep the western influence at bay for so long, are beginning to crack. Dilaogue such as 'American freestyle!' from one of the fist fighters who goes on to comment that many Thai females go over to America for prostitution, refers to the American free market and symbolises the darker side of the American dream. Also, with the use of needles and drugs, which the last fighter uses with abundance, shows that mechanical religion such as drugs and technology are replacing spirituality, as one character says, 'I am god.' So to all of you so called 'Journalists' out there who can't be bothered to take an insight to movies such as these should stick to your Hollywood saccharine, leave movies like this to the people who want something meaningful behind the visual display. Praise to the writers of this movie, well done!

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | I'll start out by admitting that I'm no expert in martial arts movies. But I have seen enough to know whether someone is mediocre, good or in Tony Jaa's case, amazing.The plot outline tells you well enough what the movie is about. Tony Jaa is off to retrieve a statue head. In all honesty, the plot is superfluous as the movie is basically a tribute to Jaa's skills. There are several stand out scenes. The first is a sequence where Jaa is being chased through a city on foot   no man will be able to watch it without wincing. The second is a sequence in a gambling den. The third is the final fight.But what really sets this movie apart is that it was all done for real. No computer effects, no wire work. It was all really done. The first is that in the aforementioned chase sequence several of the more impressive moves are shown again from a different camera angle. text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 8/10 | Explosive, authentic, and adrenaline charged, Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior redefined martial arts cinema by introducing the world to the breathtaking power of Muay Thai.Directed by Prachya Pinkaew, the film follows Ting (Tony Jaa), a young villager who journeys to Bangkok to recover the stolen head of a sacred Buddha statue. What begins as a mission of cultural and spiritual duty quickly transforms into a relentless showcase of martial arts prowess, as Ting faces underground fight clubs, criminal gangs, and corrupt forces.The film's greatest triumph is its physical authenticity. Rejecting wires, CGI, and heavy editing, Tony Jaa delivers jaw dropping stunts and bone crunching techniques that highlight the raw intensity of Muay Thai. From street chases to brutal arena fights, every sequence emphasizes agility, precision, and sheer physical endurance. The cinematography amplifies the action with fluid camerawork, ensuring audiences feel every impact.Yet, outside the action, the film is narratively thin. The plot is straightforward and sometimes predictable, functioning more as a vehicle for set pieces than as a fully fleshed out story. Supporting characters often fall into stereotypes, and emotional depth is secondary to spectacle. Still, the cultural significance of reclaiming the Buddha's head provides resonance beyond the brawls.Ultimately, Ong Bak is less about complex storytelling and more about raw cinematic energy. It propelled Thai action cinema into the global spotlight, cementing Tony Jaa as an international star of martial arts.    A groundbreaking action film that sacrifices narrative depth for physical authenticity, delivering unforgettable fight sequences that remain genre defining.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | I saw this movie recently at the Acadamy Theater in Pasadena, California. I was feeling a little under the weather at the time. There were about 20 other people in the theater, including my five year old daughter who I brought with me despite my concerns about the R rating.Suffice it to say that about thirty minutes into the movie the entire audience was enthralled and energized by this stone cold classic for eternity. My health had returned, I was completely revitalized. This movie rouses large doses of epinephrine, and succeeds on every level. I'm not a huge martial arts expert like many of the reviewers, but I was a kid in the late 60's when Bruce Lee (and Jimi Hendrix) ruled the world, and rightly so. This is the only fighting movie which I've seen since which even comes close to one of the better Bruce Lee movies. I will even contend, with some reservation, that it surpasses the Bruce Lee classics: there is humor, dramatic and sophisticated tuk tuk chase scenes, foot chase scenes, splendidly convincing archaeological sights, and obviously, absolutely SAVAGE multiple fight scenes where good defeats evil with satisfying Dirty Harry righteousness. This movie delivers the goods.Even the soundtrack is pretty good, with a pulsating type synthetic music which builds the suspense.Having been to Thailand several times and loving that country, I was very happy that this movie pays such a fitting tribute to their culture, the Thai kick boxing sport (which is HUGE in Thailand and big here in the US also), as well as the gentle and happy demeanor of their people.I should mention that by the end of the movie I had nothing but pleasure in having had my daughter watch the movie and share this unique experience. Goodness prevails over evil. Bad guys die a deserved death. Disciplined boy saves his village through courage, honor,persistence and skill. Wayward soul (Ting's cousin who has gambling debts) is reminded of his roots through observing integrity of his friend, and he finds redemption through his efforts at becoming a good guy again. Boy returns to village having honored his family and completed the mission...I'm afraid Sesame Street really would not have much a much better lesson to teach.This movie will become more famous as time goes on and people outside of the martial arts community learn about it. I left the theater stunned and enthralled. Just awesome.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | I'm a kung fu fan. I adore Hong Kong cinema. I have about sixty Jackie Chan films. In the last ten years, however, I have become completely disillusioned with Jackie Chan's efforts. Films like The Medallion and The Tuxedo have been close to appalling. The reason for these pitiful films can only be attributed to Chan's aging body, and his once minimalistic use of wires and CGI have now become his mainstay.Then, my best friend, lent me Ong Bak. He told me to watch it. He said it was good. He was wrong...it was better than good. It's a liability to Chan's dominance.I was skeptical about watching a Thai film, as opposed to a Hong Kong film, because my own preconceptions led me to think Thai cinema was extremely poor by comparison. How wrong I was.The action in this film is incredible. There is no wirework. There is no CGI. At a time where it would have been easy to use wires or computerised stunts, the makers of this film have stuck to their guns and said, 'we can make greatness on our own.' Kudos goes to them for making this decision, and they deserve a big pat on the back for pulling it off too.The undoubted start of this film is Tony Jaa. He is a truly talented martial artist, with the skills of a master, and the face of a leading man. He is a superstar who really has made a name for himself with this film. Some of the moves he pulls off in this film defy belief in much the same way Jackie Chan used to.Overall, the stunts, fighting and storyline are enough to keep anyone hooked   not just fight fans. The makers have announced that Thai cinema has something to offer, and Tony Jaa has announced that there is a new king of film fighters, and he is it.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | What is there to be said? This film was recommended to me on a UK based message board and with some apprehension, I rented it from Blockbuster, sat back and watched it.To say I spent most of the film with my mouth wide open, gawping at the amazingly fast, yet perfectly choreographed fighting scenes would be an understatement. I was simply blown away by the masterpiece that never let up.As with many 'kung fu' films, the background plot is a little thin, but it doesn't matter one bit. The story follows a young orphan by the name of Ting (Tony Jaa), who awaiting his chance to be ordained as a monk, volunteers his finely honed Muay Thai fighting abilities when the head of the village's revered Bhudda statue, 'Ong Bak' is stolen by a thief with strong links to the Bangkok criminal underworld and heads off to retrieve it. In Bangkok, it soon becomes clear that there are few people he can trust, even his own cousin who had assumed a new identity, a penchant for gambling but who had found himself at the mercy of criminals over unpaid debts.Whilst the story is weak, the action on screen certainly is not. You certainly pay little attention to the story as a whole, because much of it is somewhat disjointed but it's provided as a backdrop to what this film's really about. This is a proper raw blood and guts martial arts film. The injuries seem real (they probably are), the fighting moves are pulled off flawlessly in what seems to be a single take and the atmospheric setting of Bangkok's criminal underworld is matched by some seriously gritty and seedy locations that continue throughout to give Ong Bak it's dark edge. The action happens so fast at times that slow motion replays are shown from different angles to show off Tony Jaa's skills to full effect, and there are no stunt doubles.This is definitely a film to watch. If you're a big fan of Jackie Chan or Jet Li, you owe it to yourself to watch this too. Tony Jaa's abilities are right up there with the best of them, and it's a shame that Ong Bak received virtually no coverage at all here in the UK. If there was one criticism I had with Ong Bak, then it was because at 108 minutes, it simply felt too short.Strongly recommended.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | Twenty five years ago, I saw some Muay Thai live in it's motherland, both men's fights and   breaking with the tradition   women's fights. Both were of the fiercest kind I've seen, in comparison with any other combat sport. Ong bak is certainly a film produced with an eye on export sales, but if it had not been tampered with   in music or dubbed dialogues   one would also have a small treaty on Thai traditional values of family bonds, loyalty, justified back stepping from 'new urban values' (such as illicit games, drug abuse, stealing). If shouldn't miss the fundamental opening scene, in which the village's young men, some thirty of them, fight against a huge tree and each other to gain a simple yellow scarf. Because those blows and heavy falls from about a first or even a second floor balcony, are conducted in an open air location (marvellous set, too) and the grass is not fluffy enough to absorb the pain those guys took, besides hitting their bodies on the tree trunks, on their way down. The scene is intriguing for us Westerners, who do not know a thing about Thai culture   but then the following scene explains it all. Bravery is then a part of Ting's personality, embedded since a tender age. But so is respect for the village's religious belief, and the respect of elders. Eventually, the film narrates two stories   that of Ting, in a search for the robbed head of a Buddha statue (because there is always a fence for robbed art somewhere in OUR urban culture)   and the story of Humlee aka George, a fellow man who forgot his duty towards the Nong Pradu people, and now lives out a sordid life in the big town. The closing scene is the return to the small village, with the triumph of folklore and positive values.I saw this film in its theatrical release in Europe, and now again in «For Thai Only. Not For Export' Region 9 DVD by Bad Ram Ewec, in anamorphic widescreen but Dolby digital surround sound, Thai language only of course. I regret the loss of light in this version from the theatrical one, but the original Thai soundtrack is better, more to the point in underlining scenes than the so called French (Luc Besson) or UK versions. I had no problems watching this DVD on a multi system player, and I'm sure I will come back to it at least once a year. Even without subtitles, it's one of the best in my collection.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | Absolutely superb   the fight scenes are truly awesome; one of the best martial arts films around, and of particular interest to me as a Muay Thai enthusiast.The action scenes are well put together and some of the moves performed make you laugh with surprise as they awe inspire you.I hadn't read much about the film or the star before seeing Ong Bak, and hadn't seen any online clips, but seeing the film at the cinema today blew me away and I look forward to more films with Tony in.Muay Boran (traditional Muay Thai) has also been used in the fighting routines, as Muay Thai is the ring sport art/style of fighting, and is much more basic with very few 'fancy moves'.Muay Boran is the old style, developed for the Thais to fight the Burmese in historical wars, being much more deadly than Muay Thai, and is taught to the Thai military and police, also involving fighting off multiple attackers, as is common place in Thailand street fights, which the star of this film displays very well indeed.Krabi Krabong   Thai weapons fighting, is also shown, to great effect, and it's great to see weapons fighting done so well too.Overall, an outstanding Thai martial arts film   highly recommended!

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | I have seen several dozen Martial Arts films during the fifteen years I have spent on this world. I have seen Jet Li's best, Jackie Chan's worst and almost everything in between. And I must say, Ong Bak, quite simply blows them all out the water. True it doesn't have much of a storyline however it quite simply boasts some of the most realistic, incredible and brutal fight scenes I have ever seen. Time Magazine has boasted that Tony Jaa is the long awaited answer to Bruce Lee and Jackie Chan. I can gladly say that, that comment is without hyperbole. Muay Thai (Tony Jaa's Fighting Style) employs elements of both Jet Li's Graceful Shaolin schooled Kung Fu and the sheer devastating Brutality of Bruce Lee's Jeet Kun Do. The incredible athletic skill displayed throughout the movie by Jaa is completely natural, with the films tag line: 'No wires, no computer graphics, no equal' ringing true. In summary, if you consider yourself a martial arts lover, or action movie buff, you simply cannot afford to pass up Ong Bak.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | When I was very small and TV was making its first entrance into my life, the national network aired Bruce Lee's Enter the Dragon. And it made grown ups stand straight, talk curtly, smile coyly and gym regularly. The camera swooped down over the tree. The tree sequence began. And I was hooked line, sinker and everything attached. If any movie comes close to deserving the title 'Enter the NEW Dragon', it is this.The story didn't matter. It was good enough to string all the action together. The acting didn't matter either. What Tony Jaa lacked in silent charisma, he made up for in jaw dropping graceful action sequences. What the script lacked was made up for by an able director employing a commendable and refreshing use of the camera in an action movie without special effects (though the repeated shots tend to get a bit tedious at times).The film is a celebration of Muay Thai. The fight sequences are pure magic. And there are enough fight sequences. This movie is sex for the old school martial arts street fighting movie fan.And though this will never be the revolution that Enter the Dragon was, it may make you gape just like you did that first time you saw Lee throw a punch.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 10/10 | I'm not exaggerating   This has been the action/fighting movie I've wanted to see all my life. It puts to shame any Hollywood action movie you can name. Also no Jackie Chan nor Jet Li movie can hold a candle to it. If there were only one film I'm allowed to see in these last 3 years, ONG BAK has to be it!I give this movie . text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | This movie shows the martial art known as Muay Thai. From what I've heard it is a feared fighting style...it even scares off practitioners of the better known styles, if they are faced with it. The fights are highly choreographed here...hyper real...superior to what you see in movies like The Matrix. Just looking at some of the fight scenes in this it looks really dangerous to try and stop some of the Muay Thai moves...you'd just be better off getting the Hell out of the way!Anyway, the plot...Ting (Tony Jaa)lives in peasant village. A religious artifact (Ong Bak)is stolen from the village and Ting volunteers to retrieve for the devastated locals. His search brings him to big smoke where he moves in a murky underworld where underground fights are staged for gambling purposes. It's here where Ting gets to test out his fighting skills beyond the shadow play he has been engaging in in his village.There is an element of nationalism in this movie...Muay Thai is pitted against various other martial arts and this is meant to reflect positively on their nation...various other nations are the fall guys. For instance, Ting has to face an ugly Australian...I think it is Big Bear (played by Nick Kara). He is a particular odious character who says some nasty things...no doubt he would push all the wrong buttons with a home grown audience. I'm guessing that Big Bear would represent Thai pay back for all that sex tourism engaged in by Australians visiting their country.Speaking of Australians (of which I'm one), Ting has a side kick in Muay Lek (played by Pumwaree Yodkamol). No, she's not Australian, but she just strikes me as being the Thai equivalent of an 'ocker sheila'!This is a genuinely funny movie movie at times, with some moments right out of a Warner Brothers cartoon.Recommendations: Kung Fu shuffle   a Chinese movie which is pitched more as a comedy than Ong Bak and which consequently takes its cartoon elements to an absurd extreme. Highly recommended. This movie may just be known as 'Kung fu' in places outside of Australia.Hmm...I have vague memories of enjoying some of the Bruce Lee's later movies...they were more serious than these movies...examples might be 'Enter the dragon' and 'Game of death'.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | When you step into a comedy film you expect to laugh. When you step into a horror film you expect to pee the floor in fear. When you step into an Asian subtitled martial arts action film with the tag line 'No stunt doubles, no computer images, no strings attached' you expect to be dazzled with high flying hard hitting Muay Thai acrobatics. It's really all about expectations.The success of this kind of movie lies in 2 simple goals: butt kicking action and more butt kicking action. If there's some tertiary reason to tie together the series of otherwise pointless fight scenes then really, it's like finding money. In that regard Ong Bak should win some kind of award. Perhaps a gold plated miniature statue of a guy savagely kneeing another guy in the jaw. We'd could call it a 'Kicky'.Ong Bak is the story of Ting, a young monk to be, pursuing the evil men who stole the head from their beloved Buddha. He journeys take him from his small rural village to Bangkok, picking up a couple of sidekicks, Humlae and Muay Lek, the bumbling idiot and the girl. Hey I didn't say it was a great plot but it's more plausible, if not more interesting, than your average Jacky Chan movie. Obviously this just gives our hero an excuse to show off his nearly super human martial art talents.I thoroughly enjoyed Tony Ja's incredible athleticism, acrobatic grace and seeming disregard for personal pain. He literally requires no strings as he runs up walls, leaps over cars, slides under SUVs, and flips and somersaults his way through Bangkok. We're treated these talents in an inventive foot chase and bizarre mototaxi scenes set to a mildly pounding Matrix ish techno dance soundtrack. Couple that with his sensational Muay Thai martial arts skill and you have an 'international action superstar'! If you're at all impressed with exotic martial arts action then you'll be giddy with delight as our hero Ting pounds his opponents with an assortment of brutal elbow smashes, fierce face kicks and vicious knee attacks. Speaking of opponents, I much prefer the prolonged 1 on 1 fight scenes over the stream of nameless bad guys falling all over themselves and getting their heads smashed in by the hero scenes. I'm sure the nameless guys are very nice if you got to know them, they probably have families, wives and children. But the 1 on 1 fights appeal to that primal man versus man instinct that resides within all males. Mind you I was eating a bucket of popcorn and sucking down a soft drink at the time but I could definitely identify. And with Ting we have 1 on 1 man versus man fight scenes in the spades. Mere words cannot describe the prowess that Ja displays and the inhuman blows his opponents suffer at his hands, errr elbows.The gripes are few but I'll say them anyways. The Thai language is definitely not sexy or macho. OK I said it. It's a rich and beautiful culture but something about the high pitched and speedy dialog delivery does not jive with my North American bias of slow talking, deep voiced heroes saying pithy punchlines like 'I'll be back' or 'You've been terminated'. That and the female sidekick is pretty useless and annoying with her even higher pitched voice and faster dialog. Ugh and when she has her 'oh no someone important to me has died' scene she kicks it into overdrive with the crying and sobbing.Other than that though, if you're into visceral martial arts action then you owe it to yourself to give yourself a full dosage of a Flying Ong Bak Attack. If you're looking for an Asian version of the English Patient with a side of Muay Thai, I'm afraid you should move along.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | This is definitely one of the best action flick that Southeast Asia has produced in a very long time. text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | Let's get one thing straight here, if you come into 'Ong Bak' hoping for incredible acting, a mature and original plot and innovative new film making techniques, you're watching the wrong film. However, if you want to see a phenomenal martial arts display and some of the most eye popping, brutal fight scenes caught on camera in recent memory, this will be right up your street.Ong Bak introduces the world to Tony Jaa, an agile and highly talented kick boxing expert and the film quite rightly revolves around him. He may not have the natural charisma of Bruce Lee, or the impossible to dislike everyman charm of Jackie Chan, but boy can he fight. It takes a little while for him to actually get around to showcasing his abilities, but when he does there will be jaws on the floor all round.Consider for example the athletic prowess he demonstrates during a chase scene: he sprints through streets pursued by an army of thugs, pirouetting and gliding over, under and around all obstacles in his path, at one point leaping feet first through a ring of barb wire. Not because he has to you understand, simply because he can. And if you're impressed when he's running away from fights, you'll absolutely love it when he finally gets stuck in.His moves are fluid and graceful, but delivered with devastating effect. The ultra light stylings of Crouching Tiger...and it's ilk are replaced with bone crushing violence as we see every knee and elbow strike hitting home. Jaa's skill and stamina seem almost limitless and he goes through opponent after opponent in rapid succession with such power it'd make Bruce Lee envious were the man still around to see it. One of the early brawls Jaa engages in is a bar fight where he takes on three rival fighters one after the other, each with a different fighting style he must adapt to and ends up destroying nearly the entire club in the process. In this writer's humble opinion, this particular example is one of the best martial arts fight scenes ever committed to film.That isn't to say Ong Bak is entirely one dimensional. With it's storyline of a young monk searching for a missing Buddha statue's head, it's possible to read an underlying issue regarding the loss of religious faith in modern Thai culture. This is painted by the startling juxtaposition of Jaa's quiet and peaceful country village against the violent, sprawling metropolis of the capital city. That said, such a reading might be taking things too far and detract from enjoying this film simply for what it is meant to be; a stunning showcase of action set pieces for arguably the most talented new actor in action cinema today.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | We'll take care of the story early on. Ting (Tony Jaa), a monk in training, is sent to the 'big city' to recover the stolen head of his village's sacred Buddha statue   Ong Bak. Of course along the way, he is taken advantage of in the big city (fish out of water theme) and meets some bad dudes. Thats it. Nothing overly original, thought provoking or filled with twists and turns. This is not where the movie's strengths come from.This movie is simply a demonstration of Tony Jaa's abilities. As that, its simply amazing. The opening scene of the movie is just an indication of what we are going to see. A giant tree is the setting. Dozens of men climbing the tree, all trying to reach the yellow sash and bring it back to the ground. It is dirty, grimy and the action looks quite authentic.Ting travels to the big city and meets a parasite of a person who came from his village (George) and his highly underage female scam partner (Muay). It's all quite dull until the fight club scenes. This is the introduction to Ting's nemesis, Voicebox wheelchair dude. The bad guy talks through a voice box and smokes through a hole in his neck. I'm not sure about anyone else, but I laughed the first time he pulled out the voice box and didn't stop until he did (in the last 5 minutes he stops using the voice box). My favorite is his 'laugh'. He is suppose to be evil, but comes off way too comical.There is also a chase scene throughout the city, which has some comic elements and an opportunity to show off Tony's athletic abilities (jumps, splits, etc).Ting's second trip to 'fight club' is the queue for the non stop action to come. Here he fights a long, haired lecherous Aussie, Bruce Lee wannabe with an afro and 'Mad Dog'. All the fight scenes just make one want to cry out. You can see the hits, the dust, and practically feel the pain. Also the inclusion of slow motions shots and alternate shots help to maximize the viewing time. This isn't a Steven Seagal movie with fast cuts such that we aren't given time to examine the blows. The director is laying out the evidence right in front of us, to show us how authentic it is. He wants to make sure we got to see it all. There rest of the movie is rather predictable and only provides more opportunity for Tony to do his thing. There are numerous problems with the movie. First of all, the acting is quite atrocious, especially George and Muay. Muay's voice is quite annoying. I had given up that I could not strangle her (due to the fact that this was a movie),so I had the urge to pop my own ear drums. George's voice wasn't much better, either. Tony's acting is quite stiff and labored. He has one look for the whole range of human emotions. That could be said for most of the actors. The only emotion that were depicted properly was pain.The Tuk Tuk chase scene couldn't have been more boring. After seeing the chase scenes from Bullit, watching a three wheeled moped cab with seats race around, was like watching flies have sex. I was curious as to why the director added slow motion to some of the scenes. I thought the whole chase scene was in slow motion.George is a scumbag with a heart of gold. I mean how many times do you have to be deceived by a person before you stop believing them ?? Apparently not enough. The discovery of voice box's plot was oh so contrived and coincidental. With those odds, Tony should have probably gone and played some craps. The fact that voice box completely stops using his device at the end is quite lame. Did the director run out of batteries ? I am a big fan of this movie. I have said my peace to those elements that I thought were misplayed. At the same time, I think this movie is great for what it is : a no nonsense, bone breaking, knee to the chest, elbow to the head action movie that dispenses with the plot. Tony Jaa is amazing and I can't wait to see what he does next.I saw this movie in the theater, on a nice 5.1 audio system and through TV speakers. This movie needs a nice set of speakers (and a sub woofer) to get the full impact of the hits. TV standard speakers aren't going to do it. If you empathize with people and characters, I suggest you check with a physician before watching this movie. For everyone else and fans of actions movies, this movie is a must see.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | No wires. No people flying about in trees. No guys picking up CGI motorbikes and throwing them. Boy did the late 90s bludgeon the martial arts film genre into complete mediocrity. Part of the reason of why this film film is so important is purely that it puts the focus back on REAL stunts rather than CGI and wire work and is all the better for it. Of course there is a place for Crouching Tiger Hidden Dragon, Hero etc. as well as The Matrix Tilogy and such, but where had all the real martial arts fighting gone? Thailand. That's where the juggernaut known as Ong Bak exploded from in 2003. The plot is a pretty stereotypical plot   a small Thai village have the head of their Buddhist idol Ong Bak stolen. Ting is the village golden boy, and is very good at Muay Thai fighting, though naturally he must never use it. He gets sent to the city to find the head of Ong Bak with the help of a man who left the village many years ago. What follows is a great contrast between the 'country boy' Ting and the city folk, which gives the film an interesting subtext. In the country Ting would have probably worked the land all day and prayed, here, in the city, he is confronted by gangsters, gamblers and underground fighters all in the way to get back Ong Bak's head. Once Ting eventually gets dragged into fighting the film gets going with a barrage of action that only rarely lets up when the plot needs to advance a bit further. One of these scenes in particular was quite harrowing to watch. That pretty much sums up Ong Bak, breaking the rules, breaking the mould, breaking tables, chairs, windows, fridges and just about everything else too.

text: Movie: Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior (2003) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 7.2/10 | Rating: 7.2/10 | I saw this at an IFP screening at the Arclight in Hollywood. The running chase scenes had the bad guys waving their arms and grumbling like a dumb comedy. That silliness is more than made up by the tricks done by Jaa to get away from them.
