text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | The plot of Tony Jaa's first big movie, Ong Bak, was insanely simple: sacred statue stolen and taken to the big city, rural martial arts master goes to retrieve it, kicks butt along the way. The plot of his new film is pretty much identical, except for the statue is now a baby elephant and his mother. So one has to wonder what's with all the unfollowable subplots that happen once Jaa is in the city (Sydney, in this case). Part of the confusion probably has to do with the half hour cut by good ol' Harvey 'Scissorhands' Weinstein, but the extra plots do seem unnecessary. Then again, it doesn't really matter. When Jaa starts his special brand of butt kicking, the movie's a ball. Silly, but a lot of fun (though not nearly as fun as Ong Bak, so if you didn't like that one, go ahead and avoid this one). As many complaints as I had throughout the picture, it won me over for a couple of its fight scenes, most notably the four minute super take in which Jaa ascends several flights of stairs, wasting whoever gets in his way (think of it as Children of Men with karate!). And then there's this scene where he snaps the bones of about a hundred henchmen in a row. But nothing will prepare you for this one moment during the climactic fight. I won't spoil it for you, but I'm not kidding when I say it's the single greatest 'I can't believe they did that!' moment I've ever seen. It had me and two of my buddies laughing for several minutes afterward. We had to pause it and wait for our tears to dry. Then we couldn't resist rewinding it and watching it again. And then the movie ended, and we watched the scene in question again, and again and again, and then again in slow motion, and then again with the 'Step' button, examining it a frame at a time. So, yes, the movie is actually kind of crappy, but it's well worth seeing.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | My first experience with Tony Jaa was with Ong Bak, was with many. It is an amazing movie, flowing with one action scene after another. It was a well put together movie, fight scenes were The plot was pretty much identical to Ong Bak, with an elephant instead of a statue head, stolen by a gang and poor tony having to fight lots of people to get it back. Even his sidekick in the movie is the same actor. I wouldn't say this is a huge issue, but a little bit of originality for the fans would have been nice. Overall there are tonnes of clichés, such as the bad guys girl helping the good guy, the evil villain that dresses in black (as well as all the henchmen).Acting quality is BAD. Aside from the 2 main characters, the talent is no better than a very bad B movie. This makes it hard to feel anything for or against the characters. Tony Jaa is pretty good though, when given the chance, which doesn't happen much as there is hardly any interaction with anyone other than the elephant There was a sense of poor direction as some scenes seem to be completely irrelevant. There are several scenes in the movie which change nothing in the story, and should have been cut. You may find yourself thinking, for example someone escaping, only to be captured 5 minutes later. What was the point of the whole thing? The fight scenes tend to be a bit hit and miss. Some are absolutely excellent, but others seem to be rather poorly choreographed. For example on several occasions I spotted a few 'hits' which were a bit too far off from causing any damage. Also a lot of henchman fell a bit easily, and the fights did someones go on too long, that they made Tony Jaa look like a novice. Its a shame as Tony Jaa can really kick a$$. Still I did gasp at a few of the amazing moves he pulls off.Tony Jaa reminds me a lot of Jet Li in earlier movies; awful scripts but he carries it off. He may be the one to replace Jet Li in future martial arts epics, seeing as Jet Li as said he will not be doing anymore.Overall the movie seemed like some well thought of fight scenes, not so well choreographed, stuck together with a poor plot, bad direction and poor acting. Its only worth watching the fight scenes to spot the odd amazing move. The movie is like a chocolate cake that is too crumbly and soggy to eat and just doesn't taste chocolaty enough, except for the chocolate buttons place on top which are lovely.I'm glad I rented it, as I wouldn't recommend to buy.Alternatively, get Ong Bak, which is a lot better pulled off, and keep an eye on Tony Jaa's future movies.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 6.5/10 | While more humorous than Ong Bak at times, Tony Jaa's impressive agility and athleticism grows less impressive this time out   and this is more than simply having seen it all before (and any fan of Jackie Chan   who makes a humorous cameo here   and Jet Li will have seen it all before) but also a lack of anything to back up the fancy stunts and raw fighting prowess.The simple problem with Tony Jaa is that he has the shiny film martial arts stardom down pat, but he has absolutely no charisma. One thing that all of the action and martial arts superstars to come from China and Hong Kong have in common is that element of charisma   be it Jackie Chan's buddy next door act or Jet Li's handsome hero, Lau Ching Wan's 'my father the cop', Shieu Shek's rock star or Chow Yun Fat's tragic hero   they all really make you cheer for them, and draw you into their character. This Thai warrior needs a major lesson in on screen performance  all he does is show off his Mui Tai skills, which can carry a film only so far.I'm all for Tony Jaa breaking into the realm of martial arts stardom, but only when (and if) he can step up and bring us an actual PERFORMANCE first... .

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | If you enjoy watching martial art films, Tom yum goong will blow you away. It is alittle slow in the beginning but once Tony Jaa starts his mission, all hell breaks loose. The story, in short, is about a boy trying to rescue his pets, 2 Elephants, which was kidnapped and transferred to Austrailia at a restaurant called Tom Yum Goong.Tony Jaa shows you an array of martial art techniques used in Muay (Moo way) Thai and how his style competes against other fighting styles. He battles styles such as Wushoo (kicking style), Capoeria, Chinese Sword fighting and yes, even Wrestling. This movie will have your jaw dropped when you see how Tony Jaa adjusts and changes his style to defeat his enemies. But, he displays a style never before since on film which is so brutal, words cannot express it.Some Cons to the movie is that some of the cuts scenes could be edited better and there is a good amount talking. The ending could be done more better but how much can you expect from a foreign film. The stunts are incredible, sound effects awesome, and creative camera angles are superb. This movie will leave you gasping for air and exhausted but only wanting more. TYG has definitely raised the level of martial art films today. Check it out.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | I love this actor and I hope the best for him. His martial arts are astounding and I love Thai Boxing and it's kind of sad to see the Thai Boxing fade here and the Jet Li path start to be aped.That's what this movie brings to the table. Some of the same actors you saw in the far superior and mesmerizing ONG BAK are here again in a movie full of Thai talent making sad awkward attempts at reaching an American audience. What's sad is to see talented Thais seemingly desperate for American appeal participating in hackneyed movie scenes that integrate Australians with Thai in a pointed stab at trying to reach American audiences while staying on budget.Well  the 80's brought us gay Australian bands that we are ashamed to admit we liked and this movie is something along the same line. There's nothing really great here in a movie but you want to like it because the of the simple raw heart of the lead actor. Unfortunately, it still falls apart halfway through when it becomes obvious that we are neck high in gay Australians that can't act and watching a Thai boxer do less Thai and more Jet Li and as such, make a fool of himself in the process  I say stick to what you know. What I say  keep it raw, keep it real forget the Australians with don Johnson shadow, lip gloss and the most unconvincing tough guys ever.Ong Bak was so much better and even that was a Thai sellout halfway through in a desperate awkward grab to hit an American audience. This movie could have been a blockbuster in 1983. Today, it's just kind of sad  but really incredible technique in the acrobatics and the martial arts  they don't skimp there! The Thai boxing vs capoirea scene is especially gratifying but then quickly degrades into that sad dimension of 1980's effeminate Australian henchmen/ladymen.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | If you're someone who thrives on well choreographed fight scenes with attention to detail and gasp inducing elements, then I can recommend this movie. The filmography was very beautiful in parts, but sometimes the camera work was at a bad angle to show exactly what was going on.There's a definite animal theme in the movie, from the animals themselves, to jewelry, to statues, to sounds. This lends more of a cohesiveness to the film as it lacks it as far as trying to introduce plot points and transitioning to different scenes  a little choppy and not very seamless. Normally, I don't see a lack of comic relief as a problem, but this movie could have taken itself a little less seriously. That's a minor complaint, however.Tony Jaa is amazing as always, and gets to stretch a little of his acting muscles as well. Unfortunately, while some of the movie is in Thai with subtitles, most of the dialogue by whites is dubbed over, along with Petchtai Wongkamlao's dialogue (Humlae/George in Ong Bak). It was extremely disappointing to have dubbing, which is worsened by the fact that it's not even very good.Jaa's relationship with the elephants is touching, and it's wonderful to see another large Buddha statue  a sure sign of Jaa's spirituality. Most of the fight scenes are incredible (martial arts fans, rejoice), and the continuous shot as Jaa makes his way up four stories is worth seeing.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | Ong Bak was an extraordinary film in many ways, not being the least was the audiences' discovery of the incredible fighting presence of Tony Jaa. For the older members of the audience it was like the great Bruce Lee and Shaw Bros. films had combined and come back in the body of Jaa. There's a lot to live up to after that.Clearly Jaa is paying tribute to the movie greats he looks up to. In his first film, Bruce Lee was the obvious object of respect. Here, Jacky Chan is give some reverence, to the point that a look a like makes it seem that Chan did a walk on. A lot of the 1990's Hong Kong action film style is imitated as well. If you like this era of film making then this film is especially for you, if not well... the logic holes and the frequent cartoonish action turned me off. For me, the greatness of Ong Bak was seeing the clear influences melded into an updated style with a strong individuality of it own. The Protector seems to be more of an outright imitation down to the insane stunts with stunt men doing some absolutely crazy things.That's not to say that this film doesn't have some remarkable moments. The single take fight in the giant restaurant is a standout. The scene with the capoeira fighter is excellent as well. It's a fun film but I hope that Jaa's next film tries to blaze a new path instead of taking a well worn road.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | Tony Jaa, or whatever his name is, has reached his ceiling. Watching this movie, I got the sneaking suspicion I had already witnessed the sum total of his talents in 'Ong Bak,' and so there was nothing left for me to see in this movie except more bad guys being thrown off tall things. The lights came up and I walked out of the theater, and I realized that this is not quite so.The problem is not with Tony Jaa, who actually has no ceiling. The problem is director Prachya Pinkaew, who indeed used up all of HIS talents on his previous film. In 'Ong Bak,' Pinkaew told a coherent story with a beginning, middle, and end, with a minimum of continuity errors and several interesting characters. All of these things are missing in 'The Protector,' where it seems Pinkaew is trying to show off his many creative talents, and prove himself to be a 'serious filmmaker.' Unfortunately, he has no creative talents, and shows all the dramatic range of a bad student director.First rule of making a martial arts film: each martial arts sequence must be more impressive and exciting than the one before it. The instant an action sequence underperforms the previous one, the audience gets bored. Pinkaew, struggling to keep up, never got this memo.I should have realized there were problems when a friend asked me, pre movie, what 'The Protector' was about, and I realized I didn't know. Guess what he turned out to be protecting? Elephants. Seriously. That's the plot. He's got to fly from Thailand to Australia to rescue a baby elephant and its living parent (I was never clear on the gender of the living one). The elephants were stolen by the criminal underworld, who wants to do you really care? Does anyone? The first martial arts sequence is probably 20 minutes into the film, and it's the best bit in the movie, with Jaa literally flying onto the screen onto a half dozen gangsters. The ensuing fight is immediately followed by a boat chase that comes out of nowhere a boat chase which is poorly shot, edited, conceived... you name it. It climaxes with Jaa turning his boat sideways, so one of the chasing boats can hit him, catch air, and impact a helicopter (also out of nowhere), and the two can explode in the worst edit/CGI combo since the last time you saw a Sci Fi Channel Original Movie.Later there's a fight in a warehouse: Tony vs. the BMX bandits. The editing and pacing is such he's trying to emulate Jackie Chan, but leaving his own mark on it (he run up a plate glass window seconds before a 4 wheeler crashes through it. Why the 4 wheeler would go full speed toward a plate glass window, or why a plate glass window would be on the 2nd story of a warehouse, is beyond me). Jaa mostly succeeds, but the camera work was so bad I felt like I missed half the choreography. And suddenly the fight was over.Most notable, if you've heard anything of the movie at all, is the 4 minute unedited sequence in the back room of a hotel (and when the characters call it a 'back room,' they apparently mean 'another 4 story hotel behind this first hotel.') Tony Jaa is marketed as a master of a martial art called 'Muay Thai,' and I learned what it looked like in 'Ong Bak.' Apparently the director didn't, because it is virtually non existent during this 4 minute scene. The film making is student film, at best; I kept waiting for the camera man (dutifully hanging back a few feet from Jaa) to bust out with a chainsaw for backup, a la 'Doom.' The final fight sequence of the movie isn't so much climactic as it is incredibly repetitive and boring. Tony breaks the arms or legs of 30 consecutive black clad bad guys, and by the 6th one, all the attacks started to look alike. Get on with it, already.'Ong Bak' was an action film, but if Jaa truly can run up walls, it's time for him to launch past that ceiling, and find himself a new creative team. 'The Protector,' story wise, seems to stop at country Thai philosophy, which would be fine, if his earlier film hadn't shown so much promise. 'Ong Bak' can enjoy multiple viewings, either for the story, or just skipping to the action. 'The Protector' shows you nothing you haven't seen before, and what's worse, makes it less interesting.Basically, if this is your first Tony Jaa experience, 'The Protector' is somewhat interesting. If you've seen 'Ong Bak,' then this film is unwatchable.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | Tony Jaa has already established himself as an up and coming action star and can hopefully recreate the lost brilliance of Asian martial arts pictures. However, if he is going to do this he is going to have to do a damn sight better than this attempt. Whilst being a good effort, I have some issues with Warrior King, first of all i am not that great a fan of Tony Jaa's style of fighting, it has that Bruce Lee esquire feel of invincibility, there is barely any hits received by our hero, this, for me makes the whole 50 bads guys pointless there is not this feeling of fear that our lead could be hurt. I'm also not a great admirer of the short nature of the fight sequences. Whilst Tony Jaa appears to have the ability to knock men down with one or two strikes i am much more a fan of the more balletic and rhythmic hong Kong style of hand to hand combat, but that is a personal preference.Secondly the editing of this film is in places horrendous with it making some of the fight sequences appear unnatural and causing a loss of fluidity of, and with the editing being a crucial part of any fight scene, i feel it is something that is going to have to be improved to maximise Mr. Jaa's action potential.Thirdly, i have a sneaking suspicion that Tony Jaa is only going to be a one trick pony, with there being not that much difference in choreography from his other films such as Ong Bak, giving his films a sense of 'seen it before', something that the greats like Jackie Chan and Sammo Hung always managed to avoid.However, for it's faults, Warrior King is beautifully shot with some stunning use of the camera and some amazing cinematography, with a special mention to the fight scene in the burning, flooded temple which is a visual orgasm! There is also nice use of slow motion in this film to demonstrate the full power of the punishment dished out, all though i do feel that slow mo was at times over used.The story, script and acting i won't mention because when sitting down to watch an Asian action movie you watch for the action and there is nothing notably different or outstanding in either the script, story or acting to really give it a mention.All in all, Warrior King is a stylishly shot Martial arts film with some good moments, but i feel it could've been improved by improving on the basics of action film making. So overall good, but not great.

There is even one long fight sequence that rivals Beatrix Kiddo's fight with the 'Crazy 88' in Kill Bill. You will be entertained, even if you don't tend to like martial arts movies. 10 out of 10

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 9/10 | If you're looking for great choreographed fight sequences, or just a fan of fighting movies, this does not disappoint. Most of the fight scenes are quite impressive. There were a bunch of scenes were I thought to myself, as did another reviewer, 'I don't care if you're a stunt man, that must hurt.' To me it seemed this movie had a lot more money backing it, than Ong Bak as well. If you thought OB looked like a 2 hour hand held backyard movie with great fighting, this is a step up. There are a couple special effects during the movie (green screen, cgi   can be though forgiven as this isn't Hollywood, its Thailand) but none of it is during the fighting. You're still watching Tony kick the crap out of people without strings, or computer graphics. They have a lot more sound effects of kicks and punches and bones breaking too. I thought there was a little to much though and ¾ through the movie I found it harder to believe the moves even though I know it was all real. It can be forgiven though seeing as this is the same director of Ong Bak and only his second movie. It just seemed like the same mentality as an eight year old that just learned how funny farting noises are. But you eventually can get used to it and forget it's there.Just like Ong Bak, you're not watching this movie for the plot you will be disappointed. Tony Jaa must leave his small village to get revenge of a bunch of people who stole an elephant. Not to degrade the story, they put a lot of emphasis on the first 20 minutes of the landscape and the relationships Thai have with elephants so much so that there aren't any fight scenes whatsoever. But it does help international audience I would think instead of fighting to bring back a sacred head. Visually there are some nice shots of Thailand in those scenes though.The same actor who played Dirty Balls in Ong Bak is here as well, in a lot more comedic and less annoying role. A lot of the actors here talk some English, which can be a little difficult to understand with their thick Thai accents though. There are a few cameos like the female lead from Ong Bak and a Jackie Chan look a like as well, which makes this film a little bit funnier.In my opinion, I like the production a little bit better than Ong Bak, and I was not disappointed in the fighting scenes. If I would rate it on the action alone I would give it a , but because of the reasons I stated above, I give it a 7/10.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | When I saw Ong Bak, I was truly impressed with the stunts and fight choreography. I have been looking forward to The Protector for quite a while as a result. The end result was good, but not great. There were a number of plot holes and overly convenient coincidences that made the story a bit painful. But like most people, I didn't want to see this movie for the plot.First off, I have to say I was amazed that I was the only one in the theater who seemed to recognize Jackie Chan in his cameo (in the Syndey Airport). Jackie Chan's influence on martial arts movies is clear in this work. Plenty of impromptu acrobatics to avoid attackers and group fight scenes.The main problem was it was a bit hard to see. The director chose to go with the grainy filming style(or maybe it was just a lower budget than I thought) which I find distracts greatly from what is on the screen. Basically everything looked really flat, which is bad for an action movie.The action scenes were pretty decent overall, although the group fight scene at the end kind of grew tedious (a bunch of henchmen run out, Ton Jaa fights each in turns breaking arms, or legs before moving on to the next one). The best fight scenes were when Tony Jaa fought the expert fights, particularly Johnny, and the Capoeria fighter.I know this reviews mainly pointed out the weak points of the movie, but that was because I had high expectations and was a bit disappointed. If you go in with a bit lower expectations, then you will have a lot more fun.

He continues the same great quality of fight scenes that he did in the Ong Bak trilogy, which was his career starter.The plot of the movie is fairly simple but you're not going to see this movie to see a plot that's going to win the screenwriter any academy awards. text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | First of all I wonder why the English title for this movie ended up as 'Warrior King' on the DVD, when the movie is titled 'Tom Yum goong' or 'The Protector'. But irregardless, the movie is entertaining. Do take into account that is it a very milked recipe; one man against countless scores of bad guys.Yeah, there are some similarities between 'Ong Bak' and 'The Protector', which were a bit weak plot wise and in originality.The story is about Kham, a peaceful guy tending to elephants, who has to go to Sydney in order to get his two beloved elephants as they have been stolen, but the road is full of obstacles and the opposition is bountiful.As for the action, well if you are familiar with Tony Jaa then you know what you will get, and he doesn't fail to deliver. text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | I bought Warrior King on DVD this morning in a double box set with Ong Bak and i'm glad i did, i never really thought about seeing a Tony Jaa movie before until a mate and i were watching Resident Evil: extinction and talking about how fit Milla Jovovich was and that she was quite good at fighting, gradually the conversation went into martial arts and i suggested he should watch 'Kiss of the Dragon' starring Jet Li when he said 'thats old school fighting you should watch Warrior King with Tony Jaa' and i was about to show him the meaning of 'old school fighting' when Milla started chopping up zombies with Gerka knives so i decided against it. I don't know much about Tony Jaa but being a martial arts fan and myself having studied in Akido,Kickboxing and Karate i know when someones got speed, agility and genuine skill and Jaa provides every thing whether its kicking grapples or elbows to the face he can move and i don't think iv'e ever seen someone do a back flip and kick a guy in the head without some form of help but he does all his stunts without wires and he is very good at what he does. text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | This film exhibits many fine points, and is much more interesting than the average martial arts movie. In past years, 90 percent of this movie type has come from Hong Kong, and has relied heavily on a predictable formula for its plot. From this perspective, this movie deserves much applause, because it tends to differ from the norm. Especially with the style of fighting that is presented here, very unique in that there have been precious few movies showcasing Muay Thai. The plot about missing elephants and revenge is quite believable considering the cultural origin of the idea, and the direction and editing is done with more sensitivity and engineering than most similar films. This strength is similarly enhanced and driven home by the incredible skill of Tony Jaa. He shows remarkable athleticism and agility.The inescapable flaws of this movie type, and specifically of this movie, relate to the direction and fight sequence choreography trying just a little bit too hard. In a real life fighting situation, where life and limb are truly at stake, it is unlikely that you would see so much flying through the air with the greatest of ease, or the constant screaming and yelling that permeates this movie from almost the beginning to end. Instead of Jaa using realistic Muay Thai fighting techniques, he is relegated to constantly being a flying and screaming showman. And to make matters worse, all of his adversaries are screaming equally as loud.It is likely that much of the audience that went to this movie did so expecting to see somewhat of a continuation of the first installment, Ong Bak. In that movie, it seems we saw just a little bit more authenticity. That authenticity sets both of these movies apart from the average Kung Fu installment, and the audience has the opportunity to see the difference between the two fighting styles.All in all, this is a fine martial arts vehicle, and a good one to see for fans of the genre.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | In truth, you should probably see this movie just for the action. Because it's really that cool. Every fight scene is as visceral as it is stylish, even the scenes where he's just smashing thugs. And the one on one fight scenes (even with the big guys that just threw things and the lady) are simply awesome. It's hands down some of the best fights I've seen in a while.But unfortunately, that's where the movie ends. What little plot it has is pretty much the exposition at the beginning, and after that there is practically no plot development. Stuff happens, Cam fights, goons run back to the Dragon Lady, Cam yells for his elephant (kinda like that episode of the Simpsons where Bart wins an elephant in a radio contest). Hell, they never even fully explain what the Dragon Boss Lady steals the elephant for, only vaguely referring to 'the power of the kings' that she wants. The history surrounding the Protector is interesting, but that's sparsely covered. The only real character connection is between Cam and the elephants. The fat buddy cop? I don't even remember his name. He was just there. The girl? Well, other than being a convenient (and hot) plot device, she was just there. And I guess the Dragon Lady was an OK villain, but other than that, the characters had no substance. The only reason you could connect to Cam was because he kicked ass and liked animals.All in all, look for the great action, try to ignore the flaws and the lax plot and character development.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 6/10 | What would you risk if the only family you had left was taken from you? The Protector (known in Thailand as Tom Yum Goong) delivers its answer through relentless action and the singular presence of Tony Jaa.The story is deceptively simple: Kham, a young man from rural Thailand, travels to Australia after his cherished elephants are stolen, only to confront an international crime syndicate. The narrative primarily serves as a framework for showcasing martial arts sequences rather than developing a complex plot. Yet, this very simplicity allows the film to function as a pure action vehicle, emphasizing physicality above dialogue or complexity.From an analytical perspective, the film's strengths are clear. Tony Jaa's athleticism is staggering; long takes, fluid choreography, and the now famous four minute staircase fight scene demonstrate a commitment to practical stunt work rarely seen in modern cinema. The use of Muay Thai and 'elephant style' techniques provides cultural specificity, distinguishing the film from generic action fare. Cinematography accentuates speed and impact, immersing the viewer in a visceral physical experience.However, weaknesses lie in uneven pacing, thin supporting characters, and melodramatic storytelling. The dialogue often feels perfunctory, and attempts at emotional weight particularly surrounding Kham's bond with his elephants are underdeveloped. As a result, while the action soars, the drama lags.    A showcase of breathtaking martial arts and cultural flair, but hampered by shallow narrative and uneven character work.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | The opening of this film is absolutely beautiful, and having thoroughly enjoyed 'Ong Bak', I was ready to give myself over to this film completely.But after the first half hour, it became obvious that the audience was just going to get one stunt after another.Somewhere in the mix is a story about the Asian mob in Australia and some psycho transvestite. But all this (besides being a little silly on its own terms) was merely prop for the stunts.And don't get me wrong: the stunts here are magnificent. But by the time of the most thrilling stunt of all, a mad dash off a skyscraper at a helicopter   I confess I found myself too stunt numbed to respond with awe as I would have liked.Jackie Chan is now going through a kind of mid life crisis in his own films. My suggestion is that he hire himself out as consultant   not about stunts, but about narrative. Because Chan always knew how to package his stunts with solid story with interesting characters.Well, there are interesting characters here, but there's no real story for them to play out   just one stunt after another.Enjoyable; but could have been so much better.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | I just watched the 83 minute version, and it was AMAZING! This film was a great martial arts picture. The DVD I bought was the 'Ultimate Edition', so it also came with the much longer (110 min) International version. I can't wait to check that out, and see if any good fight scenes were edited out of the US version. The scene where Tony Jaa is climbing the stairs, and fighting bad guys all the way up, was simply stunning. Best steady cam scene I have ever seen. And it was captured in one continuous 4 minute take, very impressive.I have been a fan of Martial Arts movies for years, but this one truly stands out. Unfortunately, with the success of the Once Upon a Time in China series of films, most of the martial arts movies emerging from Hong Kong these days are following the same tired formula; heavily wired, invincible good guy performing impossible stunts, and far too many moronic sidekicks having Ernest type moments. What ever happened to serious fight scenes? Why does there always have to be some bozo grabbing his toes and hopping around while making ridiculous faces? Why does Wong Fei Hung always have to perform incredibly obvious wire stunts instead of at least attempting to keep it realistic? The answer to all of those question is Tony Jaa. All of his fight sequences in this movie were incredible, and none were wire guided. There were no 3 Stooges moments, instead they kept the tone serious. He was also a vicious fighter; in many movies they go to great lengths to show how bad the bad guys are, but then the hero merely knocks them down. Here, Tony Jaa shows no mercy at all. He breaks more bones than 10 Jet Li movies combined. He drives his opponents mercilessly into statues, breaks them in half, and cripples them. No punches are pulled, this is all out war.A fabulous Martial Arts film, one of the best I have ever seen.R.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | STAR RATING: Jodie Marsh Michelle Marsh Kym Marsh Rodney Marsh * Hackney Marsh Okay, it's a martial arts film, lets get the plot out of the way. It fails and by the end WK has simply become a very long and boring slog. In the earliest stage of his career, Jaa has gone from one extreme to another with one great film and one dire one. I wonder where he'll go from here. *

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.5/10 | Tony Jaa and Prachya Pinkaew know how to butter their bread, and make it extra toasty for anyone interested in martial arts movies let alone die hards. After the success of Ong Bak, they went on to make another film that had a slightly sillier story   Tony Jaa's character is a 'protector' of a baby elephant and its parent or uncle or whatever, and after the two elephants are kidnapped he goes on a rampage to find the people who did it. Of course, this means Pinkaew and the writers have to concoct one of those plots in martial arts movies loaded with bad guys and some cops too, and other side characters of some value like a guy who sticks up convenience stores, badly, or that other guy who, frankly, is one of the only real matches to Jaa.These 'plot' scenes aren't too bad, and keep the story rolling and contain some decent performances. But we didn't go into the Protector to see an actual story, did we? It's actually kind of superfluous, and if it weren't for the significance of elephants in Thailand, it could be a MacGuffin. The story is, frankly, second to what the Protector really shines at: showing off Tony Jaa kicking ass and not having the time to take names since he kicks ass every other second. Jaa here more than proves his worth; like Jackie Chan he had the 'no stunt double' thing going on, as happened in Ong Bak, but here unlike in Ong Bak there isn't super fast cutting in the action and fight scenes. Indeed there's a scene that reminds one of Oldboy, where a five minute long take shows Jaa going up a stair case (all in stedi cam, not hand held thank goodness) and mercilessly beating the crap out of any henchman that gets in his way. It's so powerful because we know already Jaa can do it, and because the mis en scene is so relentless. In terms of grace and skill, if not service to the story, it even tops Oldboy.Oh, and that's not all. Some scenes seem to go forever with Jaa fighting off the ridiculous onslaught of henchman and thugs, which include a pack of wild skaters. And when it comes to that last showdown  where we see how a tragedy knocks up Jaa's 'I'll kill you all!' meter a thousand points  it's breathtaking. It's hard to recommend The Protector for any other reason than for Tony Jaa and his meticulous, daunting, eye popping array of technique and skills with his body as a martial artists. He's at the top of the crop of people who have ever appeared on celluloid doing this, up there with Bruce Lee and Chan. If the movie itself doesn't quite live up to it (albeit still relatively well made and with its touches of humor), it's fine.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | (This review concerns the full length version of the film and not the American version which runs 20 to 25 minutes shorter)Tony Jaa, star of Ong Bak, is back in a rather dull action film concerning stolen elephants.The story begins as the young Tony Jaa is raising an elephant with his father for the emperor of Thailand. When Jaa has grown up the elephant and its child are brought to the big city where they are stolen and taken to Sydney Australia. Jaa follows and begins to leave a trail of broken bodies in his path to getting the elephants back.I do understand that more often than not the plot of an action movie is purely an excuse to string action scenes together, but it helps if the non action scenes are interesting and move the story along. Here while they do move the plot along they are rather dull. You don't really care as they spin out the story of Jaa's quest (which seems to involve beating every person he meets up) and the parallel story of a Thai cop in Sydney. It doesn't help that the cop, played by Petchtai Wongkamlao, one of my favorite Thai actors, speaks with such a heavily accent that his English is pretty much gibberish (If the DVD I saw had subtitled everything it would have been better). Worse, none of the non action scenes made me feel any sense of danger or urgency, yes there was humor but little else. They are often so dull they pretty much kill the rest of the movie.The action sequences are often stunning. The boat chase in Thailand is fantastic, if a bit fantastical. The fight scenes are often brutal but they tend to go on forever. The film has been charged with having repetitive fight sequences and despite the counter argument that there is only so many ways people can fight (which I understand) I have to agree with the argument that most of the action suffer from repetition.Look at the early fight scene in Sydney where Jaa breaks up a drug sale and is set upon in the tram warehouse. The fight starts and he's set upon by ever increasing numbers of fighters. First on foot, then on skates, then bikes, then motorbikes, then an ATV shows up. All seem intent on hitting him with long florescent light bulbs. Do they have any effect? None but they keep hitting him with them because it looks cool. There seems to be a sort of loose drill as Jaa is driven to one side of the warehouse by those on foot and then back to other way by the bike,motor bike or ATV. What transpires are basically the same sequence repeated with a different vehicle or different big stunt in the middle. The larger scale action scenes are full of this machine like construction that is repetitive.The smaller sequences are also riddled with repetitive moves. Jaa will kick a bad guy repeatedly in the chest, hit him somewhere else then go back to kicking them. Its basically the same set of moves repeated in different locations. Its as if thats all Jaa can do or remember. Well not all, Jaa also will throw any bad guy through any window or pain of glass that happens to be near by. If its glass it gets broken. Its so bad that you begin take bets on which piece of glass will remain unbroken.I've seen thousands of movies over the years and rarely have I ever seen a movie repeat its fight choreography so many times as this one does. Its so bad that it basically kills any fun the action scenes provide.I really can't recommend this movie, at least for what it will cost you to see it in the movies. Sure the fights are often spectacular over come the dull script and plot, but even they become tiresome after awhile (about half an hour in give or take a kick to the chest). I'd either wait for DVD where you can play around with the fight scenes to see how they're done or wait for it to show up on cable so you don't end up spending too much money on it.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 9.4/10 | This is a 'B' quality production, but this Tony Jaa is far superior to the vehicle which displays his talents. Tony bears a strong resemblance to Jai of Ron Ely/Tarzan fame (Manuel Padilla Jr.), and is noted at least once as being 'pretty.' He definitely carries a fantastic on screen presence, although he doesn't seem to have a singular style, but rather demonstrates proficiency in a myriad of techniques and martial arts styles. Muay Thai seems to be his base, but I believe it is more Bokutor, mixed with Prodalserey (a more modern form of the ancient Muay Boran or Bokutor). From that ancient and diverse base, he draws from Jeet kun do, Ninjitsu, Jujitsu, Judo, and a plethora of other styles, including full on Akido at the end! This kid looks like Jackie Chan one minute, Bruce Lee the next, and then Stephen Seagal back when he was young and still rock and rolled! You see a strong Jet Li esquire style, with Chow Yun Fat undertones, with the mastery of fury of Bolo Yeung. He demonstrates some amazing skill! It's like he (Jaa) has studied every possible style and has mastered each one! Aside from giving the viewer a total appreciation for this 'new' talent (Jaa), this film an emotionally strong, well developed story involving the Protectors who train and then protect the Imperial Elephants of Thai Royalty.All in all? If you are a fan of the martial arts venue, I would highly recommend this film, though it is a 'B' flick, with a 'C' budget and film quality. Tony Jaa is a name to remember! We were highly entertained, and look forward to great things from this young Master.It rates a  on the 'B' Scale. That should equate somewhere around a 7.6/10 on the 'A' Scale, from...the Fiend :.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | THE PROTECTOR (the heavily edited U.S. version of TOM YUM GOONG) is another Thai action flick that features the trademark collaboration of director Prachya Pinkaew, stunt/fight choreographer Panna Rittikrai and of course, Tony Jaa in cutting edge action that took off in ONG BAK: THE THAI WARRIOR. This time, you get to see more of Jaa's combat specialties that rely on Muay Thai kickboxing, acrobatics, grappling and other martial art forms.Jaa plays Kham, a young Thailand native and caretaker of elephants who goes to Australia in search of his two elephants that were kidnapped by a crime organization led by an evil sinister named Madame (Xin Jing). He's forced to use his martial arts skills to take out thugs and corrupt cops with the help of Mark (Petchtai Wongkamlao  ONG BAK), a righteous cop who happens to have more trouble in his hands when a corrupt Australian cop frames him for murder.Upon Kham's (Jaa) arrival in Australia's Thai town, Sidney, his search leads him to the organization's headquarters where Madam has her operations in the 'Tom Yum Goong' Thai restaurant. He fights his way through a long line of thugs with close range attacks and arm bending takedowns while throwing them through balconys, tables, flower vases and other equipment before facing off against Johnny (played by stuntman and Wu Shu martial artist Johnny Tri Ngyuen) in a one on one martial arts brawl. Mark and Kham find themselves working together after a senior policeman, linked to the organization, frames him for the murder of another corrupt policeman and a business executive.Like ONG BAK, this movie has a simple plot which was made to allow room for non stop fights. This time, instead of traveling to recover a stolen statue, Jaa sets out to recover his two pet elephants. As a result, director Panna Rittikrai and Jaa determined to overwork the action sequences to please their fans the way Jackie Chan puts his life on the line for his.Speaking of Jackie Chan, there's one sequence, set in a wherehouse, that comes close to CITY HUNTER and RUMBLE IN THE BRONX where Jaa encounters a gang, equipped with BMX Bikes, Rollerblades, 4 wheelers and foes who wield florescent bulbs at him. This allows Jaa to showcase his stunts, martial arts and acrobatics on furnature, cars, fences and other equipment that will appeal to Chan movie lovers.Pinkaew also salutes Jackie Chan in a scene where Jaa arrives at the airport and accidentally bumps into a man who turns out to be a direct look a like of Chan that will have you thinking twice.The film is packed with loads of spectacular fights to check out. One fight concerns Jaa being challenged by three skilled fighters in a burning Buddhist temple, flooded with water. The first one is played by Zero Gravity Stunt Team Member and gymnast Lateef Crowder, who puts on an incredible display of Capoeiria. His second foe is played by Jackie Chan Stunt Team member Jonathan Foo, who engages in Wu Shu kung fu and uses traditional swordsmanship. Jaa's third challenger is played by Australian wrestler Nathan Jones, who out matches Jaa by size, weight and strength. Jones is probably best remembered as the wrestler who fought Jet Li in FEARLESS, he battled Brad Pitt in TROY and even wrestled in the WWE years earlier for a short time. Jones delivers a variety of wrestling moves and leaves the battle unresolved, at least until the finale.Some of the most notable fights take place in a five story circular room where Jaa battles countless bad guys from the bottom floor to the top, and the finale where he uses freestyle martial arts against 50 henchmen with some bone crushing grappling moves, close range takedowns and a variety of combination attacks.Some mixed events fall in place during the film as Mark and Kham hide out from the police while Kham continues his one man martial arts attack on the operators of Tom Yum Goong. Madame takes over the family business by killing off the owners. Kham comfronts her and her army of henchmen as they go out to do battle while Mark goes out to rescue his kidnapped sister who's also a victim of Madam's evil doings.The overall rating of THE PROTECTOR was a downfall because of the solid story but thankfully, it can be overlooked with the trademark tools of Jaa, fight choreographer Panna Rittikarai and director Prachya Pinkaew who help put the film in the shape of a cutting edge martial arts piece that can be appreciated without being framed as a bad National Geographic nature program on elephants.It was good to see ONG BAK co star Petchtai Wongkamlao, remembered as the humorous con artist, re team with Jaa and make people laugh with his comedic humor and jokes. Johnny Tri Ngyuen delivered some of his martial arts skills against Jaa but it should have been a longer fight. He deserved more screen time and his supporting role revealed him as a talented actor that will hopefully give him bigger roles in future projects.Hopefully, Jaa's next movie will improve on some of the flaws that THE PROTECTOR suffered from and his proteges will create better character development for his acting and a creative plot to go along with it so he won't be looked at as only a martial artist. The results of his screen fighting expertise can possibly put him in the category with his heroes Bruce Lee, Jackie Chan and Jet Li as America's next action star.The good news about this film is that distributor 'Dragon Dynasty' gave it the ultimate treatment on DVD and included the original uncut TOM YUM GOONG version to unravel all the missing material not shown in the American version along with it's original dialogue that will definitely please the fans (familiar with the original).

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | The director and stars of Ong Bak reunite for this incredible tour de force of martial arts mayhem which, although lacking somewhat in decent narrative, certainly packs a punch where it counts. Once again, top Thai Tony Jaa kicks and punches his way through scenery and extras as though his life depended on it, and if you don't go away from this movie impressed by the amazing physical feats on display, then, quite frankly, you ought to stop watching action flicks.Jaa plays Kham, a talented fighter who travels to Australia in search of his two elephants which have been stolen by a nasty gang of criminals, led by the evil Madame Rose. But before he can complete his mission, he must do battle with a variety of highly trained opponents.This basic premise is simple enough and more than adequate for a film that solely exists in order to showcase Jaa's amazing fighting skills; unfortunately, a subplot about framing a Thai policeman for an assassination and some rubbish about a struggle for power within the gang, plus quite a few poor English language scenes, undermine the movie's effectiveness. The result is slightly less well rounded film than Ong Bak, but one that still demands a viewing.Unlike Jaa's breakthrough movie, this one takes a while to get to the action, spending the first 20 minutes or so developing the strong bond between Kham and his tusked chums. These scenes are beautifully shot and integral to the film.I had figured, however, that once Kham's pachyderm pals had been abducted, the remainder of the running time would be wall to wall fisticuffs (and kneesicuffs and elbowicuffs). Instead, Kham is like a snowball rolling downhill, gradually picking up momentum, growing more and more dangerous, until he eventually becomes a massive destructive power that destroys all in his path. And whilst I think it's a good idea to build the action slowly like this, the earlier stuff between fights is generally inconsequential guff that diminishes the overall impact of the film.The martial arts scenes, on the other hand, are superb; Jaa fights all manner of foes who use several different styles, and the standard is always exceptional. The first couple of mêlées are impressive (including a breath taking speedboat chase, and a scene where he fights against rollerbladers and BMX ers), but the best action is definitely towards the end of the film: A 'Game of death' inspired sequence sees Kham ascending a spiral staircase, encountering bad guys at each level; a battle against a Brazilian capoeira fighter and a huge bald headed brute in a waterlogged temple; a bone crunching battle against a multitude of attackers (which resembles the Crazy 88 scene from Kill Bill, minus the swords); and a great finale in which Kham fights several men twice his size and a lady boy with a whip!Even if none of that appeals to you (and you really shouldn't be wasting your time reading this if it doesn't), then watch this film if only to see the amazing sight of a baby elephant being thrown through a window (don't worry, I'm pretty sure it was done with special effects!).

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | Where to begin? Well I'll start with the story. Story? Well there actually is one though they managed to make it much worse then Ong Bak's story. The story in Ong Bak was sort of okay. But this one... OK, you don't watch this kind of film for a good story. But what matters is indeed the action and camera work. The action was very badly choreographed. Right in the first action scenes you can see Tony Jaa kicking around being worried about not to stumble over his own feet to keep his balance. I don't know how the director could let this happen with such a good action star like Jaa. The rest of the fighting scenes look a bit better but are still far from the quality of the ones seen in Ong Bak. Way too much slapstick action and quickly done moves. Sometimes the encounters try to take some Jackie Chan style for granted which fails because they lack the rhythm. Moreover I missed the Muay Thai fighting that we saw in Ong Bak. Very seldomly Jaa uses his elbows. More of really hastily done kicks and jumps which don't look great. In some takes you may think they ran out of ideas. Over and over you see the same bone breaking techniques again and again till you yawn.Between the action scenes you see some bad jokes and poor story development. That is not what we want to see. Advice: If the story is the weak side of the movie then by all means don't stretch it!!!Instead of spending money in flying boats and car chases which can't be up to the American level due to the budget, the bucks should have been spend to a good choreographer and a better director. Together this would have unlocked the full potential of Tony Jaa. Which IMHO is a real shooting star. One should only think about what a REAL director like John Woo would make out of this guy. (Remember Woo even managed to make Van Damme look good!)I'm a huge action movie fan and I gave Ong Bak a 10 but since the movie contained so many downs including nearly all the action scenes I rate it 4.5 and an extra point for Tony Jaas performance even if he can't save this mess. Rating 5.5

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | This Tony Jaa martial arts film follows Kham; a Thai villager whose father's elephants have been stolen with the help of corrupt local officials. He learns that the two elephants have been taken to Sydney so he heads to Australia to search for them. Here he soon getting into trouble as he confronts a variety of unsavoury characters. He also meets up with Thai born Australian policeman Sergeant Mark as he finds himself confronting a senior officer who is in league with the criminals.The story here is pretty basic but that doesn't matter; I doubt many people will be watching for a complex plot and subtle twists... this is all about martial arts action and here it really delivered. There are numerous fights; each seems more exciting than the one before. This action is brilliantly choreographed and at times fairly wince inducing as our protagonist snaps limbs and severs tendons! Tony Jaa is great in these scenes. Petchtai Wongkamlao brings some humour as Sergeant Mark; a likeably character is funny without being silly. As well as the numerous fights there are a couple of fine chases; this includes a short car chase in Sydney and a thrilling boat chase in Thailand. Overall I'd say this is definitely one to watch if you are a fan of martial arts films.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | My first thoughts of seeing this movie were 'what can he do any different from Ong Bak'. Let me tell you if you loved Ong Bak, Tom Yoom Goong aka The Protector will blow you away. Tony Jaa is an excellent martial artist who exhibits very extreme behavior throughout the entire movie not to mention the fight scenes are spectacular. I honestly felt that this movie would use the same fight sequences but they don't and the story is very exciting(how often do you save an elephant). Like most spectators I was marvelled at Jaa's ability to not have very much dialog's and still tell a convincing story. If you're a training martial artist like myself then you will enjoy The Protector and the over all performance of Tony Jaa.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | 'The Protector' in my eyes is easily one of the greatest action films of all time. Tony Jaa is amazing in this movie about a young boy who was trained and raise to protect elephants. Not to go into too much detail but the elephants are very important to their culture and beliefs and that they believe that elephants give people some type of power. I will leave it at that not so I don't get into any religious/cultural debate. Two of these elephants are stolen, and Jaa goes on a violent rampage to find them. The action in this movie is almost never stopping and phenomenal. You will see various forms of martial arts and fighting from Muay Thai to Caperoia to guys on roller blades. The camera work is incredible as well, capturing Jaa and others amazing skills and fights. One of my favorite scenes is when he fights the Caperoia fighter in a flooded temple. Amazing sequence. Another great one is when he climbs the different floors of a restaurant battling men all the way to the top (reminds me a bit of Tower of Death). ANY action fan will definitely love this film. ANY martial arts fan will really love and appreciate this film. Jaa is incredible and I have a feeling we will be seeing a lot more great films from him.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | When I first watched this film, I was still pretty green when it came to assessing what good film making and bad film making constituted. Over the past decade plus I have gone on a new road to find joy in terrible, poorly made films that have a certain joy and energy to them. They stink, but dang someone had a vision.I think we all wanted to see another Ong Bak, but The Protector is something else entirely. While I am sure the longer international version is more coherent, for us dumb Americans we got an inexplicable mess with spotty dubbing and strange editing choices. It's as if we had no sense of patience or something.Anyway, the action scenes we get are pretty darn amazing, but utterly ridiculous in their scope. Tony Jaa not only takes on an endless stream of hench men, he battles an extreme sports brute squad, a group of roided up strongmen and a whip lashing trans woman. It all makes sense? I mean, the story is steeped in cultural cues from Thailand but it seems that was all taken out for the sake of allowing us to get to the bone breaking faster. And damn, there is a lot of bone breaking. I felt bad for the one guy that saw like 20 of his friends get their limbs rearranged, and then Tony Jaa breaks his neck. Also, a tag line in this movie should have been 'no window is safe.'I generally do like the mission our main character Kham goes on, for being a vegan it helps make the power fantasies that swim in my mind come to life, especially since I am a fat pudgy dude in real life and there is no way I could fight 20 guys and run up five flights of stairs. If anything, I just imagine the elephant is one of my dogs and boom, totally immersed.I have to say I'm glad they didn't do too much CGI, for the moment where Jaa and Khon are walking the streets of Sydney is utterly hilarious. Anyway, watch this film for the silly factor. It ain't that great but you won't be bored.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | I watched this movie in Thailand when it was released in 2005. A few of the fight scenes are good, but the movie itself is horrific. It is almost worth seeing just for the laughs. I really can not imagine them releasing the complete version as shown in Thailand, including the really bad product placements, the bizarre anti piracy scenes and a sudden blast of pro Thailand propaganda. There is a scene where the Australian bad guys blow a horn and all over the city dozens of teenage extreme sports kids show up to fight the main guy. Complete with in line skaters, BMX riders, Motor cross riders, etc. The really bad part is they decide to chase him around with fluorescent light bulbs. It looks great on the posters and previews, that is what convinced us to see it, but don't be fooled. It is a B movie at best with A movie money backing it. This guy will not be the next Jackie Chan or Jet Li, especially if he is going to be forced to make more movies like this one.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | Alright, lets first get one thing straight. The Protector is not a highly plot centric movie. The story, while damn good for the genre, is just there as a clever excuse for Tony Jaa to fight people. That, my fellow fans of gratuitous violence, is the real draw of the film. Jaa kicks a lot of ass in a very short amount of time.That being said, Tony Jaa is absolutely stunning as a martial artist and stuntman. The only barrier standing between him and a major U.S. breakthrough is that he does not speak English. He has everything else going for him. His style is pretty unique and very raw, his technique is flawless, his acting is as solid as can be expected, and his stunts and acrobatics are beyond belief. I don't understand how the human body is capable of pulling off some of the things he does. I consider myself to be in very good physical shape, and his acrobatics, speed and raw strength are nothing short of mind boggling to me. The fight choreography, which he did a large part of, is astoundingly well done, even if a couple fights come off as a bit cheesy.Overall, this is one of the better martial arts flicks I've seen in quite a while, and if you enjoy seeing raw, visceral, and highly technical fights, than you will definitely want to see The Protector.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | I have to say that tony jaa is on the rise to being one of the greatest martial artists since Bruce lee or Jackie Chan.In the styles of Muay Thai,this art involves with more punching and kicking than the acrobatics both jet and Jackie portray.But tony does excellent in this area as well.He's young,vibrant,and in the greatest shape more men would envy.I like the story behind the movie about a lone warrior who must stop the corruption that is slowly taking over the provinces of Thailand,in smaller increments.The simple villagers who live by their beliefs and training in the martial arts protects them from their enemies,but in odd cases men with guns changes those verdicts leaving behind devastation in their wake.Thus comes in with tony jaa,and his butt kicking style that will over all make the cartels see how and why that walking into someones house uninvited will get your face smashed into the ground.This story has done great since Ong bak,which i still like to this day.It gave me a real look at an art nearly forgotten by the populace,but in some cases still taught to those who really would like to learn,even in the western hemispheres.Muay Thai is taught with some changes by some schools which match the environment.Todays violence is more pronounced than yesteryear,still though people look to serenity at some level even by learning the old ways. text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: .10/10 | For some reason, I don't think that Washington Post columnist Ann Hornaday was kidding when she said that Thai martial arts sensation Tony Jaa is a 'one man CGI effect' in his latest outing 'The Protector,' which is being presented to us by none other than Quentin Tarantino. Serious. Even though Jaa does not yet speak a word of English (not that it really matters, since about 60% of the film is English language dialogue in addition to Jaa's native Thai), he somehow or another comes off as a truly heroic human being, when things are slow, that is. When it comes time for action, Jaa transforms into a 'living CGI effect'   kicking, punching, snapping bones, breaking bones, and dancing around the screen as if he does this stuff for a living (he does).Its original title in Thailand is 'Tom yum goong,' which from what I understand is a rather exquisite Thai shrimp dish. Some here at IMDb are confused as to why it was released in the United States as 'The Protector.' Well, I'll tell you why. Jaa plays Kham, a young martial artist whose family for generations has raised the elephants of Thai kings. When two of Kham's prized pachyderms are stolen by hoodlums and smuggled to Sydney, Australia, he follows in hot pursuit, kicking and punching and getting in way over his head in a battle with the Sydney underworld.There is a sense of majesty in the early scenes of 'The Protector,' as Kham is seen as a young boy rearing his elephants. Kham doesn't joke around when he says that they're his family and not his pets. He practices martial arts on them, plays with them in the fields, and even gets doused by one with water. So when they're suddenly taken away from him, you can understand his anger and frustration in having to journey to a far off land to retrieve them. Perhaps this is where the film and Jaa mostly succeed: Jaa comes from a family that raises elephants. As a matter of fact, he would practice stunts by jumping off the backs of one into a river. So maybe this is why there is some authenticity to his portrayal of Kham and the film's early scenes.Now this is where I shower praise on 'The Protector': Jaa gives quite an intense, well acted performance in this film (did I just say that?). The subtitles help, but one can easily tell from his facial expressions that he's really hurt and ticked off at the bad guys, and lets 'em have it as punishment for their misdeeds. Praise must also be given to the elephants, too, who come off as charismatic and majestic in their own light. (OK, enough of this touchy feely emotional stuff, already. What about the action, ACTION?) I was just getting to that.When Kham hits the streets of Sydney, of course he's the stranger in a strange land. Getting swept up in a war against the underworld and the local cops (many of whom are in cahoots with a vicious femme fatale gang leader), Kham takes on all comers. In an abandoned trolley yard, Jaa battles 20 or so in line skaters and BMX ers, many of whom are brandishing all manner of weaponry, not limited to their bikes, pipes and fluorescent light bulbs and when he gets hit, he bleeds. From there, the action scenes just keeping coming to us at a furious pace, with Jaa doing his best Jackie Chan impersonations as a one man army battling dozens of his sparring partners in increasingly ridiculous action set pieces. The best of these sequences is when Kham takes on all comers as he ascends a winding four story staircase, and the camera follows him in an impressive unbroken tracking shot that captures ALL of the action.Ever since being introduced to the West in 'Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior' (2003) last year, Jaa has quickly become the talk of the martial arts community, since Jet Li is set to retire from the genre with 'Fearless' later this year. Here, Jaa reunites with 'Ong Bak' director Prachya Pinkaew. Noticeably more muscular than in that film, Jaa puts his brutal Muay Thai skills to work on a legion of bad guys. In addition to Muay Thai, he also shows off admirable skills in Aikido and Tae Kwon Do and in one sequence that brings back memories of the Crazy 88 from the 'Kill Bill' movies, he snaps the arms, legs, and wrists of at least 30 henchmen. In another, he goes up against a Capoeira fighter and a guy with a broadsword in a water drenched Buddhist prayer hall. His most skilled opponent is none other than wrestler Nathan Jones (what's he doing here?).What struck me as most believable about these action scenes is the fact that for the most part, Jaa is battling opponents that are just as skilled as he is, something that he and the director didn't seem fit to do in 'Ong Bak,' and he does take quite a fair beating himself (as do most of the fighters in 'The Protector'). There is hardly any one sided showmanship here. Punches and kicks land, hard, bones crunch and snap, and it all looks and sounds like it really hurts.To conclude, 'The Protector' is most definitely a worthy follow up to 'Ong Bak: The Thai Warrior.' I won't say that it's superior but is at least on equal grounds. Tony Jaa is an incredible stunt person and martial artist, and we all do expect to see something fantastic later on

There is a 5 10min fighting scene in which Jaa works his way up a giant spiraling building defeating many 'bad guys' and performing entertaining stunts in which the camera does not cut once! Furthermore, it is very apparent that much of the time the blows dealt are full contact(ouch)! see this movie, its just good plain fun.

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | At this time of writing, the Taiwanese vcd is the only available version of this movie. It doesn't have English subtitles, though this shouldn't mar your experience of the film, as its pretty easy to follow whats going on. Also some of the film is spoken in English. This is because the film is set in Australia. Though the story isn't the most important thing here, its mostly about the superb muay thai skills of Tony Jaa.Tony Jaa loves elephants. From when he was young, we see that he loves the creatures. When his pet elephant is kidnapped by this strange gang. I couldn't quite follow this bit, but it seems as if these guys kill elephants and cook them up and take their ivory. Anyway, he is hell bent on getting his elephant back. So, in a way, the thin story is that of revenge.Pretty soon, Jaa is finding the bad guys and kicking some serious ass! His side kick from Ong Bak is also in this film, this time playing a cop. So, down to what you really want to know! The fights. At times they are even better than those seen in Ong Bak. Their are some excellent scenes such as Jaa taking on a group of guys who have bikes and roller blades. Their is often a lot of impressive aeriel moves and loads more bone breaking in this, than its predecessor.Tom Yung Goong appears to have a slightly higher budget than Ong Bak. Some of the visuals are quite impressive and some of the choreography is jaw dropping. One example of neat visuals is this fight set in water. Their is a lot of splashing, used to great visual effect.The films finale is probably the best part of the film. A highly impressive fight with loads of baddies.To conclude, this film is excellent! Tony Jaa is fully wearing the martial arts crown right now, he seems to get better and better. This is unmissable, don't hesitate to buy it without subtitles, as a US and UK version probably won't be available until late next year. So grab a slice of the action now!

text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | Tony Jaa is back and if you absolutely loved Ong Bak then you'll probably think Tom Yum Goong is OK. This movie has everything: foot chases, car chases, elephant chases, boat chases even a Segway Human Transporter chase (however later edits thankfully deleted most of that preposterous chase).Starting off in idyllic rural Thailand Tom Yong Goong quickly shifts into action with Tony Jaa's Kham chasing the men who've just killed his father and stolen his elephants. Then it just as quickly shifts out of action. A note to the director: if you're going to have a plot and characters this thin don't waste time trying to develop them. The action picks up again later... a lot later.One of the best scenes is the 5 or so minute continuously shot fight scene (according to one interview it was shot over 4 days you figure it out) up the stairs of the combination café/brothel/petting zoo. From there we enjoy an Ultimate Fighting mini contest which pits our hero against a Brazilian style martial artist (for a minute you'll think the projectionist has mistakenly put on the last reel of 1993's Only the Strong), and a giant (6' 11', 360 lbs, and absolutely no posse) who disappears at first sound of police sirens.I won't spoil the rest of the movie for you it'll do that all by itself. It's the perfect addition to your dusty collection of unwatched Thai VCDs.

That may be enough to send you looking for review comments from people who are more like you are. Otherwise, here we go.It has been a long time since I have commented on the quality of the film media itself because it's usually top notch. I kept wanting to wipe my glasses down. Let the experts speak on different film and camera properties. I'll just say that it was distracting and not entirely pleasing.The movie seemed to have some continuity for bit then, bang!! It jumped to a scene so fast that you felt like you dozed off for a few minutes and missed something in between. Then, it happened again. I started thinking about leaving the theater. Enough of the chaos! About that time it got a little smoother which was enough.What followed was an hour of seemingly non stop, in your face, bone crunching action. The Adrenaline was on high.Tony JA is not another Jackie Chan or Jet Li. His style is so different and lethal that you don't even attempt to group him with our old favorites. That is downplaying the contribution he will make to the genre.I would advise you to forget about the holes in the movie and just go enjoy it. text: Movie: The Protector (2005) 1h 23m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | Tony Jaa showcases his exceptional martial arts skill in an attempt to rescue his stolen elephants. The first major action scene (lasting 6 minutes) has Jaa eluding rollerbladers in a warehouse. One of the highlights is a multi tiered restaurant fight (lasting 8 minutes) in which 4 or so minutes are shot in a continuous take with the camera following Jaa as he fights his way up a huge spiraling staircase. Next is a three phase duel at a temple (lasting 6 minutes) where Jaa faces off against three distinct styles of fighting. Finally, the two stage showdown (lasting 10 minutes) is quite possibly the most amazing display of martial arts in the history of cinema, with Jaa first dismantling dozens of antagonists, only to then defeat 4 large bodybuilders and a whip wielding lady. This is pure martial arts insanity.As with my other IMDb reviews, I like to comment on not only the film at hand, but also the cinematic issues that transcend the film itself. When one watches 'Tom Yum Goong', one cannot help but notice that this project can be accurately classified as a 'no brain' action flick. The acting, character development, and overall storyline are mediocre at best, but the filmmakers chose to focus 99% of their efforts on superbly choreographed, mind blowing martial arts sequences. The viewer, therefore, can exert little to no thinking during the movie and simply absorb all of the acrobatics at hand.When properly executed, this type of film is highly enjoyable because it provides seemingly endless demonstrations of jaw dropping physical talent. Anyone who's even remotely interested in the discipline of martial arts (or the abilities of the human body in general) will be awestruck at the maneuvers that Jaa pulls off here. While true that some films are capable of providing both high quality action and a well written storyline (e.g., 'The Matrix', 'Kill Zone', etc.), those films are severely limited in terms of their capacity and variety of action to be conveyed on screen. Only a true 'no brain' action movie like 'Tom Yum Goong' can provide such a high number of impressive physical demonstrations because of its strategy to pack in as many high quality martial arts sequences as humanly possible into one feature length film. With this goal in mind, the filmmakers understand that time spent developing deep characters or complex story lines is quite simply wasted time.What I've just said may seem antithetical to 'good' film making, but this is why all those snobs at AFI could never appreciate a film such as this. You see, those crotchety old farts rate every single movie by the same narrow minded, restrictive standards. When every possible cinematic 'quality' you hold dear can be fit into a tiny little conceptual box, one can be certain that one will never learn to appreciate anything outside of the most boring clichés of movie making. Seriously, only a bunch of narrow minded, group think lemmings would rate 'Citizen Kane' the best American film ever made.The well known clichés of 'good' film making are nothing more than authority driven preconceptions anyways. Yes, I'll admit that I typically prefer movies with quality acting, story lines, and character development (the main reason I've moved away from American cinema), but to claim that ALL of film making is meant to showcase these few qualities is incredibly idiotic and pretentious. Sometimes I like to soak in the intense atmospherics of a horror film ('Secret Room No. 7), gaze at the over the top violence of a schoolgirl revenge movie ('The Machine Girl'), be assaulted by Sci Fi cyberpunk ('Tetsuo: The Iron Man'), or gawk at the physical prowess of a martial artist ('Tom Yum Goong'). In cases such as this, formulaic standards are not only superfluous, but detrimental  because applying cinematic 'formulas' will smother the inventive, refreshing visual/audio qualities of these films. If you are incapable of understanding this, just go back to your stuffy cave and watch another Akira Kurosawa movie (half of which are garbage when applying traditional standards anyways).Now, don't misunderstand me. This review in no way justifies the endless parade of badly made commercial fluff pieces that Hollywood churns out at an alarming rate. Contrary to what the snobs say, 'no brain' action movies do have standards. They're just too stupid to understand a set of standards that are different from the ones they use. 'Tom Yum Goong' could have been a failure if it actively chose the 'no brain' route but failed to produce stunning action sequences. That's why Bruce Lee's movies are so painful to watch  they have wafer thin characters, boring story lines, bad acting, AND mediocre action scenes to boot. Hollywood suffers from the same flaws as of late. Most of their 'no brain' movies use heaping quantities of fake CGI in completely uninteresting ways instead of using some imagination and practical effects to offer something that's actually entertaining. Instead we get uninspired sequences of CGI with horribly choreographed character movements. No thanks. I'll take the 'no brain' projects from Thailand over America any day of the week. Did you see 'Chocolate' (2008)? It was AWESOME! Am I floating off topic yet? Nope. In the cinematic dark ages that we Americans currently live in (where poorly written, juvenile rip offs like 'The Departed' win best picture), a movie like 'Tom Yum Goong' serves an important purpose. It does away with the 'formula' and delivers the proverbial 'shot to the heart' in terms of martial arts. People who cannot appreciate a quality 'no brain' action movie (and no, that's not an oxymoron) are quite possibly the most pathetic moviewatchers that have ever lived. I ponder at the possibility that they are even more pathetic than Americans who are too lazy to read subtitles. I'm serious.So just sit back, relax, and watch Tony Jaa pummel the living hell out of boatloads of baddies  and don't feel the slightest bit guilty for loving every single minute of it.
