text: Movie: The Haunted Drum (2007) 1h 38m| Official Rating: 5.1/10 | Rating: 5.1/10 | I was intrigued by this movie, as I happened to come across it by sheer random luck. And I was instantly drawn to it, because I do like Asian movies quite a lot. And Thailand have some pretty nice horror movies available, so I had expectations to 'Perng Mang: Glawng phee nang manut' (aka 'The Haunted Drum').However, my expectations were butchered quite quickly as the movie started. It was so openly clear that this was going to be a stinker given the way the movie started and how it progressed.I managed to stick with 'Perng Mang: Glawng phee nang manut' for just about 20 minutes, then I just threw the towel in the ring and gave up out of sheer boredom.The storyline was wholly pointless and lacked any kind of appeal that could make me continue to sit through this ordeal of a movie. Everything just seemed too random and too forced throughout the 20 minutes that I managed to suffer through.As for the acting in the movie, well I can't claim to be familiar with anyone on the cast list here, nor can I claim to single anyone out for being particularly memorable for good or worse.I will not be returning to 'Perng Mang: Glawng phee nang manut' to give it a second chance. It just seemed like a waste of time and effort to me, and it was a slap in the face as I had expected somewhat more from it.It manages to land a very generous two out of ten stars from me, given the production value. But take heed, 'Perng Mang: Glawng phee nang manut' is really not worth wasting your time, money or effort on. If you enjoy a good Thai horror movie, then there are far better choices available.

metadata.synopsis: Ping, a young nobleman, has retired from the service of the crown in order to become a musician. He becomes a student of Master Duang, a famous musician. Master Duang owns a mysterious drum called Perng Mang, which has the power to bring success or death to people. Meanwhile, an arrogant musician called Muan tries to convince all the students to leave Master Duang. Some students follow his advice and end up dying horrible deaths which defy explanation. When Master Duang is defeated by Muan, he calls for Ping to inherit his musical knowledge and gives him the Perng Mang. Ping is told about the secret of Perng Mang and that it was made from a woman's skin. The woman's name was Thip, the same name of the woman he has fallen in love with.

text: Movie: The Haunted Drum (2007) 1h 38m| Official Rating: 5.1/10 | Rating: 5.1/10 | Sometimes stories manage to surprise you in a good way, I was not expecting much from this Thai movie but I'm glad I saw it in the end.A traditional Thai band struggles to keep the magic of their music alive with the help of a spirit inhabiting a mysterious drum. The drum's spirit makes sure the band members keep their vows towards their group and that the tradition coming back from generations would be preserved. It is up to one young man, who manages to create a special bond with the spirit, to honor all those who give their lives for the music.It is a simple story full of color and traces of beautiful music. You really start caring for the characters while they make efforts to keep themselves faithful to the band and, at the same time, wishing for better days. It is also a story of love and loyalty with transitions of violent and bloody scenes which, strangely enough, feel natural to the melodic pace of the movie.The movie is not perfect and has several flaws and weaknesses but it is, in the end, a really nice, original and enjoyable film.

text: Movie: Kung Fu Tootsie (2007) 1h 31m| Official Rating: 5.8/10 | Rating: 4/10 | What happens when martial arts collide with campy comedy and gender bending antics? Kung Fu Tootsie sets out to parody the gangster and kung fu genres, but its exaggerated humor and uneven storytelling make it more spectacle than substance.The film centers on Tien, the flamboyant son of a powerful mafia boss, who is unexpectedly chosen as heir to the family empire. Unprepared for the cutthroat world of organized crime, Tien must balance his effeminate mannerisms with the violent demands of gangster life. Martial arts sequences are blended with over the top comedy, as the film positions him as both a parody of traditional action heroes and a symbol of queer visibility in Thai cinema.Analytically, the film's strength lies in its willingness to subvert genre expectations. By placing a queer coded character at the center of a martial arts comedy, it challenges the hyper masculine norms usually associated with gangster and kung fu films. The colorful set pieces, outrageous costumes, and playful choreography provide moments of visual entertainment, while the satire occasionally lands in poking fun at rigid gender roles.However, the execution undermines the concept. Much of the humor relies on stereotypes, reducing the central character to a caricature rather than building complexity. The plot meanders with predictable conflicts and fight scenes, though lively, it lacks the polish of more serious martial arts cinema. Tonal inconsistency swinging between parody, slapstick, and melodrama leaves the film without a stable identity. .Summary: Kung Fu Tootsie offers colorful parody and occasional satire, but its reliance on stereotypes and uneven tone make it a forgettable entry in the Thai action comedy genre.

When Tao is disabled to continue the business, Ma has to find someone to claim the rightful position as the new Godfather. So, Ma goes on a quest to find his long lost son, Tian. Tian is Tao's poor twin. He has lived with his mother since he was a child with no support from his father Ma. However, everything seems to be perfect when Tian is back to Ma and takes the next leader of the gang, but there's one thing about Tian that's absolutely imperfect for Ma. Tian is gay and loves being pretty just like a girl.

text: Movie: Rahtree Revenge (2009) 1h 26m| Official Rating: 4.8/10 | Rating: 4/10 | How many times can a ghost return before fear turns into familiarity? Rahtree Revenge (Buppah Rahtree 3.2, 2009) continues the saga of Thailand's most infamous apartment haunting spirit, yet its attempt to close the story feels more repetitive than revelatory.Picking up from Rahtree Reborn (3.1), the film resumes the haunting of the same building, where Buppah's restless spirit wreaks havoc on tenants and intruders. The narrative attempts to heighten the stakes by layering in more victims, slapstick diversions, and exaggerated supernatural encounters. While marketed as the darker and more intense conclusion, the execution leans heavily on familiar setups and predictable payoffs.Analytically, the film retains some of the franchise's strengths. The apartment block remains a claustrophobic, practical setting for contained horror. Thai ghost traditions and visual motifs pale apparitions, sudden jolts, eerie silences still generate occasional unease. The blend of humor and horror reflects the series' identity, making it accessible to audiences who prefer a mix of levity and scares.However, the problems outweigh the merits. The tonal imbalance grows even sharper here: moments of genuine fright are undercut by cartoonish comedy, draining suspense. Character arcs lack depth, with most figures serving as disposable victims or comedic props. Worse, Buppah's presence feels diluted; once a tragic and fearsome figure, she becomes an almost secondary element to recycled gags and chaotic subplots. Instead of building toward a powerful conclusion, the film circles back to the same beats, leaving little emotional or narrative payoff. .Summary: Rahtree Revenge tries to escalate the franchise's horror comedy formula but ends up repetitive and shallow, offering more noise than lasting chills.

text: Movie: Pee chang nang (2007) 1h 30m| Official Rating: 5.7/10 | Rating: 5.7/10 | You don't see a lot of horror movies from Thailand (or, at least, I don't) but the few ones that are easily available worldwide are certainly worth looking for. The recent horror flicks 'The Pool' and 'The Lake' are enjoyably eccentric and bloody creature features, and the relatively older 'Nang Nak' (1999) is a film that I personally consider to be one of the most effectively frightening folklore tales ever made.'The Screen at Kamchanod' is good as well. So good even that I'm surprised there never came a US remake. The plot revolves around a doctor who's obsessed with a strange event that took place on 29th of January 1989, when a film was shown on a big cinema screen in the woods of Kamchanod. Although nobody   apart from the projectors   attended the screening, ghosts reportedly appeared in front of the screen and disappeared again when the film was finished. The doc wants to repeat the screening and hopefully summon the ghosts again, but for that he needs the original copy of the cursed film and the help of several reluctant relatives and colleagues.The film relies on a solid (albeit far fetched) premise, a handful of genuinely disturbing moments, and lots of flashy but nevertheless spooky imagery. Notably one passage is immensely powerful, and even reason enough to recommend the whole film, namely when the group recovers the original film roll and watches it in a ramshackle and abandoned theater. The atmosphere is already tense, but nearly becomes unbearable when creaky seats are starting to get occupied. The spirits have obviously arrived to enjoy a movie! After that, and in good old 'The Ring' tradition, no one in the group will ever be the same again. All participants begin to suffer from seeing dead people and other strange visions that are often downright nightmarish!The first sixty minutes are much more compelling than the last thirty, mainly because the pacing slows down severely, and the plot focus shifts from supernatural towards melodrama and relationship issues. Doctor Yuth is not exactly a nice fella, and his girlfriend Orn is deeply unhappy and dreams about running off with the delivery boy/junkie Roj. We get her. The climax is weak, I think, but   as said   the middle section is a must see for fans of ghost horror.

text: Movie: Saep sanit sid saai naa (2006) 1h 35m| Official Rating: 6.7/10 | Rating: 7/10 | Can a bumbling underdog become a true fighter, or is comedy his only weapon? Saep Sanit Sid Saai Naa blends martial arts parody with heartfelt humor, creating a story that is both ridiculous and surprisingly endearing.The film follows Sanit, a young man desperate to prove himself but hopelessly clumsy. When he falls for a girl, he tries to win her heart by training in martial arts, despite his lack of skill. Guided by an eccentric mentor and surrounded by colorful companions, Sanit stumbles his way through comedic trials and physical gags that poke fun at the seriousness of traditional kung fu films.Analytically, the film works because it balances slapstick with sincerity. While much of the humor comes from exaggerated pratfalls and parody of martial arts tropes, Sanit's underdog journey resonates with anyone who has struggled to find confidence. The chemistry between the leads provides warmth, and the mentor student dynamic adds a playful layer of mock philosophy that sharpens the satire. The fight scenes, though intentionally clumsy, are choreographed with enough creativity to sustain both comedy and tension.Still, the film leans heavily on formula. Many jokes are predictable, and side characters often serve as caricatures rather than fully realized figures. Pacing occasionally drags, with humor stretched beyond its natural rhythm. Yet the film compensates with heart, leaving a sense of optimism beneath the chaos. .Summary: Saep Sanit Sid Saai Naa delivers a spirited mix of parody and underdog charm predictable at times, but ultimately a fun and uplifting martial arts comedy.

text: Movie: Hanuman and the 5 Kamen Riders (1974) 1h 41m| Official Rating: 5.5/10 | Rating: 5.5/10 | I had the pleasure of seeing this Thailand made title on the big screen, in Turkey no less, in the early 80's. Now, I can't imagine any distributor in Turkey hiring a translator that spoke Thai for the translation of this film, so I assume all the dubbed dialogue, some of which I still remember, was made up.Not that you really need dialogue to understand what's going on, of course. This is one of those movies where the goodies and baddies are so boldly drawn, that all you need to do is sit back and enjoy 'what' is on the screen, without giving any thoughts as to 'why'.The Kamen Riders are bike riding masked heroes, although they don't really have any superpowers. Their bikes look like 12 year old kids' bikes that they pimp up for Hallwoeen, and their powers consist of lousy karate chops, and kicks worse than a grandmother could do.The evil lord, who resembles Ultron (actually it's more appropriate to say 'whom Ultron resembles', since this is a much older production) somehow needs blood, and sends his henchmen for the job. He also kidnaps a scientist for some reason I can't remember. And the Kamen Riders help the innocent people.All this is enough to make a decent plot, but somehow Hanuman gets involved in this. Hanuman is a godly being, and tries to punish the evil lord (just like the Kamen Riders, although they don't necessarily work together). This makes the plot a bit complicated, but no less enjoyable.The real star of the film is the action and the special effects. The baddies have cheap Halloween masks instead of makeup, and the fight sequences are terrible, but this all adds to the enjoyment of the experience. I'm not one of those western doofuses that compare shoestring budget movies like this to Hollywood productions. This is a different kind of filmmaking altogether. And in terms of what it means, what it tries to do, and what it claims to give the audience, it fairly succeeds. It looks worse than a school project done by the most inept kids with the help of a hand camera and some buddies, but it will certainly stay with you longer than the latest The Fast And The Furious installment.I've read on movie sites that this is regarded as the worst Kamen Rider movie ever (also the only one made in Thailand), and that the original copyright holders, plus most fans, completely disown it and claim it doesn't exist. I can't really make any such comparison, since I haven't seen any other Kamen Rider movie, but this is something worth seeing, if you can find it. It's very cheap, very crude and by all means terrible, but still very enjoyable.

text: Movie: The Holy Man 2 (2008) 1h 29m| Official Rating: 5.3/10 | Rating: 4/10 | What happens when a sequel tries to capture the charm of a cultural comedy but ends up recycling the same punchlines? The Holy Man 2 attempts to continue the formula of its predecessor but delivers fewer memorable moments.Directed by Note Chernyim, the film follows a new monk played by Thai comedian 'Tukkie' (Chusak Iamsuk) in a rural village temple. As with the original, the monk's unconventional antics clash with those of the local villagers, creating situations that blend slapstick humor with occasional moral lessons. The premise again aims to combine reverence for Buddhism with lighthearted entertainment that is accessible to a broad audience.Analytically, the film's strength lies in its energy and cast. Nong Cha Cha Cha and other Thai comedic actors bring lively performances, and the village backdrop once again provides a culturally rich stage for parody. The film continues to satirize rural gossip, superstition, and modern influences encroaching on traditional life.Yet its weaknesses dominate. The narrative structure is episodic, offering a series of disconnected gags rather than a coherent story. Many of the jokes feel recycled from the first installment, and the balance between comedy and moral reflection feels thinner. Attempts at emotional resonance are brief and often overshadowed by exaggerated humor. For international audiences, the film's heavy reliance on cultural in jokes makes it less accessible.    The Holy Man 2 entertains in short bursts but suffers from repetition and a lack of innovation, making it a weaker sequel that leans too much on the original's formula.

text: Movie: Seven Something (2012) 2h 27m| Official Rating: 6.6/10 | Rating: 6.5/10 | This is my latest Thai film and it's an anthology. It was released quite a while back, but I'm only watching it now. Directed by three different filmmakers for three different segments. One of the them was from 'Fan Chan', also known as 'My Girl'. It was not the best Thai film I've seen, yet not much disappointed with the overall film. The reason was the anthology. When the multiple stories compressed in one film, it always depends on each segment. You might like one or two, if not all or the whole film. But the bad luck is if you do not enjoy any of it. Then it will be a shoddy work than a normal concept film in the similar state.So, you must know what the title means before jump into to watch it. 'Seven Something' is like for every seven years, love changes. That's what the tagline says. Means you know, the romance at the beginning and the same romance a few years later are not going to be the same for some people in most of the scenarios. Getting used to it is one of the ways to make it work, but what if the kind of romance you have fallen in for, is excessive at some point later in your life. That's the story of the first segment, which is named '14'.It revolves around a teenage romance. As in the todays world, there's no life without social media. How those platforms became the youngsters daily life routine was told in here. From all, 'YouTube viral' concept was the majorly focused on it. People do videos for many purposes, including profession, talent exhibit, but for some it is just for fun. This was really needed for the at present internet culture the youngsters adopted. So I felt it was a very good message, awareness part of all three stories. The slight let down was, that I am not familiar with the Thai internet culture which differs from nation to nation. Though the fame getting out of them are same everywhere in the world.❝I'm just one person. Without me, you'll be fine. You have 10,000 people who love you out there.❞The second segment was about the film actors and their torn romance. It was named '21/28'. After the good start, I anticipated it to be another fine tale, but it was not. I did not like it. It has been just a decent one. It all revolves during the time between the film called 'Sea You' and its sequel 'Sea You Again'. The whole nation knows their breakup, because of their fight in public stages. The attempt was made by them to patch, but does it work or not is the remaining is to reveal.Too sentimental, but not to be felt kind it belongs. Everything was on the screen, between the two characters, though failed to touch its viewers with its softness. If you are familiar with Thai films and its culture, that might help you to enjoy it better. I don't know. There are other actors those I've seen in other Thai films can be seen in the guest appearances. Especially the final credits have a music track where they all come to dance with a lip sync. What disappointed me the most was to learn this tale was from the 'My Girl' famed director.The third and final segment was about a middle aged TV journalist and her romance with a younger man. This part was known as '42.195'. She has a reason for her depression in life. Then one day, she accidentally meets a marathon runner which going to change her life forever. But it's not easy in the circumstance of life she's in. Their little friendship, how it develops to an unexpected level of bond is what covered in the rest of the section. And again, I liked this segment. Very meaningful and realistic. The best performances by the pair of the entire film. I think you have to be an adult like the late 20s or more to enjoy it better.The three tales are connected as they all set in the same timeline and the universe. Each one is to entertain different generation audiences. So when you watch it, you would know which is yours. Nearly 40 45 minutes for each segment. And the overall runtime was a bit excessive which could unfavours for some viewers. As well as the paces differs in all the three. Should have been improved the screenplay in a few parts, particularly the middle tale. Otherwise, it is not a bad film, but when it comes to suggesting others, I'm not sure to thumb up. It is a less known film, and like I had a mixed feeling, it might work for you as well, or even better, maybe not. So choose it wisely.

text: Movie: Seven Something (2012) 2h 27m| Official Rating: 6.6/10 | Rating: 5/10 | Ambitious in scope yet uneven in delivery, Seven Something draws on three decades of love stories to reflect on youth, maturity, and rediscovery, although its execution wavers.The film is structured as an anthology of three segments: 14 explores teenage romance derailed by the pressures of social media; 21/28 follows the strained relationship between a news anchor and an actress facing the weight of fame and fading relevance; and 42.195 depicts a middle aged woman finding new meaning in life through marathon running and unexpected companionship. Each part attempts to mirror a stage of love and life, highlighting how time reshapes emotion.The film's greatest strength lies in its ambition and variety. The first story captures the vibrancy and vulnerability of adolescence, while the final segment delivers inspiration through themes of endurance and renewal. Cinematography is polished, with each act adopting a visual style that reflects its themes bright colors for youth, subdued tones for maturity, and expansive landscapes for rediscovery.Yet, the middle act drags the narrative. Its melodramatic approach and sluggish pacing diminish the film's overall impact. Tonal inconsistency across the segments also prevents the anthology from feeling cohesive, leaving the viewer more aware of its structure than immersed in its stories.Ultimately, Seven Something is a film of highs and lows ambitious in concept but uneven in execution, leaving a lasting mark.    A mixed anthology with moments of charm and inspiration, but weighed down by inconsistency and uneven pacing.

text: Movie: Yern Peh Lay semakute (2007) 1h 32m| Official Rating: 4.7/10 | Rating: 4/10 | What happens when a film relies almost entirely on slapstick and parody without grounding its humor in a strong story? Yern Peh Lay Semakute attempts to combine martial arts spoof, gangster comedy, and outrageous farce, but the result is more noise than narrative.The film follows three quirky characters each defined by exaggerated physical traits and comedic quirks who stumble into conflicts involving martial arts rivals and chaotic adventures. Built on caricature and over the top performances, the movie leans heavily on situational gags, verbal puns, and physical comedy, aiming to entertain through sheer energy rather than plot sophistication.Analytically, the film's strength lies in its unapologetic embrace of camp. It doesn't shy away from absurd setups, and for audiences who enjoy broad slapstick, the relentless humor offers occasional bursts of fun. The chemistry among the leads brings liveliness, and the parody of martial arts tropes occasionally lands with wit, highlighting the contrast between traditional heroism and clumsy ineptitude.However, weaknesses dominate. The humor is repetitive and often overstretched, reducing its impact. Characters remain one dimensional, serving as vehicles for gags rather than engaging figures. Pacing suffers as extended comedic routines interrupt the narrative flow. Without stronger writing, the satire feels shallow, and the film struggles to sustain attention beyond its initial novelty. .Summary: Yern Peh Lay Semakute delivers bursts of slapstick energy and playful parody, but its reliance on recycled gags and thin storytelling makes it more of a noisy distraction than a lasting comedy.

metadata.synopsis: Yern, a bus driver, Lay, his cross eyed best friend, and Peh, a crippled woman who sells fish at the local market are all sick of being poor. text: Movie: Jod mai rak (2004) 1h 41m| Official Rating: 7.0/10 | Rating: 7.0/10 | Korean movies have become so popular that they are high on the export list to the film industries abroad to be remade for local audiences. Leading the pack is Hollywood, and we've recently seen The Lake House. The Thai film industry too took a Korean movie   1997's #1 Korean film, The Letter (Pyeon Ji), and gave it their own treatment in Jod Mai Rak.I haven't watched the original, but looking at the result of this Thai effort, they aren't too far behind in the ability to make a melodramatic weepie too. Jod Mai Rak tells the story of two lonely people, a country boy called Ton (Attaporn Teemakorn), and a city girl Dew (Anne Thongprasom), who meet and found each other by chance at a Chiang Mai bus terminal, and as Fate would have it, they would come together after a semi long distance courtship over the telephone.There are plenty of sweet moments interjected throughout the narrative, like the lingering shots of a bald plum tree which belongs to Ton, and the tender moments during their stay together in Chiang Mai, after personal tragedy made Dew ditch her shared apartment in Bangkok, and opt for the more rustic lifestyle in the countryside. From here, country boy teaches city girl how to live it up with the basic necessities (well, she still brought over some city artifacts like the PC), and naturally lent itself to many moments that will melt your heart.But watching a movie like that isn't interesting, and you always know that there's something extra just waiting to come. Melodramas always have you paint the perfect blissful picture, before coming down with the all too familiar terminal illness plot device. The two star crossed lovers aren't spared this either, and the latter half of the movie see them battle their fears of not having be with each other for long. It's a story of remembrance, and not forgetting the good things in life, of moving on and cherishing the good times. It's impossible for someone not to feel at least a tear in the eye as the dramatics take their full effect, especially towards the end, though there is some redeeming bittersweet feel at the end of the movie.I found the use of the letters in the movie vaguely familiar, and possibly could have been used in other movies I've seen. It's nothing supernatural, and something which is simple, yet I know is highly effective in serving its purpose. Not that I think anyone would be crazy to do something like that in real life, probably will just either freak the other person out, or really prevent someone from truly moving on.The leads Anne Thongprasorn and Attaporn Teermakorn are believable as the lovers. Girls will probably swoon at Attaporn's portrayal of Ton, the real sensitive new age dude who can cook, has green thumbs, and has so much heart and positivity in life. Anne's Dew initially started out quite unlikable, at least to me, with her tendency to be spoilt and taking things much for granted and in a minor way, mistreating Ton perhaps? But thankfully there is a character change as the movie progresses.Directed by Pa oon Chantornsiri, Jod Mai Rak is a perfect date movie which centers much on the lives of the two lovers, at the expense of having some throwaway supporting characters. Then again, two's a company, and anything more is always unwelcome. Chiang Mai also makes for an awesome romantic place.

text: Movie: Headless Hero (2002) 2h| Official Rating: 4.3/10 | Rating: 5/10 | What happens when a centuries old ghost legend collides with broad Thai slapstick? Headless Hero (Pee Hua Kad) tries to deliver scares and laughs in equal measure, but ends up walking a thin line between parody and horror.The film draws inspiration from Thai ghost folklore, centering on a headless spirit seeking justice and release. Into this chilling premise enters a cast of comic misfits whose bumbling encounters with the ghost generate most of the humor. The film attempts to mix traditional supernatural storytelling with contemporary Thai comedy, reflecting a local trend in early 2000s cinema where horror and humor often overlapped.Analytically, the film's strengths lie in its cultural texture and occasional atmosphere. The rural settings, ghostly folklore, and use of practical effects evoke a sense of familiarity for Thai audiences. Some comedic performances, especially from supporting actors, bring moments of charm, and the central concept of a headless spirit is visually striking when handled effectively.However, the weaknesses are notable. The narrative is fragmented, often shifting abruptly between eerie tension and noisy slapstick, undermining both. Jokes sometimes overstay their welcome, and the ghost's story is underdeveloped, reducing emotional impact. Special effects are uneven occasionally practical but often dated which lessens the horror element. As a result, the film entertains in bursts but struggles to sustain either genuine scares or consistently clever comedy.    Headless Hero offers cultural flavor and quirky humor, but its uneven tone and thin storytelling keep it from becoming a standout in Thailand's horror comedy tradition.

text: Movie: 4 Kings (2014) 1h 38m| Official Rating: 5.1/10 | Rating: 5/10 | 'What if the perfect card trick promised glory, only to entangle you deeper in lies you can't ever fully escape?'4 Kings is a darkly comedic heist film. It sets its sights high on the world of gambling, deception, and underground prestige, blending flashy confidence with a critique of ambition unmoored from conscience.The story follows four central figures: Tode, a nimble illusionist known for sleight of hand; Zien, a seasoned conman with expertise in counterfeit amulets; Riang, his nephew whose life has been steeped in various gambles; and Sri, a coyote whose seductive charm becomes a tool in the dirty work. Their plan: cross borders to challenge Shuchai, a ruthless high stakes gambling boss in Poipet, with a scheme that weaves together card tricks, deception, and high tension.Visually and tonally, 4 Kings impresses in parts: the early scenes involving gambling set pieces deliver genuine suspense. The performances are committed Tode's sly confidence, Zien's experienced cynicism, Riang's desperation, Sri's resourcefulness all have flair. However, after the opening stretch, the film struggles to sustain momentum. The shift from a lean, suspenseful heist setup into broader, more familiar comedy tropes weakens the impact. Character backstories are hinted at, but emotional stakes often feel underdeveloped. Meanwhile, some plot conveniences luck oriented reveals, sudden reversals undermine the groundwork laid earlier.Thai Film JournalThe film's ambition to mix dark humor, crime, moral ambiguity is commendable. Yet the uneven pacing and mismatch of tone limit how deeply it can land.    Stylish and occasionally clever, 4 Kings has shiny con tricks and promise, but doesn't quite master the art of sustaining its own gamble.

text: Movie: 30+ (Single On Sale) (2011) 1h 50m| Official Rating: 5.4/10 | Rating: 4/10 | What happens when turning thirty becomes less about birthdays and more about battling social expectations? 30+ Single On Sale tries to answer with romantic comedy charm, but its uneven execution leaves more style than substance.The film follows Ing, a successful but still single woman in her thirties, who faces the cultural pressure of settling down before being deemed 'too old.' Enter a younger man who reignites her sense of romance and possibility. The premise touches on a timely theme: the tension between personal fulfillment and society's obsession with timelines for love and marriage.Analytically, the film has a promising foundation. It attempts to give voice to women navigating modern life while critiquing outdated norms. Cris Horwang delivers a spirited performance as Ing, portraying both vulnerability and independence, while the younger love interest adds freshness to the romantic arc. The film also benefits from slick production design, stylish costumes, and a lively soundtrack that appeals to urban audiences.Yet its weaknesses outweigh its ambition. The narrative relies heavily on predictable romantic comedy tropes, from clichéd misunderstandings to formulaic reconciliations. Emotional conflicts are often treated lightly and resolved too quickly to have a lasting impact. While the comedy has moments of wit, it usually slips into exaggeration, undermining the sincerity of the central theme.    30+ Single On Sale excels in its concept and lead performance, but stumbles with shallow storytelling, offering more gloss than genuine insight into love after thirty.

text: Movie: Edge of the Empire (2010) 1h 57m| Official Rating: 5.3/10 | Rating: 5.3/10 | EDGE OF THE EMPIRE is a film of two halves that aims to cover the same kind of patriotic Thai history as BANG RAJAN. The first half, a lower key exploration of the plight of the Thai people who find themselves increasingly oppressed under the Han Chinese dynasty, is very effective because it homes in on individual characters to explore their misery and you feel yourself caught up in their woes.A shame, then, that the second half is so different and completely throws away the build up that's come before. The second half tries to be a sprawling war epic, without the budget to offer more than one or two semi standard mêlée battles with minimal combatants. Instead, there's way too much to ing and fro ing and a distinct lack of the full blooded and heartfelt drama that the film promises at the outset.A cast of forgettable characters, disorientated editing and a distinct lack of focus (at one stage the storyline jumps on four years in the blink of an eye) finally combine to make EDGE OF THE EMPIRE a dud, a film spoilt by its own ambitions. It's a shame, because BANG RAJAN was the perfect template of how to make a film like this good, by keeping it simple and focusing on a single village rather than trying to depict huge events that you don't have the budget to do justice to.

text: Movie: Edge of the Empire (2010) 1h 57m| Official Rating: 5.3/10 | Rating: 5.3/10 | Edge of the Empire documents the various struggles and the various tirades a small, Thai based village set hundreds of years ago must wade through so as to attain a sort of peace with themselves and everyone in the land. The continuous, trudging on through a whole host of battles and skirmishes led by fierce Generals and his bloodthirsty troops are demoralising and quite painful; we, the audience, sharing said pain in that ambling one's way through Nirattisai Kaljareuk's film and its various episodes of warfare is a monumental drag of similar proportions. The film, monstrously all over the place in tone and with a disgusting pseudo politic reading 'war may well be absolute Hell for those involved, but can more often than not end up being a bloody good; visceral; stylish time for those watching', is rather a poor effort and probably one of the worst films I've seen from recent times to have come out of the continent of Asia that I have seen from recent times. Given the size of Asia, that's quite an achievement; the film's lone. The piece is a badly judged, ill disciplined effort; one of which, that, by the time it has rolled on past what I think the film though were intrinsic narrative double crosses as well as the umpteenth blood soaked battle sequence, and we've reached the hour mark having witnessed a game of strip chess, no less, we are ready for it to just end.Edge of the Empire's uneasy overall feel begins with a title sequence imbued by that of graphic novel iconography, with it a voice over detailing the horrific liquidation of various villages and those of whom were young enough to escape and set up new societies. These people live in peace with one another, they accept the past and do not seek vengeance; they fight, but it is preordained for means of sport between the various newfound establishments and stands in stark contrast to that of later societies invading their space. The film covers young Lampoon (Thanakorn), a man whom, in spite of existing many centuries ago and in poverty, is a toned and muscular individual. With Lampoon arrives his sister Bunchawee (Sontirod), a young woman whom spends most of her screen time looking like a model who has just arrived following the engaging in a specially themed Native American princess shoot. She's in love with a young lad, someone who's actually in the nearby Han dynasty, those guilty for the liquidation during the opening – a dynasty still rather angry that some of them got away.Things kick off when a young Han warlord arrives with a group of anonymous henchmen to invade the peaceful; tranquil; butterfly ridden haven of the village – but he and his men are easily dispatched. This angers Qin, the Han chief, and he dislodges the village's mayor of sorts with his own: a cackling, sadistic, power mad individual named Litongjia (Suwanbang) whom we first see making use of a brothel's facilities, despite already being married. With Litongjia arrive scenes of the man that are drenched in a hue of blood red, echoing his overall role of bringing about murder; a sense of fire and brimstone enrapturing all around him additionally arriving as he stands on his perches dishing out pain and punishment, something that sees Kaljareuk construct a demon like presence about the man. With his coming to power, Litongjia happens to illegalise all actions and ways of life that Lampoon and Bunchawee live by; so no relationships with Han's and no more weapons allowed rendering Lampoon, a sword maker, redundant: what a coincidence.The villagers in the various townships, and their now oppressive living conditions, combine their fighting spirits and create a droll, repetitive arc for the film to bed into; something which depressingly draws on inspiration from that of video games in that with each General arriving and failing, the next 'level' of bosses or antagonists that the characters must effectively foil becomes apparent – the whole thing building, as is in a standard video game framework, to that of a huge confrontation with the 'big' boss and his armies. A terrible sequence sees an archer remarkably intercept three of Litongjia's arrows with that of his own, and yet is unable to just put one through the guy's neck thus saving all manner of bother and life. Throughout, Kaljareuk strikes us an an enthusiastic director but one with a lot left to learn; his hopping from an awfully executed rape sequence to the casual execution of helpless innocents, which is incidentally shot as if an action sequence in its rabid cutting and crash zooming, reeks of a man drawing the audience into offense as things escalate from rape to genocide to that of the threat of a child being murdered.Kaljareuk's film is mostly, if not entirely, complete nonsense from its beginning to its end; principally, the film falling into that deathly unforgivable trap of entrusting sequences of warfare happening to double up as sequences of action, and as a result, ought to be shot accordingly; that spectacular scenes of on rushing 'sides' in a battle is exciting, and that the capturing of it as sheer spectacle is how it ought to be done. Some of its content wouldn't necessarily go amiss in a film like Schindler's List, other content wouldn't necessarily feel out of place in a Stephen Chow movie, whereas the persistent overhanging sense of it geared towards that of a juvenile audience distracts greatly from what should essentially be a harrowing tale of tyranny and oppression. If one were to be caught looking for a recent film, from that continent of Asia, about war and oppression and all the nastiness that comes with that, but explored properly as well as played truthfully and correctly, then one must incline one towards seeing Chuan Lu's City of Life and Death; and by all means possible, are recommended to steer clear of this nonsense.

text: Movie: The Angel of Bar 21 (1978) 2h 15m| Official Rating: 5.6/10 | Rating: 5.6/10 | Needless to say that I had actually never heard about this 1978 Thai movie titled 'Thepthida Bar 21' (aka 'Bar 21' or 'Angel of Bar 21') prior to stumbling upon the movie here in 2023. Sure, I was a little bit hesitant given the movie's age, and this would actually make it the oldest Thai movie I have seen.The storyline in 'Thepthida Bar 21' was actually good, however, the movie would have been a whole lot more enjoyable if they had opted to not delve into the musical. It just felt awkward when the cast went into singing and dancing in the middle of something. Either go full in on it, not halfhearted like director Euthana Mukdasanit did in 1978.Anyway, I was actually adequately entertained by the movie, and thus could manage to get through the rigid and awkward song and dance routines. And as such, I will say that director Euthana Mukdasanit's 1978 movie is actually fair enough for a single viewing.I wasn't familiar with the cast ensemble in the movie, but the leading actress really carried the movie quite well with her performance.My rating of 'Thepthida Bar 21' lands on a six out of ten stars.

text: Movie: Friday Killer (2011) 2h 19m| Official Rating: 6.4/10 | Rating: 5/10 | What if the deadliest hit man you know is also the father you never understood?Friday Killer (2011) follows Pae Uzi, a hardened assassin recently released from prison, who discovers he has a daughter, Dao, a young woman raised without knowing him. Their reunion is fraught: Dao believes Pae Uzi killed the only father she ever truly knew, and her quest for vengeance collides with his desperate attempt to reclaim what family he has lost. The film blends action, drama, and surprisingly emotional stakes under the direction of Yuthlert Sippapak.On a technical level, Friday Killer delivers on its set piece action scenes, especially those that contrast the brutality of Pae Uzi's profession with quieter moments of regret and reflection. The cinematography gives Chantaburi Province a mood that is both lush and ominous, grounding the action in real landscapes rather than stylised urban gloss. The transformation of Pae Uzi's character from lethal professional to conflicted parent offers some compelling character work, especially in his interactions with Dao, who is torn between anger and longing. However, the drama occasionally leans into clichés: misunderstandings occur just in time to stretch the tension, and some plot threads such as Pae Uzi's past crimes and Dao's upbringing feel underexplored. Supporting characters are colourful but often one dimensional. Tonal shifts between intense violence, comic relief, and emotional confession are not always smooth.Despite its uneven moments, Friday Killer holds its own when it grounds its action in themes of guilt, redemption, and what it means to be a father. . A gritty and ambitious film that scores with emotional conflict and high octane action while sometimes losing its way amid genre shifts and unresolved backstories.

text: Movie: In a Small World (2012) 1h 46m| Official Rating: 6.9/10 | Rating: 6.9/10 | Three men on a trip to Pattaya, Thailand. One, a hard working Indian software engineer, has no wish to go; he's quite content staying at home with his wife and Hindu religious obligations. But his boss thinks he is in need of some recreation, so off he goes. Another, a Japanese journalist, is also sent there by his boss to, it would appear, write about Thai cuisine. However the boss has an ulterior motive, to separate the man from his daughter and if possible break up the relationship. The third, an older man, goes on his own will. He is fed up with both his wife and his life in Graz, Austria so he leaves them behind to seek a new life in Thailand.At the center of this is Jade, young Thai prostitute who must support herself, her daughter and the girl's father, who has no job or ambition. With the help of her friend, she makes contact with several foreign men who visit the country. Thus she meets the three men. However her relationship with each of them is different. In the meantime, she looks for the one man who can support her and take her out of this kind of life.The film highlights how differently people deal with being in another culture. One can't understand why things are so different and constantly looks for that which is familiar. Another takes delight in the new tastes and pleasures to be found. Another has little interest in his surroundings; his only goal is to find a woman to satisfy his desires.The film is also a visual delight, at one point shifting from one country to another, showing the building style, daily life and cultural activities of each. Well worth watching.

text: Movie: In a Small World (2012) 1h 46m| Official Rating: 6.9/10 | Rating: 6.9/10 | Fascinating indie film produced in Thailand, India, Japan, and Austria. Featuring several international visitors and a young Thai single mother as protagonists, the main action of the story occurs in Pattaya, Thailand's most famous (or infamous) red light resort city. The film humanizes the characters and their respective backgrounds/cultures without overtly moralizing on the choices that they make, a refreshing change from many mainstream American films.Despite most likely being filmed on a small budget, the picture also manages to be visually sumptuous. Its interplay of spiritual imagery (mainly Hindu and Buddhist) with the decadence and squalor of mundane settings is also fascinating, reminiscent of Ron Fricke's 'Samsara' and similar works.

text: Movie: Duk dum dui (2003) 1h 42m| Official Rating: 3.8/10 | Rating: 4/10 | 'What if a mystery safari promised thrills and terror but delivered a slapstick detour where scares and sense both get lost?'Duk Dum Dui, also circulated as The Safari, follows four Thai men sent to an African backcountry to probe a string of killings, only to collide with spirits, shamans, and cannibal rumors after their transport breaks down. The premise has pulp allure and clear adventure horror DNA, but the film leans hard into sketch comedy rhythms that undercut any sustained dread. Director Suthep Po ngam stages the material as a broad ensemble romp, a choice consistent with his comedic roots but at odds with the story's supernatural stakes.Structurally, the movie plays like a string of gags stitched to a monster of the week outline: spooky caves, cursed artifacts, and frantic chases arrive in quick, disconnected bursts. The result is tonal whiplash humor interrupts tension just as it begins to build. Occasional location atmosphere and practical make up achieve modest creepiness, yet the editing seldom lets moments breathe, and the stakes feel weightless. Synopsis materials across releases promise a survival mystery with folkloric menace; on screen, we get punchlines where character development should be, and set pieces that reset instead of escalate.As a cultural curio, Duk Dum Dui is interesting: a Thai commercial comedy grafted onto an adventure horror chassis, complete with alternate English market titling. But as a sustained film, it struggles supporting players are archetypal, world building is thin, and suspense dissolves into noisy chaos. Viewers seeking camp value may grin; viewers seeking a coherent thriller will likely drift.    Conceptually playful and occasionally atmospheric, but scattered tone and stop start storytelling keep it from landing either the laughs or the scares.

text: Movie: Hor Taew Tak 6 (2018) 1h 43m| Official Rating: 3.4/10 | Rating: 2/10 | What happens when a once colorful comedy horror series runs out of fresh scares and relies on recycled laughs? Hor Taew Tak 6 shows the fatigue of a formula stretched far too thin.This sixth entry returns with the familiar flamboyant transgender caretakers who stumble into yet another ghostly encounter. The film promises outrageous comedy, eccentric spirits, and slapstick chaos, but instead delivers a patchwork of skits strung together by a fragile storyline. The haunted setting, once a playground for campy parody, now feels secondary to exaggerated routines and overextended jokes.Analytically, the film's strengths are minimal. The ensemble cast retains its trademark energy, and there are brief flashes of creativity in visual design, with brighter effects and a few set pieces that attempt to escalate the spectacle. However, these moments are fleeting. The narrative is skeletal, functioning as a loose excuse for comedic sketches rather than a coherent plot. Attempts at horror are undermined by shrill humor, while emotional beats are quickly brushed aside.The overreliance on caricatures and recycled gags further weakens the experience. Instead of evolving, the series circles back on itself, offering familiarity at the expense of innovation. For longtime fans, it may serve as nostalgic camp, but for most viewers, it is a shallow and exhausting watch.    A tired sequel that mistakes noise for comedy and spectacle for storytelling, leaving the franchise haunted by its own repetition.

text: Movie: Ma mha 4 khaa khrap (2007) 1h 30m| Official Rating: 6.1/10 | Rating: 7/10 | What if a pack of abandoned dogs could teach us more about loyalty, hope, and survival than many humans do?Ma Mha 4 Khaa Khrap (2007) (also known as Mid Road Gang) follows Makham, a Thai Ridgeback dog who once had a home, and his companions, strays cast aside by society, on a journey to find Dogtopia, a promised land where all dogs are safe, fed, and loved. Abandoned, pursued by dog catchers, and blocked by human cruelty, they must cross a dangerous highway and face trials that test their courage, friendship, and instincts.From a detailed and analytical angle, the film stands out in its ambitious blend of animal point of view storytelling and real world stakes. The use of real dogs (with voiceovers) rather than animation adds weight. Makham's expressions, body language, and interactions with his pack are surprisingly expressive and rooted in reality. Cinematography balances gritty urban alleys and slum torn neighborhoods against moments of tenderness, such as stray dogs sharing food or seeking comfort in one another. The pacing allows danger to ebb and flow: pursuits, hunger, and threat build up to the highway crossing arguably the film's emotional centerpiece.Yet the film is not without weaknesses. Some plot points particularly the motivations of the human antagonists feel thin or underdeveloped. The vision of Dogtopia sometimes leans into idealism that clashes with the gritty realism elsewhere. Also, humour and drama alternate in a way that occasionally breaks immersion; tonal shifts from comic relief among the dogs to dire danger can feel abrupt. . A heartfelt, visually engaging family film that utilizes its animal heroes to explore resilience and hope, imperfect yet moving enough to leave a lasting impression.

text: Movie: Mon Love Sib Meun (2015) 1h 37m| Official Rating: 5.4/10 | Rating: 4/10 | 'He must earn a fortune, but can he find love along the way or is the price higher than he thought?'Mon Love Sib Meun is a romantic comedy set in rural Thailand that revisits the classic '70s rom com trope of the poor but earnest country boy trying to win over a wealthy girl. The story follows Klao (New), a peasant farmer deeply in love with Thong Kwao, a beautiful young woman from a well off family. To win Thong Kwao's hand, Klao must raise a lavish dowry a task that sends him to Bangkok, confronting city life, class divides, and his own limitations.One of the film's strengths is its setting and contrast. The rural landscape offers charm, simplicity, and a sense of community, which Klao must leave behind. Bangkok represents opportunity but also alienation the bustle, the cost of living, and cultural pressures that test Klao's resolve and ideals. The performances are likable: Klao's roles sincerely portray both innocence and determination, while Thong Kwao's character is warm, though her internal conflict (between love and family expectation) could be better explored. Emotional stakes are helped by earnest interactions and supporting characters who reflect both sympathy and skepticism.However, Mon Love Sib Meun suffers from predictability and pacing issues. The plot beats dowry hardship, misunderstandings, opportunities missed and gained are familiar. Moments of comedy and romance work, but the film rarely surprises or pushes beyond its formula. Some city segments feel rushed, and Klao's transformation lacks enough internal struggle to make his journey deeply compelling. Furthermore, the film's production values are solid, but there are scenes where dialogue feels overly expository, telling rather than showing.Overall, Mon Love Sib Meun is an enjoyable romance, especially for those who appreciate nostalgic rural city contrasts and romantic perseverance but it doesn't quite reach beyond its genre foundations.    Sweet and earnest, but too predictable and lightly drawn for lasting impact.

text: Movie: Panya Raenu 2 (2012) 1h 41m| Official Rating: 5.3/10 | Rating: 5/10 | What happens when a charming childhood story tries to stretch into adolescence but stumbles over repetition? Panya Raenu 2 aims to rekindle the magic of the first film, but much of its freshness is lost in the attempt.Directed by Bin Bunluerit, the sequel continues the tale of Panya, the mischievous boy, and Raenu, the spirited girl from across the border. As they navigate the complexities of older childhood and its shifting dynamics, their relationship becomes more complicated friendship is tested by jealousy, competition, and the intrusion of adults. The film expands its scope with new situations, aiming to deepen the characters' emotional journeys while keeping the humor of village life intact.Analytically, the movie succeeds in retaining cultural detail. Once again, the Isaan setting is vividly brought to life through dialect, music, and community rituals, grounding the story in authenticity. The child actors remain engaging, and there are touching moments that reflect the universal awkwardness of growing up.However, the film's weaknesses are more apparent than in the original. Much of the humor feels recycled, relying on slapstick and caricatures rather than fresh wit. The pacing drags, with scenes that linger too long. Emotional beats while present lack the same innocence and poignancy of the first film, making the drama feel more forced than heartfelt.    Panya Raenu 2 maintains cultural charm and occasional warmth, but leans too heavily on repetition, resulting in a less inspired continuation of the original's heartfelt magic.

text: Movie: Mid Road Gang 2 (2012) 1h 47m| Official Rating: 4.4/10 | Rating: 4/10 | When the innocent are threatened, sometimes the smallest heroes carry the most significant weight.Mid Road Gang 2 (Ma Mha 2 / 2012) continues the journey of Jer, the intelligent dog, who has been adopted into a loving family. All seems well until disaster strikes: the baby of his family is kidnapped, setting Jer on a quest to rescue the child and restore safety. The plot quickly becomes a race against time, with human villains, dogged loyalty, and desperate hope interweaving to create moments of tension and warmth.From a detailed and analytical standpoint, the film's strength lies in Jer's perspective portrayed with empathy and surprisingly credible urgency. The voiceovers, which match canine instincts with human stakes, offer both comedic relief and emotional pull. Cinematography often frames Jer's journey from a low angle, comparable to a dog's height, reinforcing his vulnerability and resourcefulness. The pacing builds nicely in the setup introducing the joyful home life before the kidnapping but falters in the middle, where scenes meant to stretch the tension sometimes drift without enough payoff. Supporting characters are well intentioned but rarely fully explored, which weakens some of the emotional stakes. The relatively simple structure of good versus evil keeps the film accessible for families, although the villainy feels underdeveloped, lacking a clear motive beyond being a threat. Visually, there are moments of charm in everyday life Jer exploring, comforting the baby balanced with sequences of chase, confusion, and danger.Overall, Mid Road Gang 2 is a sequel that delivers heart more than innovation. It doesn't reinvent its genre, but for viewers looking for a family movie with a four legged hero, it offers some satisfying moments, albeit with an uneven rhythm. . A heartfelt family film with a promising premise and loyal themes, though its execution struggles under predictable beats and underdeveloped character arcs.

text: Movie: One Night Husband (2003) 1h 36m| Official Rating: 6.1/10 | Rating: 6.1/10 | Anyway the two movies presented were a hit and a miss, and One Night Husband turned out to be a bad miss. If many in the audience had their eyes closed at one point or another, or become fidgety in their seats, my opinion is that whatever is transpiring on screen, doesn't have enough of what it takes to hold an audience's attention. While the production value is good, it adopted the look and feel of an art movie about contemplation, isolation, and whatever that you would reckon the need for long silent moments.It begins with enough mystery to sustain anyone's attention   a newly wed couple consummating their marriage, except that after doing the deed, the groom walks out of the home after receiving an anonymous phone call. This leaves the bride Sipang (Nicole Theriault, a Thai pop star) perplexed, and she becomes anxious in finding out where her husband disappeared to after days of absence.However the movie seemed to junk this plot aside for a preference to dwell into her seeking of help from her brother in law Chat (Pongpat Wachirabunjong) and his wife Bussaba (Siriyakorn Pukkavesh), and from hereon, the focus is on the friendship developed between the two women, and probably if it fell into directors who are seduced by the GLBT themes of late, the relationship will dwell deeper than the platonic level.While the loose ends do get tied, the journey is trying. Unless you're a serious art movie lover, you might find many scenes in the movie pretty contrived and probably trying too hard. Essentially, the entire story is short film material, bloated only to include beautifully filmed moments of the mundane.

text: Movie: Polamuang Juling (2008) 3h 42m| Official Rating: 8.6/10 | Rating: 8.6/10 | Journalist Ing K, photographer Manit Sriwanichpoom, and opposition senator Kraisak Choohavan journeyed the length of Thailand to investigate a brutal attack on two teachers at a charity preschool, and its context in the rich and tortured culture of the country's southern provinces. Mostly they look and listen, leaving interpretation to their interview subjects and the viewer. The tragedy and the wisdom of their film   beyond documenting the crime scene, a dying victim's hospital bed and her home village in the north   is our observation that all of the interview subjects are good people. Leaving us to wonder, who committed this crime and who allowed it to occur?

text: Movie: Tongpan (1977) 1h| Official Rating: 7.5/10 | Rating: 7.5/10 | Living in Thailand a few years I've come to see that most movies are incredibly sallow and lucking of any political interest as discussion is not a cultural value in the country. This movie, was for that, a great surprise for me. As I studied the political movement of the three freedom years, from 1973 to 1976, I realised that this movie is one of the best representations of the student movement and it's feelings. Educated middle class people trying to get the farmers involved in their rights life. The story itself is a very common story between farmers, and its well told. But is probably the chance to see the way of living of the farmers what makes the movie so nice, as a documentary of the people in the northeast region, Isaan.I recommend this movie for the ones interested in knowing how farmers live in Isaan, and the way some people tried to help them in that moment in the history of Thailand, that sadly ended with a famous massacre in the 6th of October of 1976.

metadata.synopsis: Tongpan is a 1977 Thai 16 mm black and white docudrama that re creates a seminar that took place in Northeast Thailand in 1975 to discuss the proposed Pa Mong Dam on the Mekong. Interwoven are sequences depicting a poor farmer, Tongpan, who had lost his land to another dam some years before, and his struggles to make ends meet. Because of the film's socialist message and suspected communist sympathies of the filmmakers, it was banned by the Thai government. The 63 minute film was released on VCD in Thailand in 2006.

text: Movie: Citizen II (1984) 1h 55m| Official Rating: 7.7/10 | Rating: 7.7/10 | Even though this isn't in my Top 10 Thai films of all time (I would put it in my Top 30). But honestly, it's not about the ranking it's about how special this film really is. Citizen 2 is unlike any other Thai film I've seen so far.What makes it stand out is how it uses Bangkok as its canvas. This isn't just a movie that 'takes place' in Bangkok this is a movie where the city itself becomes the stage. We see everything: the slums, the cityscape, the night club, the prison, the police station, the factories, the little poor neighborhood shops, even abandoned buildings where the hero crashes after getting out of jail. It feels almost 'open world,' like the characters are wandering freely through a living, breathing city. Every single scene feels like a set piece.The script itself is very straightforward: a man just released from prison tries to find his child. Along the way, he gets tangled up with police, thieves, and countless struggles. There aren't a lot of twists or surprises, but that's not the point. The point is how the film captures its time, place, and atmosphere better than anything else. Even films I might rank 'higher' don't capture Bangkok with this much honesty and beauty. For me this is simply the greatest cinematic use of Bangkok ever put on screen.It's gorgeously shot. It's immersive. It's cinema in the purest sense. If you want to experience what I'd call a 'hangout movie' to walk with a man freshly out of prison, wandering Bangkok as he searches for his child, looking at the city, its people, its shadows this film is a treasure. There's not always a lot 'happening,' but that's exactly what makes it so powerful.I'm writing this because I don't see anyone else reviewing this film here, and I think it's too special to be forgotten or lost in the shuffle.It doesn't need to be a 'Top 10' masterpiece to matter. It's special in its own way, and if you can find a chance to watch it, I highly recommend it.

text: Movie: Mother (2012) 1h 4m| Official Rating: 7.4/10 | Rating: 7.4/10 | (Note: No user reviews yet) Synopsis: Mother is a hybrid of fiction and documentary. It is a portrait of the complicated, fragile, painful and realistic relationship between my mother and me. In the past, she once tried to commit suicide. Though the action was failed, she was disabled. Since the incident, my family has changed forever, and the film is my attempt to explore and understand her, myself and my family. To put it in a wider context, I analogically portrayed how Thai middle class family effect ed by Asian financial crisis in 1997(Tom Yam Kung Crisis) and explored the representation of family in Thai culture through the process of making this film. Thai media always shows Thai family with one dimension : the good and the bad. To understand the society, we need to go to the smallest institution of it : family. What is Thai family? What is its complexities? What are the ways each member deal with the world outside and inside? How does the family go through the radical change both from Thai society and the destiny and they dances around the reality and the fantasy of the familial representation.

text: Movie: Yes or No 2.5 (2015) 1h 42m| Official Rating: 5.2/10 | Rating: 3/10 | 'Returning to old seats with new questions: is love enough to undo the past?'Yes or No 2.5 picks up threads from the earlier films in the franchise, returning to lesbian romance with familiar faces Wine (Supanart Jittaleela) and Pii (Sunanta Yoonniyom), and introducing new characters particularly Fah (Chansakorn Kittiwattanakorn) whose arrival next door complicates emotions, relationships, and long suppressed feelings.One of the strengths of the film lies in its attempts to balance comfort with distance. Wine's lingering attachment to her university crush, Pii's supportive yet tensioned friendship, and Fah's fresh energy are woven to reflect both warmth and the awkwardness of growing relationships. Visually, the movie delivers polished cinematography soft lighting, neat framing of domestic interiors, and scenic Thai cityscapes that enhances its romantic mood. The musical interludes are sparse but fit the emotional rhythms.However, Yes or No 2.5 falls short in pacing and narrative weight. Scenes meant to deepen characters often linger without adding insight; others rush through emotionally critical moments, making them feel hollow or predictable. New relationships, especially Fah's, are introduced with promise but seldom followed through with sufficient tension or evolution. The comedy is mild, more gently amusing than laugh out loud, which is fine for the genre but when juxtaposed with more dramatic beats, the tonal shifts feel uneven.Overall, while it offers charming moments and value for fans of the series, the film's emotional impact is modest rather than profound.    Comforting return to familiar hearts, but too many threads under explored and too few risks taken.

text: Movie: Sub khu ku lok (2012) 1h 45m| Official Rating: 5.4/10 | Rating: 5/10 | What happens when a stoner comedy collides with a superhero parody? Sub Khu Ku Lok tries to answer with wild antics, eccentric characters, and absurdist humor, but its uneven execution leaves more smoke than fire.The film follows two underachieving friends, Sia and Yong, whose carefree lives revolve around smoking and small mischiefs. Their world turns upside down when they are unexpectedly tasked with saving the planet from an alien invasion. From that point, the narrative spirals into a mix of slapstick comedy, sci fi parody, and social satire, positioning unlikely heroes at the center of an over the top battle.Analytically, the film's strengths lie in its energy and willingness to push boundaries. It openly mocks genre conventions, from action movie tropes to sci fi clichés, and occasionally lands sharp commentary on Thai pop culture and the everyday struggles of the working class. The chemistry between the lead actors fuels much of the entertainment, and specific gags, though exaggerated, capture the playful irreverence of Thai comedy traditions.However, the flaws are equally apparent. The humor often overextends, relying on repetitive slapstick and crude setups that undercut narrative pacing. The sci fi elements, while ambitious, are thinly developed, leaving the 'save the world' premise feeling like a backdrop rather than a compelling driver of the story. Tonal shifts between parody and genuine drama feel abrupt, preventing deeper resonance. .Summary: Sub Khu Ku Lok is a chaotic blend of stoner comedy and superhero parody. It entertains in bursts but suffers from repetitive humor and shallow storytelling, making it more of a quirky curiosity than a memorable cinematic adventure.

text: Movie: Sassy Player (2009) 1h 42m| Official Rating: 4.7/10 | Rating: 3/10 | 'What if a soccer team full of stereotypes was supposed to bring laughter but instead leaves you longing for more sincerity than just punchlines?'Sassy Player (2009), also known as Taew Te Teen Raberd, is a Thai comedic romp that brings together sports, school drama, and LGBTQ+ visibility under one wildly ambitious premise. The story follows an all girls Catholic high school which starts admitting boys so it can field a soccer team only for some of those boys to be effeminate or identifying as kathoey.While the film deserves credit for attempting to include queer characters in a mainstream teen comedy, the execution often slides into caricature rather than thoughtful portrayal. Characters are numerous so many that distinguishing them becomes a challenge and much of the humor hinges on stereotypes: ostentatious makeup, exaggerated mannerisms, and broad comedy about gender expression. The story tries to balance subplots about straight acting versus effeminate youth, teacher romance, school politics, and even rival teams, but these threads compete rather than complement, leading to tonal inconsistency.Visually, the film looks lively when in its sports sequences: soccer matches, cheering crowds, colorful costuming. But off the field, lighting and pacing falter jokes are spaced unevenly and emotional moments are rushed, hardly giving weight to potential character growth.The film does offer moments of easy charm particularly from Sudarat Butrprom's performance and there's an openness in depicting queer teens and trans figures rarely seen in Thai comedies of that era. Yet the movie fails to fully embody the empathy or depth to match its comedic ambitions.    An energetic mix of game and camp with glimpses of heart, but crowded plot, shallow character development, and reliance on stereotypes make it more frustrating than fulfilling.

text: Movie: Kao... Kao (2006) 1h 58m| Official Rating: 6.3/10 | Rating: 5/10 | 'A rock band lost in time finds out fame's echo is louder in regret than in applause.'The Possible (Thai title Kao... Kao) is a musical comedy fantasy, starring Joey Boy as Toi, lead singer of a 1970s rock band called The Possible. The unique hook: the band gets transported from 1969 into 2006 via a magical pink microphone, and must navigate culture shock, forgotten glory, and the temptation of ego in a world that's far from what they remember.The film's greatest strength lies in its loving homage to Thailand's music history. The Possible's struggle to reconnect with past bandmates (some changed, some vanished, one deceased) is emotionally resonant. Scenes where they try to pay with old currency, or learn that their style no longer thrills modern audiences, create a bittersweet reflection: change is inevitable, and nostalgia, while powerful, may also isolate. The cast's charm helps sell this: Toi's arrogance softens gradually; the introduction of Nu Malee, the orphan daughter of a deceased member, provides warmth and moral grounding.On the flip side, the film sometimes plays safe. The comedic bits culture clash, outdated fashion, and 'old rockers in modern shoes' are amusing but predictable. The plot arc follows a standard 'time travel learns humility' template. Musically, while the covers are fun, the film doesn't challenge its songs beyond nostalgia; it seldom pushes for novelty. Some subplots (e.g. Romantic tension, rival band politics) feel underdeveloped.WikipediaIn sum, The Possible succeeds as a warm tribute to Thai rock, with heart and humor, even if it doesn't break new ground.    Endearing, musical, nostalgic; enjoyable for fans of the genre, but light on surprises.

text: Movie: Sudkate Salateped (2010) 1h 46m| Official Rating: 5.8/10 | Rating: 5/10 | What happens when a small town dreamer stumbles into the chaotic world of showbiz? Sudkate Salateped sets out to lampoon the entertainment industry through slapstick and satire, but its uneven balance of comedy and commentary keeps it from reaching its full potential.The story follows Sudkate, an awkward young man with oversized ambitions of becoming a superstar. As he navigates auditions, eccentric mentors, and outlandish rivals, the film uses his journey as a vehicle to parody Thailand's pop culture machine. Along the way, he learns about the value of friendship, perseverance, and the cost of pursuing fame.Analytically, the film shows strength in its cultural specificity. By spoofing talent shows, celebrity obsessions, and the absurdity of fame, it reflects the anxieties of a generation fixated on stardom. Specific comedic sequences succeed in poking fun at shallow industry practices, and the cast's energetic performances bring a sense of liveliness to the narrative. Musical numbers and colorful set pieces add visual flair, capturing the glitzy chaos of pop culture.Yet the weaknesses are apparent. Much of the humor relies on repetition and exaggerated gags, which quickly lose their impact. Character arcs, including Sudkate's transformation, are sketched broadly rather than with emotional depth, leaving the satire feeling shallow. Tonal shifts between parody and heartfelt drama feel abrupt, making it challenging to engage with the story beyond surface level comedy. .Summary: Sudkate Salateped delivers an energetic satire of Thailand's entertainment industry, but its reliance on overplayed gags and uneven tone leaves it more an amusing distraction than a sharp critique.

text: Movie: Ghost Variety (2005) 1h 44m| Official Rating: 5.1/10 | Rating: 5/10 | What happens when a variety show collides with a haunted theater? Ghost Variety (Waraitee Phee Chaluy) delivers the answer in a mix of slapstick, parody, and supernatural hijinks that reflect both the strengths and limitations of Thai ensemble comedy.Directed by Adirek 'Uncle' Wattaleela, the film brings together a collection of Thai comedians and pop culture personalities in a story that blurs the line between performance and paranormal mischief. A struggling theater troupe sets out to revive their variety show, only to find themselves stalked and occasionally upstaged by mischievous ghosts. The film plays less like a traditional horror comedy and more like a stage revue transplanted onto cinema, complete with sketch like segments, parody acts, and musical numbers.Analytically, the film's strength lies in its energy and willingness to poke fun at itself. The cast adopts exaggerated roles, and the variety show format enables a diverse range of comedy styles, from slapstick to wordplay. The inclusion of ghosts creates amusing contrasts, parodying both horror clichés and the theatrics of live entertainment.However, weaknesses are hard to miss. The narrative is thin, serving mainly as a loose excuse to string together comedic skits. Pacing can feel erratic, with certain jokes overstaying their welcome while others barely land. The humor, rooted heavily in Thai pop culture references of the mid 2000s, may not translate well internationally, limiting broader appeal.    Ghost Variety is spirited and occasionally inventive, but its sketch like structure and uneven humor keep it from becoming more than a light, forgettable comedy horror experiment.

text: Movie: Ghost Variety (2005) 1h 44m| Official Rating: 5.1/10 | Rating: 5.1/10 | Directed veteran Thai director Adirek 'Uncle' Watleela, Ghost Variety is a crazy horror comedy, well actually, more comedy than filled with horrific moments. It starts off quite aptly, in a remote village where a horror movie is being screened, and introduces the audience to a few of the usual ghosts and goblins, until we realize it's all a figment of the imagination.And there's plenty from where that came from, with scenes cutting in and out from screen reality and fantasy. Basically, it's about the story of a down and out filmmaker called Tom, played by familiar face Petchtai Wongkamiao, who starred in Tony Jaa vehicles Ong Bak and Tom Yum Goong for comedic effect, and recently seen in Chai Lai Angels. Here, his character Tom is developing a script, but keeps getting turned away as he's told only horror movies make money.It's a subtle jab at the film industry in general, with the constant reminder that what matters is something that can churn out bread and butter, and not for quality's sake. Surprisingly, this movie had a lot of Thai filmmakers and industry players making cameo appearances in spoofs of themselves, and I suppose to fans of Thai cinema, it'll be a hoot just to identify all of them (kinda lost with me and the audience during my screening).So Tom had no choice but to bury his artistic tendency and with the need for funds for his next film, he had to succumb and stoop to making a variety show for television, based on what else, ghosts. Bringing together a motley crew of relative cowards   in his two lead presenters Tik The Star (of his short films), played by Charnnarong Khanteethao, an upcoming singing supersensation The SuperNext (Boriboon Janruang), and a beautiful production assistant Paew (Pitchanart Sakakorn, who starred in two other movies I watched earlier this year, in one of the segments in the awfully bad movie Black Night, and Promise Me Not during this year's SIFF), they scour Thailand to seek out the truths behind some urban legends.Basically there are a few cheap scares in what seemed to be only 2 extended scenes   a haunted house sequence which brings more laughter than scares, and a haunted village sequence which seemed more Sci Fi than horror. Other than that, the movie turned out to be quite directionless as it flits from scene to scene, and towards the end, it leaves the audience quite bewildered because there are just too many schizophrenic endings, which might just leave one frustrated if you're looking for a clean cut storyline and resolution.However, the strength in this movie is on the comedy, and in merging horror into it, it plays along with the general consensus that yes, horror films do sell.
